model: Mood is subjective (their words); affect is objective (what you observe).
why: E.g. mood "low", affect flat.

q: What does "insight" mean in the MSE?
model: Whether they recognise they are unwell (and need treatment).
why: Affects adherence and risk.

q: AF with a pansystolic murmur and basal crackles suggests what?
hint: A leaky valve plus a failing pump.
why: Link signs into one diagnosis.

q: How long do SSRIs take to start working?
why: Warn patients so they don't stop early.

q: When should a patient under 25 starting an SSRI be reviewed?
why: Higher risk of suicidal thoughts early on.

q: Which GMC document sets the standards for doctors?
why: Students follow "Achieving good medical practice".

q: What is patient-centred care?
model: Treating the patient as a partner: their ideas, concerns, expectations and values shape decisions.
hint: The patient is at the centre.
why: It respects autonomy, including the right to refuse.

q: What is the difference between compassion and empathy?
model: Empathy is understanding and showing you understand their feelings; compassion is noticing distress and acting kindly.
hint: One is insight into their state, one is doing something kind.
why: Both build trust.

q: How should a student always introduce themselves?
why: Never misrepresent your role.

q: What should you do if you'll be late for a placement?
why: Reliability is part of professionalism.

q: When can confidential information be disclosed without consent?
acc: law / public interest / safeguard / serious harm
model: When required by law, in the public interest (serious harm) or for safeguarding.
why: Otherwise share on a need-to-know basis.

q: Which Act lists protected characteristics?
why: E.g. age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation.

q: What is the UK system for reporting patient safety incidents in hospitals?
why: Also Freedom to Speak Up Guardians.

q: Can a patient refuse to be seen by a student?
why: Always ask consent.

q: Who should you register with to look after your own health?
why: Don't self-treat; seek support early.

q: How long after diarrhoea and vomiting should you stay off work?
why: Norovirus spreads easily to patients.

q: What does the GMC say about prescribing for yourself or family?
why: Objectivity is compromised.

q: What should you say if asked something beyond your knowledge?
acc: don't know / find out / do not know
model: "I don't know, but I'll find out."
why: Work within your competence.

q: Give a strategy to reduce unconscious bias.
acc: reflect / structur / training / diverse / ask / check
model: Reflect on assumptions, use structured assessments, seek diverse views, training.
why: Bias leads to unequal care (e.g. undertreated pain).

q: What is a "never event"?
model: A serious, preventable incident that should never happen with safeguards in place (e.g. wrong-site surgery).
why: E.g. the WHO surgical checklist prevents them.

q: What do the letters PDSA stand for in quality improvement?
why: Small rapid test-of-change cycles.

q: What is the duty of candour?
model: Being open and honest with patients when something goes wrong, including an apology.
hint: Owning up when things go wrong.
why: Professional and statutory duty.

q: How should you respond to negative feedback?
model: Listen without defending, thank them, reflect and act on it.
why: Feedback drives improvement.

q: Name a member of the MDT other than doctors and nurses.
acc: pharmacist / physio / ot / occupational / dietitian / social worker / speech
model: Pharmacist, physiotherapist, OT, dietitian, social worker.
why: Know team roles.

q: What must every entry in the notes include?
model: Date, time, name, role and signature.
why: Notes must be legible, accurate and contemporaneous.

q: How do you check understanding after explaining something?
model: Teach-back: ask them to explain it in their own words.
why: Better than "do you understand?"

q: Name a source for a medication history besides the patient.
acc: gp / pharmacy / repeat / carer / summary care
model: GP record, pharmacy, repeat slip, carers.
why: Reconcile within 24 hours.

q: Who should interpret in a consultation?
why: Family members may filter information and breach confidentiality.

q: Which examinations need a chaperone offered?
why: Record their name or that one was declined.

q: What should a differential diagnosis include besides the most likely cause?
acc: can't miss / serious / dangerous / cannot miss / red flag
why: Don't miss dangerous conditions.

q: What should each investigation do?
acc: question / confirm / exclude / change management / guide
model: Answer a specific question (confirm, exclude, assess severity or guide treatment).
why: Consider pre-test probability, risk and cost.

q: What is anchoring bias?
model: Sticking to an initial diagnosis despite new information.
why: Watch for cognitive biases.

q: How many moments of hand hygiene are there (WHO)?
why: Before patient, before aseptic task, after body fluid, after patient, after surroundings.

q: Why should needles never be resheathed?
why: Dispose at point of use.

q: What is closed-loop communication?
model: The receiver repeats back the message to confirm it.
why: Reduces errors in teams.

q: What should you do when a patient's question is beyond your role?
acc: seek help / senior / team / ask / find out
model: Seek help from the team and get back to them.
why: Respond honestly within your knowledge.

q: Why does right heart failure cause ankle oedema?
model: Raised venous (hydrostatic) pressure pushes fluid out (Starling forces).
why: Apply basic science to clinical signs.

q: What process underlies most myocardial infarctions?
why: Explain mechanisms of common disease.

q: Who should you check a management plan with as a student?
why: Work within your competence.

q: What does a positive Trendelenburg test indicate?
model: Weak hip abductors on the standing side.
hint: Muscles that keep the pelvis level.
why: The pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side.

q: Which hip movement is lost first in osteoarthritis?
why: Test at 90° hip flexion.

q: What does Thomas's test detect?
why: Flex the opposite hip: the tested leg lifts off the couch.

q: How is true leg length measured?
model: From the ASIS to the medial malleolus.
why: Apparent length is from the umbilicus.

q: What is an antalgic gait?
model: A short stance phase on the painful side.
hint: Spending less time on one leg.
why: Minimises time loading the painful limb.

q: What should you check for before knee stress tests?
why: A large effusion limits testing.

q: In which position is a DRE performed?
why: Comfortable and gives good access.

q: What does a normal prostate feel like?
model: Smooth, rubbery, with a palpable median sulcus.
hint: Like the tip of your nose.
why: A hard, craggy prostate with loss of the sulcus suggests cancer.

q: Why perform a DRE in suspected cauda equina?
model: To check anal tone and perianal sensation.
why: Reduced tone suggests cauda equina syndrome.

q: Which joint does gout classically affect first?
acc: big toe / first mtp / 1st mtp / mtp
why: Called podagra.

q: Which diuretics increase the risk of gout?
hint: Two common classes for BP and oedema.
why: They reduce urate excretion.

q: Which drug lowers urate long-term in gout?
why: Not usually started during an acute attack in the first instance.

q: Why does a goitre move up on swallowing?
model: It's attached to the larynx and trachea by the pretracheal fascia.
why: A thyroglossal cyst rises with tongue protrusion.

q: What does a thyroglossal cyst do when the tongue is stuck out?
why: It's attached to the foramen caecum via the thyroglossal duct remnant.

q: Which eye signs are specific to Graves' disease?
why: Lid lag and retraction occur in any hyperthyroidism.

q: What reflex change occurs in hypothyroidism?
why: Hyperthyroidism gives brisk reflexes.

q: How should you position yourself when explaining to an older patient with hearing loss?
why: Allows lip reading.

q: What respiratory rate is a NICE red flag for sepsis?
why: Other red flags: SBP ≤90, HR ≥130, new confusion.

q: What heart rate is a NICE red flag for sepsis?
why: Along with SBP ≤90 and RR ≥25.

q: What NEWS2 score with suspected infection should prompt you to think sepsis?
why: Prompt urgent assessment.

q: What are the "take 3" of the Sepsis Six?
hint: Bottles, a blood gas value and a measurement.
why: "Give 3" = oxygen, antibiotics, fluids.

q: What lactate level suggests septic shock?
why: Escalate to critical care.

q: Which test reproduces radicular arm pain with neck extension, rotation and axial load?
why: Suggests cervical radiculopathy.

q: What sign of cervical myelopathy is found in the hand?
why: Flicking the middle finger nail causes thumb flexion: an UMN sign.

q: What ECG shows sawtooth waves?
why: Often 2:1 block with a rate of 150.

q: What ECG features suggest hyperkalaemia?
model: Tall tented T waves, flat P waves, broad QRS.
why: Emergency: calcium gluconate to protect the heart.

q: What ECG shows complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes?
why: Needs pacing.

q: Which second-degree heart block has progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat?
acc: mobitz i / mobitz 1 / wenckebach / mobitz type 1 / type 1
why: Mobitz II has sudden dropped beats and higher risk.

q: What is the difference between standard and surgical ANTT?
model: Surgical ANTT uses a critical aseptic field and sterile gloves for complex procedures.
hint: Think about the gloves and field.
why: Standard ANTT uses a general aseptic field and non-sterile gloves.

q: How many blood culture sets are taken in suspected endocarditis?
model: Three sets from different sites at different times.
why: Bacteraemia is continuous; multiple sets increase yield.

q: Which blood culture bottle is filled first with a butterfly?
why: Air in the tubing goes into the aerobic bottle, not the anaerobic one.

q: How much blood goes in each adult blood culture bottle?
why: Underfilling reduces sensitivity.

q: What usually contaminates blood cultures?
why: Leads to unnecessary antibiotics: strict ANTT.

q: Should you challenge a patient's delusions?
why: Stay calm and non-confrontational.

q: A patient pausing and looking around as if listening may be doing what?
why: Ask gently about voices.

q: What is a delusion?
model: A fixed, false belief held despite evidence and out of keeping with culture.
why: E.g. persecutory, grandiose.

q: Name a negative symptom of schizophrenia.
acc: apathy / alogia / anhedonia / withdraw / blunt / flat / avolition
model: Apathy, alogia, anhedonia, social withdrawal, blunted affect.
why: Positive symptoms are hallucinations and delusions.

q: Name a type of thought interference.
hint: Thoughts put in or taken out.
why: First-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.

q: Should you promise to keep a safeguarding disclosure secret?
hint: You may need to share it.
why: Listen, explain you may need to share it to keep them safe.

q: Does asking directly about suicide increase the risk?
why: It shows you take them seriously.

q: In the MSE, is the patient's own description of their mood objective or subjective?
why: Record your observations (affect, appearance, speech) separately as objective findings.

q: What size laryngeal mask is used for a 70–100 kg adult?
why: Size 4 for 50–70 kg, size 3 for 30–50 kg.

q: Which supraglottic airway has no inflatable cuff?
why: It has a gel cuff that seals itself.

q: Why is a supraglottic airway unsuitable with a full stomach?
why: An endotracheal tube with a cuff does.

q: What is the gold standard for confirming tracheal tube position?
why: "No trace = wrong place".

q: How long should a patient be pre-oxygenated before intubation?
why: Builds an oxygen reservoir in the lungs.

q: How should you inhale through a pMDI?
model: Slowly and deeply, then hold for 10 s.
why: A dry powder inhaler needs a quick, deep breath.

q: Why should patients rinse their mouth after an inhaled steroid?
why: Also reduces hoarseness.

q: What should you check before stepping up asthma treatment?
why: Poor technique is a common cause of poor control.

q: What type of respiratory failure has a high PaCO₂?
why: Type 1 = low O₂ with normal or low CO₂.

q: What does a venous gas not give you reliably?
why: Venous is fine for pH, bicarbonate, lactate and potassium.

q: Which test checks collateral ulnar flow before radial puncture?
why: Ensures the hand is perfused if the radial artery is damaged.

q: How long should pressure be applied after an ABG?
why: Arteries bleed more than veins.

q: What PEF defines life-threatening asthma?
why: 33–50% is acute severe.

q: What does a normal PaCO₂ mean in acute asthma?
why: CO₂ should be low from hyperventilation.

q: What IV drug is given in severe asthma not responding to nebulisers?
model: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes.
why: Relaxes bronchial smooth muscle.

q: What dose of oral prednisolone is given in acute asthma?
why: Continue for at least 5 days.

q: What should you stabilise when testing hip abduction?
model: The pelvis (hand on the opposite ASIS).
why: Otherwise pelvic tilt mimics hip movement.

q: Clubbing with fine bibasal crackles suggests what?
why: Investigate with HRCT and spirometry (restrictive).

q: What spirometry pattern does pulmonary fibrosis cause?
why: Both volumes fall.

q: What should a presentation include after positive findings?
why: Then summary, differential and next steps.

q: What is a triadic consultation?
model: A consultation with three people (e.g. patient, carer and doctor).
why: Speak to the patient first.

q: An acute onset of confusion suggests what rather than dementia?
why: Look for infection, drugs, retention, constipation.

q: Name a challenge in a triadic consultation.
acc: exclude / talk over / conflict / confidential / hidden / bias / safeguard
model: Patient excluded, conflicting accounts, confidentiality, hidden carer stress or safeguarding.
why: Speak separately if needed.

q: Suprapubic tenderness with dipstick nitrites suggests what?
why: Pyelonephritis if loin tenderness and fever.

q: New confusion with fever and suprapubic tenderness in an older person: what is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Also consider pneumonia and drugs.

q: Name a protective factor in suicide risk assessment.
acc: family / faith / pet / children / support / religio / hope
model: Family, children, faith, pets, support networks.
why: Weigh against plans, means and previous attempts.

q: Why is ABCDE ordered the way it is?
model: It deals with the most immediately life-threatening problems first.
hint: Think about which problem is fatal soonest.
why: Airway obstruction kills fastest.

q: Where is the JVP assessed?
model: The internal jugular vein, between the heads of sternocleidomastoid, with the patient at 45°.
why: Height above the sternal angle; over 3 cm is raised.

q: What feature suggests a lump is an epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst?
why: A lipoma is soft, mobile and lobulated.

q: What does a stony hard, fixed lump suggest?
why: Refer urgently.

q: How can you tell an expansile from a transmitted pulsation?
model: With fingers on each side, an expansile mass pushes them apart (aneurysm); a transmitted one lifts them up.
hint: Place one digit on each side.
why: Expansile pulsation suggests an aneurysm.

q: What must every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain have?
why: To exclude ectopic pregnancy.

q: Which contraceptive increases the risk of PID?
model: An intrauterine device (coil), mainly soon after insertion.
why: Also an ectopic if pregnancy occurs.

q: In SOCRATES, what does "E" stand for?
why: What makes it better or worse.

q: Lower abdominal pain, a missed period and shoulder-tip pain suggest what?
hint: A pregnancy in the wrong place.
why: Shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm.

q: Which side is diverticulitis usually felt on?
why: Sigmoid colon is the commonest site.

q: Name a risk factor for STIs.
acc: under 25 / young / multiple / new partner / condom / msm / previous sti / sex work / chemsex
model: Age under 25, new or multiple partners, inconsistent condom use.
why: Offer testing and partner notification.

q: What medication prevents HIV in high-risk people?
why: Offered to MSM and others at high risk.

q: In a rapid A–E in the critically ill, how should the team work?
why: Treat problems as you find them.

q: When should findings of an intimate examination be discussed?
why: Dignity and comfort.

q: Can a patient stop an intimate examination partway through?
why: Consent is ongoing and can be withdrawn.

q: Where should the pad of the finger press during a rectal examination in men?
why: Sweep round the whole rectal wall for masses.

q: How many beats of ankle clonus are abnormal?
why: Sustained clonus is an UMN sign.

q: What does an upgoing plantar response indicate?
model: An upper motor neuron lesion (Babinski sign).
why: Normal in infants under 1.

q: What does a positive Romberg's test indicate?
why: The patient sways when the eyes are closed.

q: Which root supplies sensation to the dorsum of the foot?
why: L4 medial leg, S1 lateral foot.

q: What is a high-stepping gait a sign of?
model: Foot drop (e.g. common peroneal palsy or L5 radiculopathy).
why: The patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes.

q: In Schober's test, by how much should the marked distance increase on full flexion?
hint: A hand's width… roughly half of one.
why: Less suggests restricted lumbar flexion (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis).

q: What does pain down the leg on straight leg raise suggest?
hint: Irritation of the lowest nerves of the lumbar plexus.
why: Positive between 30 and 70°.

q: At which vertebral level are the iliac crests?
why: Used to find the space for lumbar puncture.

q: When listening for mitral stenosis, how should the patient lie?
model: In the left lateral position, using the bell.
why: Brings the apex close to the chest wall.

q: Name a finishing step after a cardiovascular examination.
acc: bp / blood pressure / peripheral pulse / ecg / fundi / urine
model: BP, peripheral pulses, ECG, fundoscopy, urine dip.
why: State them at the end.

q: Name a finishing step after a respiratory examination.
acc: sats / pefr / peak flow / sputum / cxr / chest x
why: Mention them to finish.

q: What does leuconychia suggest?
why: White nails from low protein.

q: Where is V1 placed?
why: V2 at the same level on the left.

q: Where is V4 placed?
why: V5 and V6 at the same level, further out.

q: Which limb lead colour goes on the right arm?
why: "Ride Your Green Bike": red RA, yellow LA, green LL, black RL.

q: What is the standard ECG paper speed?
why: One small square = 0.04 s.

q: What does a negative lead I suggest?
acc: lead reversal / limb lead / arm lead / dextrocardia / swapped
why: Check electrode placement.

q: What ABPI indicates peripheral arterial disease?
why: Below 0.5 is severe; above 1.3 suggests calcified arteries.

q: Which leg pulse is felt deep in a fossa with the knee slightly bent, using the fingertips of both hands?
why: It lies deep against the back of the femur and tibia; an easily felt one may be an aneurysm.

q: What does pallor of the leg on elevation below 20° indicate (Buerger's test)?
why: Then reactive hyperaemia (rubor) when the leg hangs down.

q: Where are venous ulcers usually found?
model: The gaiter area (above the medial malleolus).
why: Arterial ulcers are on the toes and heels, punched out and painful.

q: Breathlessness lying flat that is relieved by sitting up is called what?
why: A feature of heart failure.

q: Which score is used for stroke risk in AF?
why: Guides anticoagulation.

q: Calf pain on walking relieved by rest suggests what?
why: Ask about walking distance.

q: Which MRC grade means movement only when gravity is eliminated?
why: Grade 3 is against gravity.

q: Which observation falls late in hypovolaemic shock?
hint: Compensation keeps it up until late.
why: Tachycardia, cool peripheries and narrow pulse pressure come first.

q: What size cannulae are used in hypovolaemia?
why: Flow ∝ radius⁴.

q: What is the "lethal triad" in haemorrhage?
why: Each worsens the others.

q: Within what time should tranexamic acid be given in trauma?
why: Later use may increase harm.

q: Why avoid large volumes of crystalloid in major haemorrhage?
why: Replace blood with blood products.

q: Where can blood be hidden in trauma ("on the floor and four more")?
acc: chest / abdomen / pelvis / long bone / thigh
why: Plus external loss.

q: What is the usual MSK exam structure?
model: Look, feel, move (then special tests and neurovascular).
why: Then examine the joint above and below.

q: How are pack-years calculated?
why: A pack is 20 cigarettes.

q: Which questionnaire screens for alcohol misuse?
why: Followed by brief intervention.

q: What should you do at the end when explaining a diagnosis?
acc: safety net / safety-net / teach back / written / check
model: Safety-net, check understanding and give written information.
why: Make sure they know when to seek help.

q: What must be documented about the chaperone after an intimate examination?
model: Their name (or that one was offered and declined).
why: Protects the patient and the examiner.

q: Where is a high vaginal swab taken from?
why: For bacterial vaginosis, candida and trichomonas.

q: What does pain in the groin on hip movement suggest, compared with lateral thigh pain?
model: True hip joint pathology (e.g. OA); lateral pain over the greater trochanter suggests bursitis.
why: Hip joint pain is felt in the groin.

q: What does a positive anterior drawer test suggest?
why: Posterior drawer = PCL.

q: Which joint is tender in an acromioclavicular injury, and which test stresses it?
model: The ACJ; stressed by the scarf (cross-body adduction) test.
why: Pain on top of the shoulder.

q: Until what age do you correct for prematurity on growth charts?
why: For babies born before 37 weeks.

q: What does height falling across centiles with weight preserved suggest?
acc: endocrine / hypothyroid / growth hormone / gh / steroid
model: An endocrine cause (e.g. hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, steroids).
why: Undernutrition affects weight first.

q: What does head circumference crossing centiles upwards suggest?
model: Hydrocephalus (raised intracranial pressure in an infant).
why: Needs urgent assessment.

q: What is the most common cause of faltering growth?
why: Take a detailed feeding history.

q: By what age should a newborn regain their birth weight?
why: Up to 10% loss in the first days is normal.

q: Name a serious cause of abdominal pain in a toddler with "redcurrant jelly" stools.
why: Bowel telescopes into itself.

q: What temperature in a baby under 3 months is a NICE red feature?
why: Needs urgent paediatric assessment.

q: What respiratory rate is a red feature in a child?
why: Plus grunting and moderate or severe indrawing.

q: What colour of vomit is a red flag in a child?
why: Suggests bowel obstruction (e.g. malrotation with volvulus).

q: Why examine ears and throat last in a child?
why: Keeps the child calm for the rest.

q: Name a sign of dehydration in a child.
acc: dry / sunken / tears / crt / capillary / turgor / nappies / lethargy
model: Dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle or eyes, no tears, prolonged CRT, few wet nappies.
hint: Look at the mouth and eyes.
why: Ask about wet nappies.

q: What phrase often reveals a hidden agenda at the end?
acc: while i m here / while i'm here / by the way
why: Ask early: "Is there anything else?"

q: Give a common hidden agenda.
acc: cancer / mental / sexual / domestic / substance / sick note / drug / alcohol
model: Cancer fears, mental health, sexual health, domestic abuse.
why: Respond without judgement.

q: What is shared decision making?
model: Discussing options with risks and benefits and agreeing a plan together.
why: Respects the patient's values.

q: How should the thyroid be palpated?
model: From behind, while the patient swallows.
why: Feel both lobes and the isthmus; check lymph nodes.

q: What should you confirm at the start of a remote consultation?
model: Identity, location (for emergencies), privacy and who else is present.
hint: Name, whereabouts and whether they can talk freely.
why: Then consent.

q: Name a situation unsuitable for a remote consultation.
acc: very unwell / safeguarding / examination / language / hearing
model: Very unwell patient, safeguarding concerns, need for examination.
hint: When you need to see them.
why: Lower threshold for face-to-face review.

q: What Wells score leads straight to CTPA?
why: 4 or less: D-dimer first.

q: What is usual first-line treatment for PE in the UK?
why: For at least 3 months.

q: How long is anticoagulation usually given for a provoked PE?
why: Longer if unprovoked or ongoing risk.

q: Why should "units" never be abbreviated to "U"?
model: It can be misread as 0, causing tenfold overdoses.
why: Write "units" in full.

q: Should basal insulin be withheld in type 1 diabetes when nil by mouth?
why: Risk of DKA; use VRIII plus basal insulin.

q: Name a long-acting basal insulin.
acc: glargine / detemir / degludec / lantus / levemir / tresiba
hint: Given once a day as background.
why: Once-daily background insulin.

q: What is a VRIII?
hint: Five letters, one of them repeated three times.
why: Used when nil by mouth.

q: Which part of the finger is used for capillary glucose testing?
why: Less painful than the pad.

q: What does NEWS2 stand for?
why: Track-and-trigger system for deterioration.

q: Which core procedures should you be able to perform by the end of Year 1?
acc: venepuncture / cannula / blood culture / injection / ecg / abg / urinalysis / bmi
model: Venepuncture, cannulation, blood cultures, injections, ECG, urinalysis, BMI.
why: Practise them alongside A–E and the core examinations.

q: Name the two shockable cardiac arrest rhythms.
acc: vf / ventricular fibrillation + vt / ventricular tachycardia
why: Asystole and PEA are non-shockable.

q: When is adrenaline first given in a shockable arrest?
why: Then every 3–5 minutes (alternate cycles).

q: What dose of amiodarone is given after the third shock?
why: A further 150 mg after the 5th shock.

q: Name one of the 4 Ts in cardiac arrest.
why: The reversible causes alongside the 4 Hs.

q: Where do the defibrillator pads go?
model: One below the right clavicle, one in the left midaxillary line (V6 position).
why: Current passes through the heart.

q: Should compressions continue while the defibrillator charges?
why: Minimises the pause before the shock.

q: Which murmur is heard best with the patient sitting forward in expiration?
why: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.

q: Which murmur has an opening snap and is linked to rheumatic fever?
why: Mid-diastolic rumble at the apex.

q: Which way do you pull the pinna for adult otoscopy?
why: Straightens the ear canal; down and back in children.

q: In sensorineural hearing loss, where does Weber's test lateralise?
why: In conductive loss it goes to the affected ear.

q: What is normal on Rinne's test?
model: Air conduction louder than bone conduction.
hint: Compare the two routes sound can take.
why: Bone > air means conductive loss.

q: Why examine the male genitalia standing first?
hint: Things that fill up on gravity.
why: They are more obvious when standing.

q: A swelling around the testis that glows with a torch is likely what?
why: Solid tumours don't transilluminate.

q: Which side is a varicocele usually on?
why: The left testicular vein drains at right angles into the left renal vein.

q: Sudden testicular pain with a high-riding horizontal testis suggests what?
why: Emergency surgery within 6 hours.

q: How do you test the accessory nerve (XI)?
model: Shrug the shoulders and turn the head against resistance.
hint: Two movements of the neck and shoulders.
why: Tests trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.

q: Which way does the tongue deviate in a hypoglossal palsy?
model: Towards the side of the lesion.
why: The working genioglossus pushes it over.

q: What does forehead sparing in facial weakness indicate?
model: An upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke).
why: The forehead has bilateral cortical supply.

q: What does the swinging light test detect?
why: Optic nerve disease.

q: Within what time should a 12-lead ECG be done in chest pain?
why: To pick up a STEMI quickly.

q: What dose of aspirin is given in suspected ACS?
why: Chewed or dispersed.

q: Within what time should primary PCI be possible in STEMI?
model: Within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given.
why: Otherwise give fibrinolysis.

q: What number is dialled for an in-hospital cardiac arrest?
why: The national standard.

q: How often should compressors swap?
why: Fatigue reduces compression quality.

q: Name a non-shockable rhythm.
why: Give adrenaline as soon as possible.

q: What must you say before delivering a shock?
why: Check everyone is clear.

q: What does a pinhole improve?
why: If acuity improves, glasses will help.

q: What does yellow sclera indicate?
why: Bilirubin over about 40 µmol/L.

q: Which eye do you use to examine the patient's right eye with an ophthalmoscope?
model: Your right eye (ophthalmoscope in the right hand).
why: Avoids "kissing" the patient.

q: What does a swollen optic disc with blurred margins suggest?
why: Investigate urgently.

q: An absent red reflex in a child suggests what?
why: Urgent ophthalmology referral.

q: AV nipping and cotton wool spots suggest what?
why: Diabetic retinopathy has dot-blot haemorrhages and microaneurysms.

q: Which cranial nerve supplies lateral rectus?
why: "LR6 SO4, rest 3".

q: Which cranial nerve supplies superior oblique?
why: Depresses the eye when adducted.

q: Which nerve carries the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
why: Parasympathetic fibres to the sphincter pupillae.

q: At what distance is a Snellen chart read?
why: 6/6 is normal.

q: What visual field defect does a pituitary tumour cause?
why: It compresses the optic chiasm.

q: A stroke in the occipital cortex causes which field defect?
hint: The same half in both eyes.
why: Same side of the field in both eyes.

q: Sudden painless vision loss with jaw claudication suggests what?
why: High-dose steroids immediately to protect the other eye.

q: New floaters and flashes with a curtain over vision suggest what?
why: Same-day ophthalmology referral.

q: How long should face sutures stay in?
why: Scalp, trunk and arms 7–10, legs and feet 10–14.

q: Which sutures are used for skin closure?
why: Absorbable (Vicryl) for deep layers.

q: At what angle should a suture needle enter the skin?
why: Helps evert the wound edges.

q: Which instrument everts the wound edge when suturing?
why: They grip without crushing.

q: What should you check about a wound before closing it?
acc: tetanus / foreign body / tendon / nerve / bite / clean
model: Tetanus status, foreign bodies, tendon or nerve injury, contamination (bites).
why: Contaminated or old wounds may need delayed closure.

q: What is the maximum dose of plain lidocaine?
why: 7 mg/kg with adrenaline.

q: How many mg/mL are in 1% lidocaine?
why: 1% = 1 g per 100 mL.

q: What is the first sign of local anaesthetic toxicity?
why: Progresses to seizures and arrhythmias.

q: What treats local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
why: It soaks up the drug.

q: Why aspirate before injecting local anaesthetic?
why: Prevents toxicity.

q: Why must you try to "get above" a scrotal swelling?
model: If you can't get above it, it's probably an inguinoscrotal hernia.
hint: Could it come from the abdomen?
why: A true scrotal swelling has a palpable upper edge.

q: What size speculum should you choose for otoscopy?
why: Gives the best view.

q: What does SPIKES stand for?
acc: setting + perception + invitation + knowledge + emotions + strategy
model: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary.
why: A framework for breaking bad news.

q: What is a "warning shot" in breaking bad news?
acc: prepare / warn / not the news / afraid
model: A phrase that prepares the patient ("I'm afraid it's not the news we were hoping for").
why: It gives them a moment to brace.

q: What should you do after giving bad news?
why: Then respond to emotions with empathy.

q: What communication technique confirms instructions in a team crisis?
why: The instruction is repeated back.

q: What does a bitemporal hemianopia suggest?
model: A lesion at the optic chiasm (e.g. pituitary tumour).
why: Crossing nasal fibres are compressed.

q: Which type of diarrhoea stops when the patient fasts?
model: Osmotic diarrhoea stops on fasting; secretory continues.
hint: Something in the gut lumen is pulling water in.
why: Unabsorbed solutes (e.g. lactose, laxatives) hold water in the lumen by osmosis. Remove them by fasting and the diarrhoea stops; secretory diarrhoea is driven by active ion secretion, so it carries on.

q: Name a stool test that helps tell IBD from IBS.
model: Faecal calprotectin is raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
hint: A neutrophil protein measured in faeces.
why: Calprotectin comes from neutrophils, so it rises when the bowel wall is inflamed (IBD, infection) but stays normal in functional IBS.

q: Which channel is driven open by cholera toxin to cause secretory diarrhoea?
model: Cholera toxin keeps Gs on → ↑ cAMP → CFTR Cl⁻ secretion; water follows.
hint: The chloride channel that's faulty in cystic fibrosis.
why: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs so it stays active; cAMP rises and CFTR pumps chloride into the lumen, with sodium and water following.

q: Why is loperamide avoided in bloody diarrhoea with fever?
acc: dysentery / invasive / toxic megacolon / toxin / keeps
model: It slows transit, keeping invasive organisms and toxins in the gut (risk of toxic megacolon).
hint: Think about what the gut is trying to flush out.
why: Antimotility drugs stop the gut flushing out invasive organisms and their toxins, which can worsen colitis and precipitate toxic megacolon.

q: First-line oral treatment for C. difficile?
model: Oral vancomycin; fidaxomicin second line. Stop the culprit antibiotic and PPIs.
hint: An oral glycopeptide that isn't absorbed from the gut.
why: Vancomycin given orally isn't absorbed, so it reaches high concentrations in the colon where C. difficile lives; IV vancomycin doesn't reach the gut lumen.

q: Which electrolyte does the colon secrete, explaining why diarrhoea causes its loss?
model: The colon secretes K⁺, so diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia.
hint: Low levels cause U waves and flat T waves.
why: Colonic cells secrete potassium (more so under aldosterone), so large-volume diarrhoea drains K⁺ and causes hypokalaemia.

q: Where in the gut are vitamin B12 and bile salts absorbed?
hint: The last part of the small bowel.
why: The terminal ileum carries the receptors for the B12–intrinsic factor complex and the transporters that reclaim bile salts, so ileal resection or Crohn's affects both.

q: Which transporter absorbs glucose with sodium in the small intestine?
model: SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled); fructose uses GLUT5; both exit via GLUT2.
hint: The reason oral rehydration solution contains salt and sugar together.
why: SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to pull glucose in; each glucose brings sodium (and water) with it, which is why oral rehydration solution combines the two.

q: Which plasma protein provides most of the oncotic pressure?
hint: Made by the liver; low in nephrotic syndrome.
why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and too large to leave capillaries easily, so it generates most of the colloid osmotic pressure.

q: Name a cause of oedema due to low oncotic pressure.
acc: nephrotic / cirrhosis / liver / malnutrition / protein-losing / hypoalbuminaemia
model: Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy.
hint: Think about where albumin is lost, or not made.
why: Low albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid filters out into tissues: lost in the urine (nephrotic), not made (cirrhosis) or not built (malnutrition).

q: Which glands in the duodenal submucosa identify it histologically?
hint: Alkaline mucus glands named after a Swiss anatomist.
why: Brunner's glands secrete alkaline mucus to neutralise acid arriving from the stomach; their submucosal position is unique to the duodenum.

q: Which spirometry ratio confirms airflow obstruction?
hint: Volume blown out in one second over the total.
why: Obstruction slows how fast air leaves, so FEV1 falls more than FVC and the ratio drops below 0.7; restriction lowers both, keeping the ratio normal.

q: Which pneumocytes produce surfactant?
hint: The cuboidal ones, not the flat gas-exchange cells.
why: Type II cells make surfactant, which lowers surface tension so small alveoli don't collapse; type I cells are thin for gas exchange.

q: Name the enzyme imbalance behind emphysema.
hint: Too much breakdown enzyme, too little inhibitor.
why: Neutrophil elastase from smoke-driven inflammation digests elastin in alveolar walls; α1-antitrypsin normally neutralises it, so the balance tips towards destruction.

q: Which type of emphysema is linked to α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
model: Panacinar, lower lobes (centriacinar, upper lobes, in smokers).
hint: Affects the whole acinus, mainly the lower lobes.
why: Without the inhibitor, damage hits whole acini evenly and is worst where blood flow is greatest (the bases); smoking damage starts centrally in the upper lobes.

q: Which two inhaler classes are combined at step 2 in COPD without asthmatic features?
why: When one long-acting bronchodilator isn't enough and there are no asthmatic features, NICE adds the other class (LABA plus LAMA) rather than a steroid.

q: Which inhaled drug class raises pneumonia risk in COPD?
hint: The anti-inflammatory added for triple therapy.
why: Inhaled steroids suppress local airway immunity, so COPD patients on ICS have more pneumonia; that's why ICS is reserved for asthmatic features or frequent exacerbations.

q: In what form is most CO₂ carried in blood?
model: ~70% as bicarbonate; also carbamino compounds and dissolved.
hint: Carbonic anhydrase makes it inside red cells.
why: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells rapidly turns CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H⁺ (buffered by haemoglobin) and bicarbonate that moves into plasma.

q: What acid–base disorder does vomiting cause?
model: Metabolic alkalosis (loss of HCl), with hypokalaemia.
why: Vomiting loses HCl, leaving bicarbonate unopposed; volume loss then drives aldosterone, which wastes K⁺ and H⁺ and keeps the alkalosis going.

q: Name a cause of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
acc: dka / ketoacidosis / lactic / lactate / uraemia / methanol / ethylene glycol / salicylate / aspirin
model: DKA, lactic acidosis, uraemia, toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates).
why: A high anion gap means an unmeasured acid has been added (ketones, lactate, uraemic acids, toxins), consuming bicarbonate without raising chloride.

q: Name a factor that shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
acc: co2 / carbon dioxide / acid / h+ / temperature / heat / 2,3 / bpg / dpg / exercise
hint: The Bohr effect: conditions in busy tissue.
why: Active tissues are warm, acidic and full of CO₂; these conditions lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it releases more where it's needed.

q: Why does pulse oximetry mislead in carbon monoxide poisoning?
acc: carboxy / cohb / reads / normal / can't distinguish / cannot distinguish
model: It reads COHb as oxyhaemoglobin, so sats look normal. Use co-oximetry.
hint: The probe can't tell oxyhaemoglobin from another bound form.
why: Standard oximeters use two wavelengths and can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ looks normal while oxygen delivery is poor.

q: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which roots?
hint: "Three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive."
why: The diaphragm develops in the neck and descends, taking its nerve supply from C3–5 with it, which is why high cervical injuries stop breathing.

q: How do you calculate alveolar ventilation?
hint: Subtract the air that never reaches the alveoli.
why: Only air reaching the alveoli takes part in gas exchange, so the dead-space portion of each breath is subtracted before multiplying by the rate.

q: Name the three levels of prevention.
hint: Before disease, early detection, limiting harm.
why: Primary prevention stops disease starting (vaccines), secondary finds it early (screening), tertiary limits harm once established (rehab).

q: Name the two main causes of peptic ulcer disease.
hint: One bacterium and one class of painkiller.
why: H. pylori damages the mucosa and raises acid; NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that maintain mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow.

q: Name a non-invasive test for H. pylori.
acc: urea breath / breath / stool antigen / stool
model: Urea breath test or stool antigen test (stop PPI 2 weeks before).
hint: One you blow into a bag after a labelled drink; one is a faecal sample.
why: H. pylori's urease splits labelled urea into labelled CO₂ that you breathe out; the stool test detects bacterial antigen. PPIs suppress the bacteria and cause false negatives.

q: How does H. pylori in the antrum lead to duodenal ulcers?
hint: It damages the antral D cells that act as a brake.
why: Antral infection kills somatostatin-producing D cells, removing the brake on gastrin; more gastrin means more acid pouring into the duodenum.

q: What is UK first-line H. pylori eradication therapy?
model: 7 days of PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole.
why: A PPI raises gastric pH so the antibiotics work better, and two antibiotics reduce resistance; clarithromycin or metronidazole is chosen by allergy and previous use.

q: Which enzyme do PPIs block?
hint: The final step of secretion in parietal cells.
why: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the final common step of acid secretion, so blocking it stops acid whatever the stimulus (histamine, gastrin or vagal).

q: Which area of the brain detects drugs and toxins to trigger vomiting?
hint: Outside the blood–brain barrier, in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
why: The area postrema lies outside the blood–brain barrier, so it can sample blood for toxins and drugs and relay to the vomiting centre via dopamine and 5-HT3.

q: Which gastric cells make acid and intrinsic factor?
hint: Lost in pernicious anaemia; found in the gastric body.
why: Parietal cells make both, which is why autoimmune gastritis against them causes low acid and B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).

q: Which brush-border enzyme activates trypsinogen?
hint: A duodenal enzyme; its older name ends in -kinase.
why: Enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes; activation happens in the gut, not the pancreas.

q: What is the metaplasia seen in Barrett's oesophagus?
model: Squamous → columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).
hint: The squamous lining is replaced by the type lining the bowel.
why: Chronic acid reflux makes the squamous lining change to acid-resistant intestinal-type columnar cells, which can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

q: Name the characteristic cell of diffuse gastric cancer.
hint: Mucin pushes the nucleus to one side.
why: Diffuse gastric cancer cells fill with mucin that pushes the nucleus aside, and they infiltrate the wall to make it rigid (linitis plastica).

q: Which two-level score guides DVT investigation?
model: Two-level Wells score: D-dimer if unlikely, USS if likely.
hint: Also used for PE; named after a Canadian.
why: Wells sorts DVT as likely or unlikely: unlikely gets a D-dimer first (a negative rules it out), likely goes straight to ultrasound.

q: At what point after starting IV antibiotics should they be reviewed?
model: At 48–72 hours (stop, switch IV to oral, narrow, continue).
hint: Start Smart then Focus: after two to three days.
why: By 48–72 hours cultures are back and the patient's course is clearer, so you can stop, switch IV to oral, narrow or continue (Start Smart then Focus).

q: Name a mediator of acute inflammation that causes vasodilation.
acc: histamine / prostaglandin / no / nitric oxide / bradykinin
hint: Released by mast cells, or made from arachidonic acid.
why: Vasodilation increases blood flow (redness, heat); histamine acts immediately, prostaglandins and NO sustain it.

q: Which precautions and mask are needed for suspected TB?
model: Airborne precautions with an FFP3 respirator and negative-pressure room.
hint: Spread by droplet nuclei that hang about for hours.
why: TB spreads on tiny droplet nuclei that stay airborne, so a fitted FFP3 respirator and a negative-pressure room are needed rather than a surgical mask.

q: Why use soap and water rather than alcohol gel for C. difficile?
hint: Alcohol doesn't kill its resistant form.
why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol can't kill; washing with soap and water physically removes them from the hands.

q: Where do T cells mature?
why: T cells are selected in the thymus: positive selection keeps those that recognise self-MHC, negative selection deletes strongly self-reactive ones.

q: Which organism causes most cellulitis and impetigo?
hint: Gram-positive cocci in clusters or chains.
why: Both are skin-colonising Gram-positive cocci; impetigo is often Staph aureus, cellulitis usually Strep pyogenes.

q: What is first-pass metabolism?
model: Metabolism in the gut wall and liver before the drug reaches the systemic circulation.
hint: Oral drugs travel via the portal vein first.
why: Oral drugs pass through the gut wall and then the liver via the portal vein before reaching the circulation, so some is metabolised first (e.g. GTN is given sublingually).

q: Which cells kill virus-infected cells lacking MHC class I?
hint: Innate lymphocytes that check for "missing self".
why: NK cells kill cells that have lost MHC class I ("missing self"), a trick viruses and tumours use to hide from cytotoxic T cells.

q: Where does the thoracic duct drain?
acc: left venous angle / left subclavian / left internal jugular / left
model: Into the left venous angle (left subclavian/internal jugular junction).
hint: The junction of the internal jugular and subclavian, on one side.
why: The thoracic duct carries lymph from most of the body and empties where the left internal jugular joins the left subclavian vein.

q: Which white cell has a bilobed nucleus and red granules?
hint: Raised in allergy and parasite infections.
why: Eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and granules containing major basic protein; they rise in allergy, asthma and parasitic infection.

q: Which cytokine drives CRP production?
hint: The main cytokine acting on the liver in the acute phase.
why: IL-6 from macrophages travels to the liver and switches on acute-phase proteins, including CRP.

q: What complex forms pores in bacterial membranes?
hint: The terminal complement components assemble into it.
why: The terminal components C5b–C9 assemble into a pore that lets water in and lyses the cell; deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infection.

q: Name the three complement pathways.
hint: One antibody-triggered, one sugar-binding, one always ticking over.
why: Classical is triggered by antibody–antigen complexes, lectin by mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars, alternative by spontaneous C3 activation on surfaces.

q: What does the "inverse care law" state?
model: Those most in need of care get the least of it.
hint: Tudor Hart's observation about where good care ends up.
why: Tudor Hart noted that good care tends to be least available where it's most needed (deprived areas), because of market forces.

q: Name the criteria used to call a pleural effusion an exudate.
hint: Compares pleural and serum protein and LDH.
why: Light's criteria call an effusion an exudate if pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >⅔ of the upper normal limit.

q: Immediate treatment of a tension pneumothorax?
model: Needle or finger decompression, then a chest drain.
hint: Second intercostal space, midclavicular, or the fifth space.
why: Tension physiology (rising pressure, falling venous return) kills before an X-ray can be done, so decompress first, then place a definitive drain.

q: How does a competitive antagonist change the dose–response curve?
model: Shifts it to the right with the same maximum (surmountable).
hint: Same maximum effect, but you need more agonist.
why: A competitive antagonist binds the same site reversibly, so enough agonist can outcompete it: the curve moves right but the maximum is unchanged.

q: Which chemoreceptors drive most of the ventilatory response to CO₂?
model: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla (via CSF H⁺).
hint: They sense CSF pH in the brainstem.
why: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and lowers CSF pH, which central chemoreceptors sense; they account for most of the response to CO₂, while peripheral ones sense hypoxia.

q: Name a drug with zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
hint: An antiepileptic, or a common social drug.
why: Zero-order drugs saturate their enzymes, so a fixed amount is cleared per hour and small dose increases can cause big rises in level (phenytoin toxicity).

q: Which pharmacokinetic value determines the loading dose?
hint: The apparent space a drug spreads into.
why: The loading dose has to fill the volume the drug distributes into (dose = target concentration × Vd); clearance sets the maintenance dose.

q: Name the asbestos-related malignancy of the pleura.
hint: Long latency; not a lung carcinoma.
why: Mesothelioma arises from the pleura decades after asbestos exposure; asbestos also raises lung cancer risk, especially with smoking.

q: Name Parsons' model of the obligations of a patient.
hint: The rights and duties of being unwell.
why: Parsons said the sick are excused normal duties but are obliged to want to get well and to seek and cooperate with medical help.

q: Which nerve should you check before and after reducing a shoulder dislocation?
model: The axillary nerve (regimental badge area, deltoid).
hint: Check the "regimental badge" patch of skin.
why: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and is stretched in dislocation; check sensation over the "regimental badge" before and after.

q: Which nerve is at risk in a humeral shaft fracture?
hint: Runs in the spiral groove; injury gives wrist drop.
why: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove against the humeral shaft, so a fracture there can cause wrist drop.

q: Which collagen type is found in hyaline cartilage?
hint: One more than the type in bone.
why: Type II collagen gives hyaline cartilage its tensile framework; bone, tendon and skin are mainly type I.

q: What change in cartilage starts osteoarthritis?
model: Proteoglycan loss and fibrillation of cartilage.
hint: Loss of the water-holding molecules, then surface splitting.
why: Losing proteoglycans means cartilage holds less water and loses its springiness; the surface then splits (fibrillation) and wears down.

q: Name the four stages of fracture healing.
model: Haematoma/inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling.
hint: A blood clot, two kinds of callus, then reshaping.
why: Bleeding forms a haematoma and inflammation, fibrocartilage forms a soft callus, woven bone makes a hard callus, then remodelling restores lamellar bone.

q: Which skin layer contains melanocytes and stem cells?
hint: The deepest layer of the epidermis.
why: The stratum basale is the dividing layer: stem cells (keratinocytes) and melanocytes sit there, on the basement membrane.

q: Name a regional block for forearm fracture reduction.
model: Bier's block (IV regional) or haematoma block.
hint: IV regional anaesthesia with a cuff, named after a surgeon.
why: Bier's block injects local anaesthetic IV below a cuff to numb the whole limb; a haematoma block injects straight into the fracture site.

q: What does PICO stand for?
hint: Who, what, versus what, and what you measure.
why: PICO turns a clinical question into a searchable one: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.

q: What investigation should every patient with syncope have?
why: An ECG can show dangerous causes of syncope, such as heart block, long QT, Brugada, WPW or ischaemia, cheaply and quickly.

q: Name a red flag feature of syncope.
acc: exertion / exercise / lying / supine / ecg / murmur / family history / sudden death / heart failure
model: Exertional or supine syncope, abnormal ECG, new murmur, FHx sudden death, heart failure.
hint: Think of circumstances that point to a cardiac cause.
why: Syncope on exertion or lying down, with palpitations, a murmur, an abnormal ECG or family history of sudden death, suggests a cardiac cause needing urgent assessment.

q: First-line investigation for stable chest pain (NICE)?
acc: ct coronary / ctca / ct angiography / ct
hint: A non-invasive scan of the heart's arteries.
why: NICE uses CT coronary angiography first because it has a very high negative predictive value and shows anatomy directly.

q: Which blood test confirms myocardial infarction?
hint: A cardiac muscle protein, measured high-sensitivity.
why: Troponin is released from damaged myocytes; a rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile with ischaemic features confirms MI.

q: Which heart block has progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat?
acc: mobitz i / mobitz 1 / wenckebach / mobitz type 1
hint: Second-degree, type I, with an eponym.
why: In Mobitz I the AV node tires a little more with each beat until one P wave isn't conducted; it's usually nodal and benign.

q: What ECG pattern defines atrial fibrillation?
model: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves.
hint: Think about rhythm regularity and atrial activity.
why: Chaotic atrial activity replaces organised P waves, and the AV node conducts randomly, so QRS complexes are irregularly irregular.

q: Which coronary artery supplies the AV node in most people?
hint: The reason inferior MIs cause heart block.
why: The AV nodal artery usually comes from the RCA, so inferior MIs (RCA) often cause heart block.

q: Which heart sound marks closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves?
why: S2 is the closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole; splitting widens with inspiration as right-sided filling increases.

q: What generates the pacemaker potential in the SA node?
hint: An oddly named inward current, blocked by ivabradine.
why: HCN channels open at negative voltages and let in a slow inward Na⁺ current, so the membrane drifts up to threshold automatically; ivabradine blocks it.

q: Where are the arterial baroreceptors?
hint: Two places: the carotid bifurcation and the top of the aorta.
why: Carotid sinus receptors signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve and aortic arch receptors via the vagus to the medulla, adjusting heart rate and vascular tone.

q: When do neutrophils first infiltrate after an MI?
why: Neutrophils arrive from about 24 hours and peak at 1–3 days, followed by macrophages; this timeline is used to date infarcts.

q: Nerve conduction in demyelinating neuropathy shows?
model: Slowed conduction velocity and conduction block.
hint: Myelin speeds signals up, so lose it and...
why: Myelin lets impulses jump between nodes; demyelination slows conduction velocity and can block conduction, whereas axonal loss mainly reduces amplitude.

q: Which organism classically triggers Guillain–Barré syndrome?
hint: A curved Gram-negative gut bacterium from undercooked chicken.
why: Campylobacter jejuni carries antigens that mimic gangliosides on peripheral nerves, so antibodies made against it attack myelin (molecular mimicry).

q: What should you monitor to spot respiratory failure in GBS?
hint: A spirometry volume, not oxygen sats.
why: Falling FVC shows diaphragm weakness before oxygen sats drop; an FVC below about 20 mL/kg calls for ICU review.

q: What CSF finding is typical of GBS?
model: High protein with normal cell count.
hint: Cells normal, but something else is raised.
why: Albuminocytological dissociation: protein rises from nerve root inflammation while the cell count stays normal (often only after the first week).

q: Acute treatment for a cluster headache attack?
hint: High-flow gas plus a subcutaneous drug.
why: High-flow 100% oxygen and subcutaneous or nasal triptans work fast enough for short, intense attacks; oral drugs act too slowly.

q: Name a migraine prophylactic drug.
hint: A beta-blocker, an antiepileptic or a tricyclic.
why: Propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline reduce attack frequency; topiramate is teratogenic, so avoid it in women who could become pregnant.

q: Which ion flows in to depolarise a neuron during an action potential?
hint: Its channels are blocked by local anaesthetics.
why: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and sodium rushes in down its gradient, depolarising the membrane; K⁺ outflow then repolarises it.

q: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres?
model: III, VII, IX and X (plus S2–4).
why: Cranial parasympathetic outflow travels in III (pupil), VII (tears, saliva), IX (parotid) and X (thoracic and abdominal organs); sacral outflow is S2–4.

q: Which receptor mediates bronchodilation?
why: β2-adrenoceptors on airway smooth muscle raise cAMP and relax it, which is why β2 agonists treat asthma and non-selective β-blockers can trigger bronchospasm.

q: What neurotransmitter do sympathetic nerves to sweat glands release?
hint: The exception: the same as the parasympathetic transmitter.
why: Sympathetic fibres to sweat glands are the exception: they release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors, which is why anticholinergics stop sweating.

q: Upper age limit for walking independently?
why: Most children walk by 12–15 months; not walking by 18 months is a red flag for motor delay, muscle disease or cerebral palsy.

q: Which hand preference age is a red flag?
why: Handedness normally isn't established until about 18 months to 2 years; an early preference suggests weakness of the other hand (e.g. hemiplegic cerebral palsy).

q: Name a fracture pattern suggestive of non-accidental injury.
hint: Chest wall injuries in infants, or classic injuries at the ends of long bones.
why: Posterior rib fractures come from squeezing the chest, and metaphyseal corner fractures from shaking or twisting; neither fits accidental falls in infants.

q: What does jaundice in the first 24 hours of life suggest?
model: Always pathological: haemolysis (ABO/Rh, G6PD) or sepsis.
why: Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours; jaundice in the first day means bilirubin is rising fast, usually from haemolysis or sepsis.

q: An absent red reflex in a newborn may mean?
hint: A lens opacity, or an eye tumour.
why: The red reflex needs a clear path through the lens and a normal retina; cataract or retinoblastoma blocks it and needs urgent ophthalmology.

q: Name a core principle of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
acc: best interests / non-discrimination / heard / life / survival
model: Best interests, non-discrimination, right to life and development, right to be heard.
hint: One of four general principles, e.g. what's best for the child.
why: The UNCRC's four general principles are non-discrimination, best interests, the right to life and development, and the right to be heard.

q: What forms during gastrulation?
acc: trilaminar / three germ / ectoderm / mesoderm / endoderm
model: The trilaminar disc: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm.
why: Gastrulation turns the bilaminar disc into three germ layers: ectoderm (nervous system, skin), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood) and endoderm (gut lining).

q: Which structure induces neurulation?
why: The notochord signals to the overlying ectoderm (e.g. via sonic hedgehog) to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube.

q: Name an autosomal recessive condition.
acc: cystic fibrosis / cf / sickle / thalassaemia / pku / haemochromatosis
model: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, β-thalassaemia, PKU, haemochromatosis.
hint: Classic examples affect the lungs and pancreas, or haemoglobin.
why: Recessive conditions need two faulty copies, so carriers are healthy and the risk for each child of two carriers is 1 in 4.

q: Paternal deletion at 15q11–13 causes which syndrome?
hint: Hyperphagia and floppiness (maternal deletion gives Angelman).
why: Genes at 15q11–13 are imprinted: losing the paternal copy gives Prader–Willi, losing the maternal copy gives Angelman.

q: What hypothesis explains inherited tumour-suppressor cancers?
hint: Retinoblastoma: one copy inherited, one acquired.
why: Both copies of a tumour-suppressor gene must be lost; inherited cases are born with one hit, so they need only one more, giving earlier and bilateral tumours.

q: Painless visible haematuria in an adult should be treated as what until proven otherwise?
why: Bladder cancer classically presents with painless visible haematuria, so adults are referred on a suspected cancer pathway even if the bleeding stops.

q: Which two investigations make up a haematuria clinic assessment?
model: Flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging (CT urogram).
hint: Look inside the bladder, and image the upper tracts.
why: Cystoscopy inspects the bladder lining directly, and CT urography images the kidneys and ureters for upper-tract tumours or stones.

q: Biggest risk factor for bladder cancer?
hint: The same as for lung cancer.
why: Carcinogens from tobacco are excreted in urine and sit in contact with the bladder lining; smoking roughly triples the risk.

q: Which intravesical treatment is used for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
why: BCG instilled into the bladder stimulates a local immune response that reduces recurrence and progression of high-grade superficial tumours.

q: Gold-standard imaging for renal colic?
why: Non-contrast CT KUB detects almost all stones, gives their size and position, and shows other causes of pain.

q: Emergency treatment for an obstructed, infected kidney?
model: Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or JJ stent) + IV antibiotics.
hint: Drain it urgently, from above or below.
why: Pus behind an obstruction won't clear with antibiotics alone and can cause urosepsis, so the kidney needs draining urgently.

q: Name two hormonal functions of the kidney.
acc: epo / erythropoietin / renin / vitamin d / calcitriol
hint: Think red cells, blood pressure and bones.
why: The kidney makes EPO in response to hypoxia, renin to control blood pressure, and activates vitamin D by 1α-hydroxylation, so CKD causes anaemia, hypertension and bone disease.

q: Where is most sodium and water reabsorbed?
hint: The first segment after the glomerulus.
why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, plus nearly all glucose and amino acids.

q: Which transporter do loop diuretics block?
model: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.
hint: In the thick ascending limb of the loop.
why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, which reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered sodium, making them the most powerful diuretics.

q: Name the three drugs in the "triple whammy" for AKI.
hint: A painkiller, a RAAS blocker and a water tablet.
why: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole, ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent, and diuretics reduce volume, so together they collapse glomerular filtration pressure.

q: Which nerve and roots control the external urethral sphincter?
hint: The same nerve that supplies the perineum.
why: The external sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–4), which is why sacral damage causes incontinence.

q: What is "operant conditioning"?
model: Learning by reinforcement or punishment of behaviour (Skinner).
why: In operant conditioning, behaviour followed by reward becomes more frequent and behaviour followed by punishment less frequent.

q: Waist-to-height ratio that indicates central adiposity?
hint: NICE: keep your waist below a simple fraction of your height.
why: A ratio of 0.5 or more ("keep your waist to less than half your height") signals central fat, which predicts cardiometabolic risk better than BMI.

q: Which gut hormone increases hunger before meals?
hint: Made by the stomach; rises when fasting.
why: Ghrelin from the stomach rises before meals and falls after eating, stimulating appetite via the hypothalamus.

q: Mutation of which receptor is the commonest monogenic cause of obesity?
hint: A hypothalamic receptor in the leptin pathway.
why: MC4R sits downstream of leptin in the hypothalamus; loss of function removes the satiety signal, causing early-onset hyperphagia and obesity.

q: Name a GLP-1 receptor agonist licensed for weight loss.
why: GLP-1 agonists slow gastric emptying and act on hypothalamic satiety centres; semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (Wegovy) is licensed for weight loss.

q: Which bariatric operation is best for T2DM remission?
hint: The one that diverts food past the duodenum.
why: Bypassing the duodenum and speeding nutrients to the distal gut boosts incretin hormones, improving insulin secretion within days, beyond the effect of weight loss.

q: Name a sign of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
hint: Look at the Achilles, the knuckles and the cornea.
why: LDL receptor mutations cause very high LDL from birth, which deposits in tendons (xanthomata) and the cornea (arcus before 45).

q: How do statins lower LDL?
hint: They block the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
why: Blocking HMG-CoA reductase lowers liver cholesterol, so liver cells make more LDL receptors and pull LDL out of the blood.

q: Main determinant of basal metabolic rate?
hint: What makes up most of your body that isn't fat.
why: Muscle and organs use far more energy at rest than fat, so lean mass explains most of the variation in BMR between people.

q: Through how many degrees does the midgut rotate?
why: The midgut herniates into the cord and rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA before returning; malrotation predisposes to volvulus.

q: What is the "rule of 2s" condition from the vitelline duct?
why: Meckel's diverticulum: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric, pancreatic), often presents before age 2.

q: Name the stages of change model.
hint: From not thinking about it, through preparing, to keeping it up.
why: Prochaska and DiClemente's model: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (and relapse); match the intervention to the stage.

q: Which fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement?
why: A fall on an outstretched hand pushes the distal fragment dorsally, giving the "dinner fork" deformity; volar displacement is a Smith's fracture.

q: Where is tenderness in a scaphoid fracture?
hint: A hollow at the base of the thumb.
why: The scaphoid forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, so tenderness there suggests a fracture even if the first X-ray is normal.

q: Main complication of a scaphoid fracture?
model: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
why: Blood enters the scaphoid distally and flows backwards, so a waist fracture can cut off the proximal pole, causing AVN and non-union.

q: Which collagen dominates early tendon repair?
model: Type III, later replaced by type I.
hint: The type later replaced by type I.
why: Fibroblasts first lay down weaker type III collagen, which is gradually remodelled into stronger type I as the tendon matures.

q: Antibodies against what cause myasthenia gravis?
acc: acetylcholine receptor / achr / ach receptor / musk
hint: Postsynaptic nicotinic receptors at the NMJ.
why: Antibodies block and destroy postsynaptic ACh receptors, so fewer are available and transmission fails with repeated use (fatigable weakness).

q: What does botulinum toxin block?
hint: It acts on the presynaptic nerve terminal.
why: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins needed for vesicles to fuse, so ACh isn't released and muscles become flaccid.

q: Which drug treats malignant hyperthermia?
why: Malignant hyperthermia is uncontrolled calcium release through faulty ryanodine receptors; dantrolene blocks the receptor and stops the hypermetabolic crisis.

q: Which protein does calcium bind to start skeletal muscle contraction?
hint: Part of a complex on the thin filament, with tropomyosin.
why: Calcium binds troponin C, which moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites so myosin heads can attach and cross-bridge cycling begins.

q: What is the nocebo effect?
model: Negative expectations causing real adverse effects.
why: Expecting harm can produce real symptoms; telling patients about side effects can increase how often they're reported.

q: Name the four principles of medical ethics.
why: Beauchamp and Childress's four principles: respect autonomy, do good (beneficence), avoid harm (non-maleficence), and be fair (justice).

q: Which case set the standard for disclosure of material risks?
why: Montgomery (2015) replaced the doctor-centred Bolam standard for consent: doctors must disclose risks a reasonable patient, or this patient, would consider significant.

q: Which test defines breach of duty in negligence?
why: Bolam: a doctor isn't negligent if a responsible body of medical opinion would have acted the same way; Bolitho adds that the opinion must be logical.

q: Which conventions protect medical neutrality in conflict?
hint: A Swiss city, the Red Cross.
why: The Geneva Conventions protect the wounded, health workers and hospitals in armed conflict, and require care regardless of side.

q: Which scan confirms gestational age?
hint: First-trimester scan measuring the fetus from head to rump.
why: Crown–rump length between 10 and 14 weeks varies little between fetuses, so it dates the pregnancy most accurately and sets the due date.

q: First-line antihypertensive in pre-eclampsia?
why: Labetalol is effective and safe in pregnancy; nifedipine is the alternative (e.g. in asthma), and ACE inhibitors are avoided.

q: Treatment for eclampsia seizures?
hint: An electrolyte given IV, also used in severe asthma.
why: Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures better than antiepileptics; monitor reflexes, breathing and urine output for toxicity.

q: Name the "4 Ts" of postpartum haemorrhage.
why: Most PPH is from a uterus that doesn't contract (tone); the others are tears (trauma), retained placenta (tissue) and clotting problems (thrombin).

q: How many doctors must certify a termination under the Abortion Act?
why: The Abortion Act 1967 requires two registered medical practitioners to agree in good faith that the legal grounds are met (one in an emergency).

q: Which part of the brain links the nervous and endocrine systems?
why: The hypothalamus receives neural input and controls the pituitary through releasing hormones and direct nerve fibres, linking the two systems.

q: Where do steroid hormones bind?
hint: They're lipid-soluble, so they cross the membrane.
why: Steroids are lipid-soluble, so they cross the cell membrane and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors, which is why their effects are slower.

q: Which hormones does the posterior pituitary release?
hint: Two peptides made in the hypothalamus.
why: ADH and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic nuclei and transported down axons to the posterior pituitary, which stores and releases them.

q: What does progesterone do to the endometrium?
hint: Prepares it for implantation in the second half of the cycle.
why: After ovulation the corpus luteum's progesterone turns the thickened endometrium secretory, with glands and blood supply ready for implantation.

q: What triggers ovulation?
hint: A surge of a pituitary hormone.
why: Rising oestradiol from the dominant follicle switches from negative to positive feedback, causing an LH surge that triggers ovulation about 36 hours later.

q: Why does BP fall in the second trimester?
hint: Hormonal relaxation of the vessel walls.
why: Progesterone and nitric oxide relax vascular smooth muscle, so SVR falls and blood pressure dips in the second trimester, before returning to normal near term.

q: Which reflex drives the positive feedback of labour?
hint: Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin; an eponym.
why: The fetal head stretching the cervix sends signals that release oxytocin, causing stronger contractions and more stretch: a positive feedback loop.

q: Which joints does rheumatoid arthritis typically spare in the hand?
why: RA targets synovial joints of the MCPs, PIPs and wrists and typically spares the DIPs, which are typical in OA and psoriatic arthritis.

q: Name the X-ray signs of osteoarthritis.
model: LOSS: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts.
why: Cartilage loss narrows the joint space; bone responds with osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts (LOSS).

q: Name the inflamed synovial tissue that erodes joints in RA.
why: Pannus is inflamed, proliferating synovium that spreads over cartilage and erodes bone at the joint margins.

q: Which antibody is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
why: Anti-CCP is about 95% specific for RA and predicts erosive disease; rheumatoid factor is less specific.

q: First-line DMARD for RA?
hint: Weekly, with folic acid on another day.
why: Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD, given once weekly with folic acid on a different day to reduce side effects; monitor FBC and LFTs.

q: Which muscles stop the pelvis dropping in single-leg stance?
why: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip and hold the pelvis level when standing on one leg; weakness causes a Trendelenburg sign.

q: Name the metaplasia in a smoker's bronchus.
hint: The type of epithelium on skin.
why: Smoke irritation replaces ciliated columnar epithelium with tougher squamous epithelium, which loses mucociliary clearance and can progress to squamous carcinoma.

q: Name the CURB-65 criteria.
acc: confusion + urea + respiratory / rr + blood pressure / bp + 65 / age
hint: Each letter is a criterion, plus the number.
why: CURB-65 scores 1 for each: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, Age ≥65; higher scores mean higher mortality.

q: Name two "geriatric giants".
acc: falls / immobility / confusion / delirium / incontinence / iatrogenesis / polypharmacy
why: Isaacs' "giants" (immobility, instability/falls, incontinence, intellectual impairment/delirium, iatrogenesis) are common, have many causes and threaten independence.

q: Name the five Fried frailty criteria.
acc: weight loss + exhaustion + weak / grip + slow / walking + activity
model: Weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking, low activity.
hint: Shrinking, tiredness and three more physical measures.
why: Fried's frailty phenotype: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weak grip, slow walking and low activity; three or more means frail.

q: Which receptor does SARS-CoV-2 bind?
why: The spike protein binds ACE2 on respiratory epithelium, helped by the protease TMPRSS2, to enter cells.

q: Which drug reduced COVID-19 deaths in patients needing oxygen (RECOVERY)?
why: RECOVERY showed dexamethasone cut deaths in patients needing oxygen or ventilation by damping the inflammatory response, but not in those who didn't need oxygen.

q: How does aciclovir become active?
hint: A viral enzyme adds the first phosphate.
why: Aciclovir is phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase, so it's activated mainly in infected cells, then terminates viral DNA chains.

q: Mechanism of oseltamivir?
hint: Stops new virions leaving the cell surface.
why: Neuraminidase cuts new virions free from the host cell; blocking it traps them, which is why it works best started within 48 hours.

q: Which enzyme do retroviruses use to make DNA from RNA?
why: Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA, which then integrates into host DNA; NRTIs and NNRTIs target it.

q: What causes influenza pandemics?
why: Influenza has a segmented genome; when two strains infect the same host, segments swap (shift), producing a new subtype nobody is immune to.

q: Which vaccine is given to children as a nasal spray each year?
why: The live attenuated nasal flu vaccine is offered to children each year; it protects them and reduces spread to older relatives.

q: At what ages is the 6-in-1 vaccine given in infancy?
hint: Three doses a month apart, starting at two months.
why: The 6-in-1 (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Hib, hepatitis B) is given at 8, 12 and 16 weeks to build immunity before maternal antibody wanes.

q: How long must depressive symptoms last for a depressive episode?
why: ICD-11 and DSM need symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks to separate a depressive episode from normal low mood.

q: Name a screening tool for postnatal depression.
why: The EPDS is a 10-item self-report scale designed for the postnatal period; it avoids physical symptoms like tiredness that are normal after birth.

q: First-line drug class for moderate–severe depression?
why: SSRIs are as effective as older drugs, with fewer side effects and much lower toxicity in overdose; sertraline is often first choice.

q: Name a feature of serotonin syndrome.
acc: clonus / hyperthermia / agitation / hyperreflexia / diarrhoea / tremor
why: Excess serotonin causes a triad: mental-state change (agitation), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, sweating, diarrhoea) and neuromuscular excitability (clonus, hyperreflexia).

q: Which antidepressant class is most dangerous in overdose?
hint: The older class; look for a broad QRS.
why: TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, causing a broad QRS, arrhythmias and seizures; a few weeks' supply can be fatal.

q: Loss of dopamine in which pathway causes Parkinson's disease?
why: Dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra project to the striatum; losing them disrupts the basal ganglia loop, causing bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.

q: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory one in the brain?
why: GABA opens chloride channels (GABA-A) that hyperpolarise neurons; benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol enhance it.

q: Prevalence equals incidence multiplied by what?
why: Prevalence counts existing cases, so it depends on how often new cases arise (incidence) and how long they last (duration).

q: Name a non-medical source of support for mental health.
acc: mind / samaritans / social prescribing / peer / charity / self-help / citizens advice / hafal
model: Charities (Mind, Samaritans), social prescribing, peer support, self-help.
why: Non-medical support such as charities, peer groups and social prescribing addresses loneliness, finances and purpose, which drive many mental health problems.

q: How much more common is depression in women than men?
why: Depression is about twice as common in women, reflecting hormonal, psychosocial and reporting differences; men are less likely to seek help and more likely to die by suicide.

q: Which joint is classically affected first in gout?
acc: first mtp / 1st mtp / big toe / metatarsophalangeal
why: Urate crystallises most easily in cooler peripheral joints under stress, so the big toe MTP joint is the classic first site (podagra).

q: Name a drug that raises urate and can trigger gout.
model: Thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin.
why: Diuretics and low-dose aspirin reduce renal urate excretion, raising serum urate; ciclosporin does the same.

q: What crystals are seen in gout under polarised light?
hint: Think shape and the sign of birefringence.
why: Gout shows needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent under polarised light; pseudogout shows rhomboid, weakly positive crystals.

q: When should serum urate be rechecked after a flare?
model: At least 2 weeks after the flare (it can be normal during one).
