q: Fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation?
why: A fall on an outstretched hand angulates the distal radius dorsally, giving a dinner-fork deformity.

q: Fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck?
why: Punching with a closed fist drives force through the 5th metacarpal, fracturing its neck (boxer's fracture).

q: Name a normal variant that mimics a fracture.
acc: epiphys / growth plate / accessory ossicle / sesamoid / bipartite
model: Unfused epiphyses, accessory ossicles, sesamoids, bipartite patella.
why: Children's growth plates and accessory bones look like fracture lines, so know normal variants and compare with the other side.

q: Fracture with more than two fragments?
why: A comminuted fracture has more than two fragments, usually from high-energy injury.

q: Elbow X-ray sign of an occult fracture?
why: An effusion lifts the posterior fat pad out of the olecranon fossa so it becomes visible; with trauma this suggests an occult fracture (radial head in adults, supracondylar in children).

q: Fat–fluid level in the knee means?
why: Fat from the marrow leaking into the joint floats on blood, so a fat–fluid level means a fracture extends into the joint.

q: "Lightbulb" humeral head suggests which dislocation?
why: In posterior dislocation the humeral head is internally rotated, so it looks round like a lightbulb on an AP film; it follows seizures or electric shocks.

q: Commonest shoulder dislocation?
why: About 95% of shoulder dislocations are anterior, from forced abduction and external rotation.

q: Scaphoid fracture complication?
model: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
why: Blood enters the scaphoid distally and flows backwards, so a waist fracture can leave the proximal pole without supply (AVN).

q: Name a part of fracture description.
acc: site / bone / pattern / type / displacement / angulation / open / closed / comminution
model: Bone, site, pattern, displacement, angulation, open/closed.
why: A structured description (bone, site, pattern, displacement, angulation, open or closed) communicates the injury clearly and guides management.

q: Name an emergency fracture finding.
acc: open / neurovascular / pelvic / compartment / spinal / cervical
model: Open fracture, neurovascular compromise, unstable pelvic fracture.
why: Open fractures risk infection, neurovascular compromise threatens the limb, and unstable pelvic fractures can cause major bleeding.

q: On which side of the femur is the linea aspera?
why: The linea aspera is a ridge on the back of the femur where many thigh muscles attach.

q: Main artery to the femoral head?
why: The medial circumflex femoral artery gives the retinacular vessels that supply most of the femoral head.

q: Which nerve is at risk in posterior hip dislocation?
why: The sciatic nerve lies directly behind the hip, so posterior dislocation can stretch or injure it, causing foot drop.

q: Where is the great saphenous vein at the ankle?
hint: In front of a bony bump.
why: The great saphenous vein lies just in front of the medial malleolus, a reliable site for venous cut-down.

q: Root value of the knee jerk?
why: The knee jerk tests the femoral nerve, roots L3–4.

q: Root value of the ankle jerk?
why: The ankle jerk tests S1 via the tibial nerve; it's lost in S1 radiculopathy.

q: Foot drop after a fibular neck fracture: which nerve?
hint: It wraps around the fibular neck.
why: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, so fractures there can damage it, weakening dorsiflexion and eversion.

q: Which sacral plexus nerve injury gives a Trendelenburg gait?
why: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus; without them the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg.

q: Through which foramen does the sciatic nerve leave the pelvis?
why: The sciatic nerve leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, entering the buttock.

q: Muscle supplied by the coccygeal plexus?
why: The coccygeal plexus (S4–Co1) supplies coccygeus and part of levator ani, and the skin around the coccyx.

q: Through which opening does the obturator nerve reach the thigh?
why: The obturator nerve runs along the pelvic wall and passes through the obturator canal into the medial thigh.

q: Main muscle group supplied by the obturator nerve?
why: The obturator nerve supplies the adductors of the thigh, so injury weakens adduction.

q: Where does the small saphenous vein drain?
why: The small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus and up the calf to join the popliteal vein.

q: Which way do perforator veins carry blood?
why: Valves in the perforators direct blood from superficial to deep veins; when they fail, blood flows outwards, causing varicose veins.

q: Main mechanism of venous return from the leg?
why: Contracting calf muscles squeeze deep veins, and valves stop backflow, pumping blood towards the heart.

q: Name the boundaries of the femoral triangle.
why: The femoral triangle lies between the inguinal ligament (above), sartorius (lateral) and adductor longus (medial).

q: Order of femoral structures, lateral to medial?
why: From lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, then lymphatics in the femoral canal (NAVY); the nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

q: Continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee?
hint: Through the hiatus in adductor magnus.
why: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery behind the knee.

q: Name the anastomosis around the hip.
why: The cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses connect branches of the internal iliac and femoral arteries, providing collateral flow around the hip.

q: Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse felt?
model: Lateral to the EHL tendon on the dorsum of the foot.
hint: Next to the big toe's extensor tendon.
why: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

q: Where is the posterior tibial pulse felt?
why: The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, where it can be felt.

q: Nodes enlarged by a melanoma on the heel?
model: Popliteal (lateral heel) or superficial inguinal nodes.
why: The lateral heel drains with the small saphenous vein to the popliteal nodes; most of the foot drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

q: Line disrupted on a pelvis X-ray in a neck of femur fracture?
why: Shenton's line runs along the inferior femoral neck and the superior pubic ramus; a break suggests a displaced neck of femur fracture.

q: Name a symptom of left heart failure.
hint: Worse lying flat or at night.
why: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing breathlessness that's worse lying flat (orthopnoea) or waking the patient at night (PND).

q: Heart sound in heart failure?
why: An S3 is rapid filling into a stiff or overloaded ventricle in early diastole; in adults over 40 it suggests heart failure.

q: First blood test in suspected chronic heart failure?
why: NT-proBNP is released when ventricles are stretched; a normal level makes heart failure unlikely, and high levels prompt urgent echo.

q: Investigation that confirms heart failure?
hint: A bedside scan that measures ejection fraction.
why: Echo shows ejection fraction, valve disease and structure, confirming the type of heart failure and guiding treatment.

q: EF cut-off for HFrEF?
hint: The same as the lower bound of "mildly reduced".
why: HFrEF is EF 40% or below, the group with proven mortality benefit from ACEi/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i.

q: Mechanism of sacubitril?
hint: Stops natriuretic peptides being broken down.
why: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, which breaks down natriuretic peptides; higher levels cause vasodilation and natriuresis.

q: How long must ACEi be stopped before sacubitril/valsartan?
why: Neprilysin also breaks down bradykinin, so combining sacubitril with an ACE inhibitor greatly raises angioedema risk; a 36-hour washout is needed.

q: Name an SGLT2 inhibitor used in heart failure.
why: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin reduce death and heart failure admissions in heart failure, with or without diabetes.

q: Which drug treats congestion but doesn't improve survival?
why: Loop diuretics relieve fluid overload and symptoms but haven't been shown to improve survival.

q: Name a non-drug measure in heart failure.
acc: weight / salt / fluid / rehab / vaccin / smoking / exercise
model: Daily weights, rehab, flu/pneumococcal vaccines, salt advice, smoking cessation.
why: Daily weights catch fluid build-up early; cardiac rehab, vaccinations, salt advice and smoking cessation improve outcomes.

q: Name a neurohormonal system activated in heart failure.
model: RAAS and the sympathetic nervous system.
why: Low cardiac output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system, which retain salt and water and constrict vessels; useful short term, harmful long term, which is why blocking them helps.

q: Which law links ventricular size to wall stress?
why: Laplace: wall stress is proportional to pressure × radius ÷ wall thickness.

q: Why does dilation worsen function?
model: Higher wall stress raises oxygen demand.
hint: A bigger radius means more tension.
why: A dilated ventricle has a bigger radius, so wall stress and oxygen demand rise, worsening ischaemia and remodelling.

q: Name a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure.
why: Bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol reduce mortality in HFrEF by blocking harmful sympathetic activation; start low and increase slowly.

q: Drug added for HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥75 despite β-blocker?
why: Ivabradine blocks the funny current in the SA node, lowering heart rate without lowering blood pressure, only in sinus rhythm.

q: Device for HFrEF with LBBB and wide QRS?
why: In LBBB the ventricles contract out of sync; biventricular pacing (CRT) resynchronises them, improving output and survival.

q: Name a surgical option in heart failure.
acc: cabg / valve / lvad / transplant / crt / icd
why: Revascularisation (CABG), valve repair or replacement, ventricular assist devices and transplant treat underlying causes or support failing hearts.

q: Type of joint at the inferior tibiofibular joint?
why: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis held by strong ligaments; injury (high ankle sprain) widens the ankle mortise.

q: Name a superficial calf muscle.
why: The superficial calf muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris) join to form the Achilles tendon and plantarflex the foot.

q: Nerve of the anterior compartment of the leg?
hint: A branch of the common fibular.
why: The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior compartment muscles (dorsiflexors) and the skin between the first and second toes.

q: Commonest compartment for compartment syndrome in the leg?
why: The anterior compartment has tight fascia and bone boundaries, so swelling after tibial fractures raises pressure quickly.

q: Which ankle ligament is most often sprained?
why: Inversion injuries in plantarflexion stress the anterior talofibular ligament first, as it is the weakest lateral ligament.

q: Medial ankle ligament?
why: The deltoid ligament is a strong fan-shaped ligament on the medial side that resists eversion.

q: Main dorsiflexor of the ankle?
hint: The muscle at the front of the shin.
why: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot; weakness causes foot drop.

q: Which ankle position is least stable?
why: The talus is wider at the front, so it fits tightly in dorsiflexion but loosely in plantarflexion, making sprains likelier then.

q: Ligament supporting the medial longitudinal arch?
hint: Runs from the calcaneus to the navicular.
why: The spring ligament supports the head of the talus, holding up the medial arch; failure contributes to flat foot.

q: Main evertors of the foot?
why: Fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment evert the foot.

q: Nerve to the evertors?
why: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the lateral compartment (evertors) and most of the dorsum of the foot.

q: The medial plantar nerve is equivalent to which hand nerve?
why: Like the median nerve in the hand, the medial plantar nerve supplies a few intrinsic muscles and sensation to the medial 3½ digits.

q: The lateral plantar nerve is equivalent to which hand nerve?
why: Like the ulnar nerve, the lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic foot muscles and the lateral 1½ digits.

q: Heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning?
why: Plantar fasciitis is degeneration of the plantar fascia at its calcaneal attachment; pain is worst with the first steps after rest.

q: How many layers of muscle are in the sole?
why: The sole has four layers of muscles, from superficial (abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis) to deep (interossei).

q: Most effective first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding?
why: The LNG-IUS releases progestogen locally, thinning the endometrium; it reduces blood loss more than other medical options and lasts years.

q: Mechanism of tranexamic acid?
why: Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen activation, reducing breakdown of clots in the endometrium and cutting menstrual blood loss.

q: Blood test confirming ovulation?
why: Progesterone made by the corpus luteum peaks about 7 days before the period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle); a high level confirms ovulation.

q: Test of tubal patency?
why: HSG or HyCoSy pushes contrast through the uterus and tubes; spillage into the pelvis shows patency.

q: First-line drug for ovulation induction in PCOS?
why: Letrozole blocks oestrogen synthesis, increasing FSH to stimulate follicles; it gives higher live birth rates than clomifene in PCOS.

q: Pain, bleeding and a positive test with an empty uterus: suspect?
why: A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound suggests an ectopic, which can rupture and bleed.

q: Drug used for medical management of ectopic pregnancy?
why: Methotrexate stops trophoblast cells dividing (it's a folate antagonist), so a small, unruptured ectopic resolves without surgery.

q: Hormone that makes fibroids grow?
why: Fibroids are oestrogen-sensitive: they grow in pregnancy and shrink after menopause; GnRH agonists shrink them before surgery.

q: Fibroid surgery that preserves fertility?
why: Myomectomy removes fibroids while keeping the uterus, so fertility is preserved.

q: Commonest ovarian tumour in young women at risk of torsion?
why: Mature cystic teratomas contain hair, fat and teeth; they're heavy, which makes torsion likely.

q: Tumour marker in the RMI?
hint: A serum marker of ovarian cancer.
why: The RMI multiplies ultrasound features, menopausal status and CA-125 to estimate cancer risk and decide referral.

q: Commonest bacterial STI in the UK?
why: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI, often asymptomatic, which is why young people are screened.

q: Treatment of gonorrhoea?
why: Gonorrhoea has developed resistance to many antibiotics, so a single high dose of IM ceftriaxone is used, with a test of cure.

q: Treatment of uncomplicated chlamydia?
why: A week of doxycycline cures chlamydia more reliably than single-dose azithromycin.

q: Which body regulates IVF in the UK?
why: The Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority licenses and regulates fertility clinics and embryo research.

q: Muscles forming the pelvic floor?
hint: One big sheet plus a small posterior muscle.
why: Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus form the pelvic diaphragm that supports the pelvic organs.

q: Name the screening criteria.
why: Wilson and Jungner's criteria (1968) set out when screening is worthwhile: an important condition, a suitable test, an early stage and effective treatment.

q: First test in cervical screening?
why: Persistent high-risk HPV causes nearly all cervical cancer, so HPV is tested first; only HPV-positive samples go on to cytology.

q: What is the age range for breast screening in Wales?
hint: Every three years in middle age.
why: Breast Test Wales invites women aged 50–70 every three years for mammography.

q: Leading cause of infant death in the UK?
why: Most infant deaths in the UK follow preterm birth and congenital anomalies, ahead of infection and SIDS.

q: Menopause is diagnosed after how long without periods?
why: Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without periods, reflecting loss of ovarian follicles.

q: Name a vasomotor symptom.
why: Falling oestrogen unsettles the hypothalamic thermostat, causing hot flushes and night sweats.

q: Premature ovarian insufficiency is menopause before what age?
why: Menopause before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency; it needs hormone replacement to protect bones and heart.

q: Name a cause of premature ovarian insufficiency.
acc: chemo / radiotherapy / oophorectomy / surgery / autoimmune / turner / fragile x / idiopathic
model: Idiopathic, chemo/radiotherapy, surgery, autoimmune, Turner, fragile X.
why: POI can follow chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery, or be autoimmune or genetic (Turner, fragile X premutation); many cases are unexplained.

q: Name a long-term health risk after menopause.
why: Oestrogen protects bone and blood vessels, so after menopause osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease become more common.

q: Why add a progestogen to HRT in women with a uterus?
model: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
why: Oestrogen alone stimulates the endometrium, risking hyperplasia and cancer; a progestogen protects it in women with a uterus.

q: Which HRT route doesn't increase VTE risk?
why: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first-pass liver metabolism, so it doesn't raise clotting factors or VTE risk like oral oestrogen.

q: Name a contraindication to HRT.
acc: breast cancer / oestrogen-dependent / undiagnosed bleeding / vte / liver / pregnancy
model: Breast cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active VTE, liver disease, pregnancy.
why: Hormone-sensitive cancers, undiagnosed bleeding, active VTE and liver disease can be worsened by HRT, so it's avoided in them.

q: Name a psychological symptom of menopause.
acc: low mood / anxiety / irritab / brain fog / memory / concentration / sleep
model: Low mood, anxiety, irritability, brain fog.
why: Fluctuating oestrogen affects mood and cognition, causing low mood, anxiety, irritability and "brain fog".

q: Name a key question in a gynae history.
acc: lmp / cycle / intermenstrual / postcoital / postmenopausal / smear / screening / contraception / obstetric
model: LMP, cycle, IMB/PCB/PMB, smear history, contraception, obstetric history.
why: Menstrual history (LMP, cycle, abnormal bleeding), screening history, contraception and obstetric history narrow the differential.

q: Which speculum is used for routine cervical visualisation?
why: Cusco's bivalve speculum holds the vaginal walls apart to show the cervix for smears and inspection.

q: Framework for structured handover?
why: SBAR structures handover (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) so information isn't lost.

q: Unilateral pelvic pain + positive pregnancy test: what must you exclude first?
why: An ectopic pregnancy can rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding, so it's excluded first with ultrasound and serum hCG.

q: Organisms usually causing PID?
why: PID is usually ascending infection by chlamydia or gonorrhoea, often with anaerobes, which is why treatment covers all three.

q: Name a long-term complication of PID.
model: Infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.
why: Tubal scarring after PID causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain; risk rises with each episode.

q: Perihepatitis in PID?
why: Infection spreads to the liver capsule, causing right upper quadrant pain and "violin-string" adhesions (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis).

q: Outpatient PID regimen (BASHH)?
model: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days.
hint: An IM injection plus two oral drugs for 14 days.
why: Ceftriaxone covers gonorrhoea, doxycycline covers chlamydia and metronidazole covers anaerobes; 14 days treats upper genital tract infection.

q: Device for endometrial biopsy in clinic?
why: A pipelle is a thin flexible tube that sucks out an endometrial sample in clinic, without anaesthesia.

q: Speculum used to examine prolapse?
why: A Sims speculum retracts one vaginal wall at a time, so the opposite wall can be inspected for prolapse.

q: Instrument for an assisted vaginal birth with suction?
why: A ventouse applies a suction cup to the baby's head to help delivery; forceps grip the head instead.

q: Name a differential for pelvic pain in a woman of reproductive age.
acc: ectopic / pid / endometriosis / ovarian torsion / cyst / appendicitis / uti
model: Ectopic, PID, endometriosis, torsion, ruptured cyst, appendicitis.
why: Gynaecological (ectopic, PID, endometriosis, torsion, cysts) and surgical (appendicitis) causes overlap, so pregnancy testing and imaging are key.

q: Loading dose of aspirin in STEMI?
why: 300 mg of aspirin gives rapid, near-complete platelet inhibition in acute coronary syndromes.

q: How long is dual antiplatelet therapy given after MI?
why: Dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months after MI prevents stent thrombosis and recurrent events, balanced against bleeding.

q: Statin and dose after MI?
why: High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg lowers LDL and stabilises plaques after ACS, reducing further events.

q: Antidepressant of choice after MI?
hint: The SSRI from the SADHART trial.
why: Sertraline is safe after MI: no significant QT effect or hypotension, and the SADHART trial showed it was safe in cardiac patients.

q: Antidepressant class to avoid after MI?
why: Tricyclics prolong QRS and QT, cause arrhythmias and postural hypotension, so they're avoided after MI.

q: Name a discharge advice point after MI.
acc: driving / dvla / rehab / gtn / smoking / sex / work
model: Driving rules, cardiac rehab, GTN use, smoking cessation, return to work.
hint: What they can and can't do in the next few weeks.
why: After MI, patients need advice on driving (DVLA rules), cardiac rehab, GTN use, smoking cessation and returning to work and exercise.

q: A neck lump that moves with tongue protrusion?
why: A thyroglossal cyst is a remnant of the duct the thyroid travelled down, still tethered to the tongue base, so it rises when the tongue is stuck out.

q: Eye sign specific to Graves' disease?
why: Thyroid eye disease (exophthalmos, lid retraction) is caused by TSH-receptor antibodies acting on orbital tissue, so it's specific to Graves'.

q: How do you show a goitre moves on swallowing?
model: Ask the patient to swallow water.
why: The thyroid is wrapped in pretracheal fascia attached to the larynx, so it moves up with swallowing.

q: Line separating the greater and lesser pelvis?
acc: pelvic brim / linea terminalis / pelvic inlet
why: The pelvic brim (linea terminalis) separates the greater (false) pelvis above from the lesser (true) pelvis below.

q: Name a palpable pelvic landmark.
acc: asis / iliac crest / pubic tubercle / ischial tuberosity / psis / pubic symphysis
model: ASIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle, ischial tuberosity, PSIS.
why: Palpable landmarks (ASIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle, ischial tuberosity, PSIS) guide examination and procedures.

q: Which ligaments create the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
why: Sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.

q: Type of joint at the pubic symphysis?
why: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilage disc; it loosens slightly in pregnancy.

q: Name a boundary of the pelvic outlet.
acc: ischial tuberosit / coccyx / pubic arch / sacrotuberous / pubic symphysis
model: Pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, coccyx.
why: The outlet is diamond-shaped: pubic symphysis at the front, ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities at the sides, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx at the back.

q: Female pelvis subpubic angle compared with male?
why: A wider subpubic angle (about 90°) and rounder inlet give more room for the baby's head during birth.

q: The perineum divides into which two triangles?
why: A line between the ischial tuberosities divides the diamond-shaped perineum into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.

q: Main nerve supplying the pelvic floor?
acc: pudendal / s4 / nerve to levator ani
model: S4 (nerve to levator ani) and pudendal nerve.
why: The nerve to levator ani (S4) supplies the muscle from above and the pudendal nerve (S2–4) from below.

q: From which structure does levator ani arise laterally?
acc: tendinous arch / obturator fascia / arcus tendineus
model: Tendinous arch of the obturator fascia.
hint: A thickening of the obturator internus fascia.
why: Iliococcygeus arises from the tendinous arch, a thickening of obturator internus fascia on the pelvic side wall.

q: Name a structure passing through the female pelvic floor.
why: In women the urethra, vagina and anal canal pass through the pelvic floor, which is why childbirth can weaken it.

q: What is the perineal body?
model: The central tendon of the perineum.
hint: A central meeting point for muscles.
why: The perineal body is a fibromuscular node where perineal muscles meet; it's important for pelvic floor support and is cut in an episiotomy.

q: Which structure passes under the uterine artery?
why: The ureter runs under the uterine artery near the cervix ("water under the bridge"), so it's at risk of being clamped during hysterectomy.

q: Origin of the ovarian artery?
why: The ovarian arteries come straight off the abdominal aorta because the gonads develop high up and descend.

q: Pudendal nerve roots?
hint: The same roots as the pelvic splanchnics.
why: The pudendal nerve arises from S2–4 and supplies the perineum, external sphincters and genitalia.

q: Landmark for a pudendal nerve block?
why: The pudendal nerve passes around the ischial spine, which can be felt vaginally, so local anaesthetic is injected there.

q: Function of Bartholin's glands?
why: Bartholin's glands secrete mucus to lubricate the vulva; a blocked duct forms a cyst or abscess at 4 or 8 o'clock.

q: Lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity?
why: The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity, so fluid, blood or pus collects there.

q: Lymph drainage of the ovaries?
why: Ovarian lymph follows the ovarian vessels up to the para-aortic nodes, because the ovaries developed near the kidneys.

q: Lymph drainage of the vulva?
why: The vulva drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so vulval cancers spread to the groin.

q: First imaging for most pelvic gynae pathology?
why: Transvaginal ultrasound gives detailed views of the uterus and ovaries without radiation, so it's the first test for most pelvic problems.

q: Name a cause of haemoptysis.
acc: lung cancer / cancer / tb / tuberculosis / pe / bronchiectasis / pneumonia / vasculitis / mitral stenosis
model: Lung cancer, TB, PE, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, vasculitis.
why: Haemoptysis can come from infection (pneumonia, TB), bronchiectasis, cancer, PE or vasculitis; age, smoking and travel history narrow it.

q: How do you position a patient with massive haemoptysis?
why: Lying on the bleeding side keeps blood out of the healthy lung, protecting gas exchange while the source is treated.

q: Wells score at which PE is "likely"?
why: A Wells score over 4 makes PE likely, so go straight to CTPA; 4 or below, check a D-dimer first.

q: Imaging for suspected PE?
why: CT pulmonary angiography shows clots in the pulmonary arteries directly; V/Q scanning is used if contrast is contraindicated.

q: Commonest ECG finding in PE?
why: Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding in PE; the classic S1Q3T3 pattern is uncommon.

q: Commonest inherited thrombophilia?
why: Factor V Leiden resists inactivation by activated protein C, so clotting continues, raising VTE risk.

q: Name a VTE risk factor.
acc: surgery / immobility / cancer / pregnancy / pill / cocp / hrt / previous / obesity / travel
model: Surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogens, previous VTE.
why: Surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogens and previous VTE all act through Virchow's triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability).

q: How do DVTs reach the lung?
acc: ivc / right heart / venous / vena cava
model: Via the venous return (IVC) through the right heart.
hint: Through the right side of the heart.
why: A DVT breaks off, travels up the IVC, through the right heart and into the pulmonary arteries.

q: Mean PAP threshold for pulmonary hypertension?
why: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg at rest (lowered from 25 in 2022).

q: Mechanism of pulmonary hypertension in chronic lung disease?
why: Alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles to match perfusion to ventilation; when chronic, the vessel walls thicken and pressure rises.

q: Right heart failure caused by lung disease?
why: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular failure from lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, causing raised JVP and oedema.

q: Name a drug class for pulmonary arterial hypertension.
acc: endothelin / bosentan / ambrisentan / pde5 / sildenafil / prostacyclin / prostanoid / epoprostenol
why: PAH treatments target three pathways: block endothelin, boost nitric oxide (PDE5 inhibitors) and add prostacyclin.

q: Treatment of massive PE with shock?
why: Massive PE with shock causes right heart failure, so the clot is broken down quickly with thrombolysis.

q: Minimum anticoagulation for a provoked PE?
why: A provoked PE (e.g. after surgery) has low recurrence risk once the trigger is gone, so 3 months is usually enough.

q: Anticoagulant in antiphospholipid syndrome?
why: DOACs perform worse than warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome (especially high risk), so warfarin is used.

q: Name the three steps of Very Brief Advice.
why: Very Brief Advice: Ask about smoking, Advise that the best way to stop is medication plus support, and Act by referring or prescribing.

q: Mechanism of varenicline?
why: Varenicline partially activates nicotinic receptors to ease cravings and blocks nicotine from binding, reducing the reward from smoking.

q: Who sets "Outcomes for graduates"?
why: The GMC's "Outcomes for graduates" sets what newly qualified doctors must know and be able to do.

q: Which of the four ethical principles concerns fair distribution of resources?
why: Justice is about fair distribution of resources and treating people equally.

q: What should you do at the limits of your competence?
why: Patient safety requires recognising your limits and asking for help early.

q: Name a protected characteristic (Equality Act).
acc: age / disability / gender reassignment / marriage / pregnancy / race / religion / sex / sexual orientation
model: Age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, pregnancy, marriage.
why: The Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics, including age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, pregnancy and marriage.

q: FEV1/FVC ratio diagnostic of COPD?
why: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 shows persistent airflow obstruction, confirming COPD.

q: COPD in a young non-smoker suggests?
why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes, even without much smoking.

q: What does OARS stand for in MI?
why: OARS (open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries) are the core skills of motivational interviewing.

q: Low pH, high PaCO₂, normal HCO₃⁻?
why: High CO₂ with low pH and normal bicarbonate means acute respiratory acidosis; the kidneys haven't had time to compensate.

q: Low PaO₂, low PaCO₂ in an asthmatic?
why: A low PaO₂ with low CO₂ means type 1 failure; the patient is hyperventilating, typical of acute asthma before they tire.

q: Name a key symptom in a cardiorespiratory history.
acc: chest pain / breathless / cough / haemoptysis / palpitations / wheeze / orthopnoea / syncope / oedema
model: Chest pain, breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis, palpitations, syncope.
why: Chest pain, breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis, palpitations and syncope are the core cardiorespiratory symptoms to explore.

q: Pleural plaques suggest exposure to?
why: Pleural plaques are benign markers of asbestos exposure, common in shipyard, construction and insulation workers.

q: Farmer's lung is which type of disease?
acc: hypersensitivity pneumonitis / extrinsic allergic alveolitis / eaa
why: Inhaled antigens from mouldy hay trigger a hypersensitivity reaction in the alveoli (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

q: Name a sign of right heart strain on examination.
acc: raised jvp / jvp / parasternal heave / rv heave / loud p2 / oedema
model: Raised JVP, RV heave, loud P2, peripheral oedema.
why: Pulmonary hypertension strains the right ventricle: raised JVP, a parasternal heave, a loud P2 and peripheral oedema.

q: How can a venous clot cause a stroke?
acc: paradoxical / pfo / patent foramen ovale / asd
why: A venous clot can pass through a patent foramen ovale from right to left atrium and reach the brain (paradoxical embolism).

q: Why are bronchopulmonary segments surgically important?
model: Each has its own bronchus and artery: resectable alone.
why: Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own bronchus and artery, so it can be removed without affecting neighbouring segments.

q: How many segments in the right lung?
why: The right lung has 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left has 8–10, depending on how they're counted.

q: Where does the pulmonary trunk divide?
acc: t4 / t5 / sternal angle / under the aortic arch / concavity
model: Under the aortic arch, at about T4–5.
hint: The same level as the second costal cartilage.
why: The pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries under the aortic arch, at about T4–5 (the level of the sternal angle).

q: Name the two blood supplies of the lung.
hint: One for gas exchange, one systemic.
why: The pulmonary circulation brings blood for gas exchange; the bronchial circulation (systemic) supplies the airways and lung tissue.

q: Bronchial arteries usually arise from?
why: Bronchial arteries usually arise from the descending thoracic aorta, so they carry blood at systemic pressure.

q: Which circulation causes most massive haemoptysis?
why: Bronchial arteries are at systemic pressure, so when they bleed (e.g. in bronchiectasis or TB) bleeding can be massive; they can be embolised.

q: Name the three parts of Virchow's triad.
why: Virchow's triad: stasis (immobility), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma) and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, thrombophilia).

q: Embolus type after a long bone fracture?
why: Fat from marrow enters veins after long bone fractures, causing fat embolism syndrome (hypoxia, confusion, petechial rash).

q: Name a non-thrombotic embolus.
acc: fat / air / amniotic / tumour / septic / cholesterol / foreign
model: Fat, air, amniotic fluid, tumour, septic.
why: Emboli can be fat, air, amniotic fluid, tumour or septic material, not just thrombus.

q: Which cells make surfactant?
acc: type ii / type 2 / pneumocyte ii / type two
why: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant and can divide to replace type I cells after injury.

q: Which cells line most of the alveolar surface?
why: Type I pneumocytes are thin and flat, covering about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange.

q: What term describes the combined physical, psychological, social and spiritual suffering behind a patient's pain?
hint: Coined by the founder of the hospice movement.
why: Cicely Saunders, founder of the modern hospice movement, described how pain is made worse by fear, isolation, money worries and spiritual distress, so treating only the physical cause often fails.

q: Does palliative care aim to hasten or postpone death?
model: Neither: it aims to improve quality of life.
hint: Its goal is quality of life.
why: The WHO definition says palliative care affirms life, regards dying as normal and neither hastens nor postpones death, focusing on symptom relief and support.

q: Which enzyme converts codeine into morphine?
why: Codeine is a prodrug; poor CYP2D6 metabolisers get little pain relief, while ultra-rapid metabolisers can get morphine toxicity, which is why codeine is avoided in under-12s and breastfeeding mothers.

q: Which weak opioid can cause serotonin syndrome and seizures?
hint: A step-2 drug with antidepressant-like actions.
why: Tramadol also inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, so it lowers the seizure threshold and can cause serotonin syndrome, especially with SSRIs.

q: What must be co-prescribed with a regular strong opioid?
why: Opioid-induced constipation affects almost everyone on regular opioids and doesn't wear off, unlike nausea and drowsiness.

q: Name a sign of opioid toxicity.
acc: myoclonus / pinpoint / drowsiness / confusion / hallucination / respiratory depression / slow breathing
model: Drowsiness, confusion, hallucinations, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.
why: Toxicity is more likely with rising doses, renal impairment (morphine metabolites accumulate) and dehydration.

q: Over what duration does pain become persistent (chronic)?
why: Pain persisting beyond normal tissue healing time (about 3 months) is classed as chronic, which changes the approach from finding a cause to managing function, mood and beliefs.

q: What is allodynia?
acc: light touch / non painful / not normally painful / innocuous
model: Pain from a stimulus that isn't normally painful (e.g. light touch).
why: Allodynia points to neuropathic pain and central sensitisation; screening tools such as DN4 ask about it.

q: Which pain scale is designed for people with dementia who can't report pain?
why: These observational scales score vocalisation, facial expression, body language, behaviour and physiological changes.

q: What is the "surprise question" in palliative care?
model: "Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?"
why: If the answer is no, the patient may benefit from palliative care input and advance care planning (Gold Standards Framework).

q: Name a non-cancer condition that benefits from palliative care.
acc: heart failure / copd / dementia / mnd / motor neurone / kidney / renal / liver / frailty / parkinson
model: Heart failure, COPD, dementia, MND, end-stage kidney or liver disease, frailty.
why: Palliative care is needed by anyone with a life-limiting illness, and non-cancer patients are often referred late or not at all.

q: Which nerve fibres carry fast, sharp, well-localised pain?
why: Thinly myelinated Aδ fibres carry "first pain"; unmyelinated C fibres carry slow, dull, burning "second pain".

q: Where in the brainstem does descending pain inhibition start?
why: The PAG projects to the rostral ventromedial medulla, which inhibits dorsal horn transmission using serotonin, noradrenaline and endogenous opioids; opioids act here.

q: Which receptor drives central sensitisation ("wind-up")?
why: Repeated C-fibre input activates NMDA receptors in the dorsal horn, amplifying pain; ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, can help resistant pain.

q: Which theory explains why rubbing a painful area helps?
why: Large Aβ touch fibres activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, "closing the gate" on nociceptive input; TENS uses the same principle.

q: Name a first-line drug for neuropathic pain (NICE).
hint: A tricyclic, an SNRI or an α2δ ligand.
why: NICE CG173 offers a choice of these four (except for trigeminal neuralgia, where carbamazepine is first line), switching if one doesn't work.

q: Which drug is first line for trigeminal neuralgia?
why: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pains in the V2/V3 territory triggered by touch, eating or wind; carbamazepine is very effective.

q: Name a drug class NICE says not to start for chronic primary pain.
acc: opioid / nsaid / paracetamol / gabapentinoid / benzodiazepine / gabapentin / pregabalin
model: Opioids, NSAIDs, paracetamol, gabapentinoids or benzodiazepines.
why: NICE NG193 found little evidence of benefit and real harm; exercise, CBT/ACT, acupuncture and some antidepressants are offered instead.

q: What fraction of the 24-hour opioid dose is the usual breakthrough dose?
hint: A small fraction of the daily total.
why: Breakthrough doses cover pain between regular doses; how many are used guides daily titration of the regular dose.

q: Which opioid is preferred in severe renal impairment?
why: Morphine's active metabolites (morphine-6- and -3-glucuronide) accumulate in renal failure, causing toxicity.

q: What is a typical starting dose of regular oral morphine for an opioid-naive palliative patient?
hint: Two or three tens per day.
why: NICE CG140 suggests e.g. MR morphine 10–15 mg twice daily with 5 mg immediate-release for breakthrough, then titrate.

q: Which drug treats pain from liver capsule stretch or raised intracranial pressure?
why: Steroids reduce oedema around tumours, relieving capsular pain, nerve compression and raised ICP headache.

q: Name the four domains of holistic palliative care.
why: Holistic care addresses the whole person and their family, including practical needs like finances and carers, and spiritual concerns about meaning and faith.

q: Who in the MDT usually provides spiritual support in hospital?
why: Chaplains support people of any faith or none with questions about meaning, fear and rituals at the end of life.

q: Which advance care planning document is legally binding in England and Wales?
model: An advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT).
why: A valid and applicable ADRT is legally binding; refusal of life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and say "even if my life is at risk". A statement of wishes is not binding.

q: Who can make health decisions for a patient who lacks capacity, if appointed in advance?
acc: lpa / lasting power of attorney / attorney
model: An attorney under a lasting power of attorney (health and welfare).
why: The LPA must be registered; the attorney can consent to or refuse life-sustaining treatment only if this is expressly stated.

q: Is a statement of wishes and preferences legally binding?
model: No, but it must be considered in best-interests decisions.
why: It records what matters to the person (e.g. preferred place of death) so decisions reflect their values.

q: Which antiemetic is first line for opioid- or metabolic-induced nausea?
hint: A D2 antagonist also used for delirium.
why: Chemical nausea acts on the chemoreceptor trigger zone (dopamine D2 receptors), which haloperidol blocks.

q: Which antiemetic should be avoided in complete bowel obstruction?
why: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic, so it can worsen colic and perforation risk in complete obstruction; cyclizine is used instead.

q: Which drug helps breathlessness in palliative care when the cause can't be reversed?
why: Opioids reduce the sensation of breathlessness; a fan, positioning and breathing techniques also help; oxygen only if hypoxic.

q: What dose of dexamethasone is given for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression?
why: High-dose steroids reduce cord oedema while urgent whole-spine MRI (within 24 h) and radiotherapy or surgery are arranged.

q: How is hypercalcaemia of malignancy treated?
model: IV fluids then an IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid).
hint: Rehydrate, then stop the bones releasing it.
why: Rehydration lowers calcium and restores renal excretion; bisphosphonates reduce osteoclastic bone resorption.

q: Which drug is used for terminal agitation?
why: Midazolam is a short-acting SC benzodiazepine used as an anticipatory medicine; look for reversible causes (urinary retention, pain) first.

q: Which anticipatory medicine treats noisy respiratory secretions in the last days?
why: Antimuscarinics reduce secretions; repositioning helps too; explain to relatives that the noise rarely distresses the patient.

q: Name a sign that a person may be entering the last days of life.
acc: bedbound / drowsy / sleep / swallow / intake / mottl / cheyne / breathing / peripheries
model: Bedbound, drowsier, reduced intake, unable to swallow tablets, changed breathing, mottled cool peripheries.
hint: Think eating, alertness and skin colour.
why: Recognising dying (NICE NG31) allows an individualised care plan, stopping unnecessary interventions and prescribing anticipatory medicines.

q: What are yellow flags in persistent pain?
acc: psychosocial / belief / fear / avoidance / mood / catastroph
model: Psychosocial factors predicting poor recovery (fear-avoidance, belief that pain means harm, low mood, catastrophising).
hint: Psychological rather than physical warning signs.
why: They predict long-term disability better than physical findings, so they are targets for psychological therapy.

q: Above what daily oral morphine equivalent does opioid harm rise without extra benefit in persistent pain?
why: "Opioids Aware" (Faculty of Pain Medicine) advises review and tapering when doses exceed this.

q: Name a spiritual need to ask about in end-of-life care.
acc: meaning / faith / religio / legacy / ritual / relationship / afraid / purpose
model: Meaning, faith and rituals, legacy, unresolved relationships, fears about dying.
why: Spiritual distress worsens pain and anxiety; asking "What gives you strength?" opens the conversation.

q: Which outcome tool assesses symptoms and concerns in palliative care?
why: It covers physical symptoms, emotional concerns, information needs and practical problems.

q: What are the four parts of the capacity test under the Mental Capacity Act?
model: Understand, retain, weigh up and communicate the decision.
why: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed unless shown otherwise; failing any one of the four means lacking capacity for that decision.

q: Who is appointed to represent a patient lacking capacity with nobody else to consult?
why: An IMCA must be involved for serious medical treatment decisions when there is no family or friend to consult.

q: Can relatives without an LPA make treatment decisions for a patient who lacks capacity?
model: No: they inform the best-interests decision, which the clinician makes.
hint: They are consulted, not decision makers.
why: Only a valid ADRT, a health and welfare attorney or a court deputy can make the decision; families are consulted about the patient's wishes and values.

q: What does NURSE stand for when responding to emotion?
why: NURSE statements show empathy, e.g. naming the emotion ("You seem frightened") and exploring it.

q: A daughter asks you not to tell her father he is dying. What should you do first?
why: Collusion usually comes from love and fear; then explain the patient's right to information and ask the patient how much they want to know.

q: What feature distinguishes inflammatory back pain from mechanical back pain?
acc: exercise / morning stiffness / better with activity
model: It improves with exercise and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>30 min).
why: Axial spondyloarthritis starts before 40, is insidious, worse with rest and wakes patients in the second half of the night.

q: Leg pain on walking relieved by sitting or bending forward suggests what?
why: Flexion widens the spinal canal; vascular claudication is relieved by standing still.

q: Name a red flag for cauda equina syndrome.
acc: saddle / retention / incontinence / bilateral sciatica / bladder / bowel / sexual
model: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, bilateral sciatica, sexual dysfunction.
hint: Think about the sphincters and the perineum.
why: It is a surgical emergency needing immediate MRI and decompression.

q: Which test is positive in L2–L4 nerve root irritation?
hint: Done with the patient lying face down.
why: With the patient prone, flexing the knee stretches the femoral nerve roots, causing anterior thigh pain; the SLR tests L5/S1.

q: Which reflex is reduced in an S1 radiculopathy?
why: S1 also causes weak plantarflexion and sensory loss on the lateral foot and sole.

q: What examination findings suggest cord compression rather than root compression?
acc: umn / upper motor / brisk / upgoing / sensory level / clonus
model: UMN signs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, clonus) and a sensory level.
why: Root compression causes LMN signs in one myotome and dermatome.

q: Is paracetamol alone recommended for low back pain (NICE)?
why: NICE NG59 found paracetamol alone ineffective; NSAIDs at the lowest dose for the shortest time are recommended, with exercise.

q: Which intervention is offered for acute, severe sciatica?
hint: An injection near the nerve root.
why: NICE considers it for acute severe sciatica; discectomy if pain persists with concordant MRI findings.

q: Which procedure treats chronic facet joint back pain after a positive diagnostic block?
why: Heat lesions the medial branch nerves supplying the facet joints.

q: Which Act classifies drugs into Classes A, B and C?
why: The Act sets penalties; the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 put drugs into Schedules for prescribing, storage and records.

q: Which Schedule includes morphine, oxycodone and fentanyl?
why: Schedule 2 CDs need full prescription requirements, safe custody and a CD register.

q: Which Schedule are gabapentin and pregabalin in?
why: They were reclassified in 2019 because of misuse; CD prescription requirements apply.

q: Which Schedule are benzodiazepines such as diazepam in?
why: Fewer controls: no CD prescription requirements, but the prescription is valid for 28 days.

q: How long is a Schedule 2 CD prescription valid for?
why: Good practice is to prescribe no more than 30 days' supply.

q: What must be written in both words and figures on a CD prescription?
model: The total quantity (or number of dose units).
why: e.g. "twenty-eight (28) tablets"; it prevents fraudulent alteration.

q: Is "as directed" acceptable as a CD dose?
why: The dose must be clearly stated; "one tablet twice daily" is acceptable.

q: How do you convert oral codeine to an equivalent oral morphine dose?
why: Codeine 240 mg/day ≈ 24 mg oral morphine per day.

q: How do you convert oral morphine to subcutaneous morphine?
why: SC morphine is about twice as potent as oral because it avoids first-pass metabolism.

q: How do you convert oral morphine to subcutaneous diamorphine?
hint: Diamorphine SC is three times as potent as oral morphine.
why: Diamorphine is very soluble, useful for large SC doses.

q: Why reduce the dose by 25–50% when switching to a different opioid?
why: A patient tolerant to one opioid may be more sensitive to another, risking toxicity.

q: A patient takes MR morphine 30 mg twice daily. What is the SC morphine dose over 24 hours?
why: 60 mg oral ÷ 2 = 30 mg SC; breakthrough SC dose 5 mg (one-sixth).

q: Over how long does a palliative syringe driver usually run?
why: Doses are prescribed as the total over 24 h, with separate PRN SC breakthrough doses.

q: Which diluent is usually used in a palliative syringe driver?
why: Some drugs (e.g. cyclizine) precipitate in sodium chloride; check compatibility.

q: Should a fentanyl patch be removed when a syringe driver is started?
why: It continues background analgesia; the driver adds for extra needs (take specialist advice).

q: What complications follow a "long lie" after a fall?
model: Rhabdomyolysis, pressure ulcers, hypothermia, dehydration, pneumonia.
why: Lying on the floor for over an hour is a marker of frailty; check CK and renal function.

q: Name a drug class that increases the risk of falls.
acc: benzodiazepine / sedative / antihypertensive / diuretic / antidepressant / antipsychotic / opioid / hypnotic / z drug
model: Sedatives (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs), antihypertensives, diuretics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids.
hint: Drugs that sedate or lower BP.
why: They cause drowsiness, postural hypotension or confusion; medication review is part of falls assessment.

q: What fall in systolic BP on standing defines postural hypotension?
model: 20 mmHg or more (or 10 mmHg diastolic) within 3 minutes.
why: Measure lying for 5 min then standing at 1 and 3 min.

q: What Timed Up and Go result suggests high falls risk?
why: Stand from a chair, walk 3 m, turn, walk back and sit.

q: Which blood test checks for muscle damage after a long lie?
why: Raised CK indicates rhabdomyolysis, which can cause AKI.

q: What DEXA T-score defines osteoporosis?
why: −1 to −2.5 is osteopenia; T-score compares to a young adult mean.

q: Which hormone loss after menopause speeds bone loss?
why: Oestrogen normally restrains RANKL-driven osteoclast activity.

q: How should alendronic acid be taken?
model: Once weekly, first thing on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, staying upright for 30 minutes.
why: Reduces oesophageal irritation and improves absorption.

q: Name a rare serious side effect of bisphosphonates.
model: Osteonecrosis of the jaw (or atypical femoral fractures).
why: Check dental health before starting; review treatment after about 5 years.

q: Why shouldn't denosumab be stopped suddenly?
model: Rebound bone loss with multiple vertebral fractures.
why: It's a 6-monthly anti-RANKL antibody; follow with a bisphosphonate if stopping.

q: Name a tool for estimating 10-year fracture risk.
why: They combine age, sex, BMI, previous fracture, steroids, smoking and alcohol.

q: By how much must creatinine rise within 48 hours to define AKI?
why: KDIGO/NICE: a rise of ≥26 µmol/L in 48 h, or ≥1.5 × baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 hours.

q: What urine output defines oliguria in AKI?
model: Less than 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours.
hint: Half a mL per kg per hour.
why: Accurate output needs a fluid balance chart, often a catheter in the critically ill.

q: What creatinine level automatically makes AKI stage 3?
why: Stage 3 is also ≥3 × baseline or needing renal replacement therapy.

q: What is the most common category of AKI?
why: Hypovolaemia, sepsis and drugs reducing perfusion cause most hospital AKI; prolonged pre-renal AKI can progress to acute tubular necrosis.

q: What does SADMANS stand for in sick day rules?
acc: sulfonylurea + ace + diuretic + metformin + arb / arbs / angiotensin receptor + nsaid + sglt2
model: Sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, Diuretics, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors.
why: These are paused during dehydrating illness to reduce AKI, hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis/ketoacidosis risk, then restarted 24–48 h after eating and drinking normally.

q: Name a patient risk factor for AKI.
acc: 65 / age / ckd / heart failure / diabetes / liver / sepsis / previous aki / cognitive / contrast
model: Age ≥65, CKD, heart failure, diabetes, liver disease, sepsis, previous AKI, cognitive impairment.
hint: Think birthdays and chronic organ disease.
why: NICE NG148 recommends assessing risk in anyone acutely unwell, with U&E monitoring and avoiding nephrotoxins.

q: Which protein do light chains precipitate with in myeloma cast nephropathy?
hint: Made by the thick ascending limb.
why: Casts form in the distal tubule, obstructing it and causing inflammation; dehydration, hypercalcaemia and contrast make it worse.

q: Why does a urine dipstick miss myeloma light chains?
hint: The dipstick is tuned to one protein.
why: Heavy light-chain proteinuria can give a negative dipstick, so send serum free light chains and urine for Bence Jones protein.

q: What does CRAB stand for in myeloma?
model: Calcium (raised), Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions.
why: These end-organ features define myeloma needing treatment.

q: Which urgent blood test best detects myeloma in unexplained AKI?
model: Serum free light chains (with protein electrophoresis).
why: A very high involved light chain with an abnormal kappa:lambda ratio suggests cast nephropathy; rapid chemotherapy can save kidney function.

q: Which arteriole does angiotensin II mainly constrict?
why: This maintains glomerular pressure and GFR when perfusion is low; ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove it, so GFR can fall in hypovolaemia or renal artery stenosis.

q: What rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor is acceptable?
why: A small rise reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure (the protective effect); more suggests renal artery stenosis or hypovolaemia.

q: How do ACE inhibitors slow progression of proteinuric CKD?
model: They lower intraglomerular pressure, reducing proteinuria, hyperfiltration and fibrosis.
hint: Think about the force on the filter.
why: Angiotensin II and aldosterone drive glomerular hypertension and TGF-β-mediated scarring.

q: What urinary casts suggest acute tubular necrosis?
why: Red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis; white cell casts suggest interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.

q: What urinary finding suggests glomerulonephritis?
model: Blood and protein on dipstick (red cell casts on microscopy).
why: GN needs urgent immunology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement) and nephrology referral.

q: When should a renal ultrasound be done in AKI with suspected obstruction?
why: Hydronephrosis needs urgent decompression (catheter, nephrostomy or stent); pyonephrosis within 6 hours.

q: Which blood test identifies rhabdomyolysis as the cause of AKI?
why: Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin, which is toxic to tubules; treat with aggressive IV fluids.

q: Why is eGFR unreliable in AKI?
why: In AKI, creatinine lags behind the real fall in GFR.

q: Name a drug that causes acute interstitial nephritis.
acc: ppi / omeprazole / lansoprazole / penicillin / nsaid / rifampicin / amoxicillin
why: An allergic reaction in the interstitium, sometimes with rash, fever and eosinophilia; stop the drug, consider steroids.

q: Name a drug that causes acute tubular necrosis.
acc: gentamicin / aminoglycoside / vancomycin / contrast / amphotericin / cisplatin
model: Gentamicin, vancomycin, IV contrast, amphotericin, cisplatin.
why: Direct tubular toxicity; aminoglycoside levels must be monitored.

q: Below what eGFR should metformin be stopped?
why: Risk of lactic acidosis; review the dose below 45 and stop during AKI.

q: Below what eGFR should nitrofurantoin be avoided?
why: It's ineffective (low urine levels) and toxic (neuropathy) in poor renal function.

q: What does the STOP approach to AKI stand for?
model: Sepsis, Toxins, Optimise volume and BP, Prevent harm.
why: Treat infection, stop nephrotoxins, fluid-resuscitate and treat complications such as hyperkalaemia.

q: Name an indication for emergency dialysis in AKI.
acc: acidosis / hyperkalaemia / potassium / overload / pulmonary oedema / uraemi / pericarditis / encephalopathy / lithium / intoxication
model: Refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia or pulmonary oedema; uraemic pericarditis or encephalopathy; dialysable toxins.
why: Remembered as AEIOU.

q: What fluid bolus is given in hypovolaemic AKI?
why: Repeat boluses guided by response; beware fluid overload in heart failure and oliguria.

q: What does a high urea out of proportion to creatinine suggest?
acc: pre renal / prerenal / dehydration / gi bleed / upper gi / bleed
model: Pre-renal AKI (dehydration) or an upper GI bleed.
hint: Think fluid status and the gut.
why: Urea is reabsorbed more in low-flow states and rises with digested blood protein.

q: What is a common cause of spurious hyperkalaemia?
why: Red cells release potassium; also delayed processing and very high white cells or platelets. Repeat if no clear cause or ECG changes.

q: What is the normal serum potassium range?
why: Both high and low potassium cause arrhythmias.

q: Low sodium with high potassium and hypotension suggests what?
why: Loss of aldosterone causes sodium loss and potassium retention; check a 9 am cortisol or short Synacthen test.

q: Hypertension with low potassium suggests what?
why: Excess aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium; check aldosterone:renin ratio.

q: Name a cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia.
model: SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, psychogenic polydipsia.
why: Assess volume status first to classify hyponatraemia.

q: Which antibiotic can raise potassium?
why: It blocks ENaC in the collecting duct like amiloride.

q: Name a drug class causing hypokalaemia.
acc: loop / thiazide / diuretic / salbutamol / beta agonist / insulin / steroid
model: Loop and thiazide diuretics (also salbutamol, insulin, steroids).
why: Diuretics increase distal sodium delivery and potassium excretion.

q: What is given first in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?
why: Calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes but doesn't lower potassium.

q: How does insulin lower potassium?
model: It shifts potassium into cells (via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase).
hint: Moves it rather than removes it.
why: Given with glucose (10 units with 25 g); monitor for hypoglycaemia.

q: What is the maximum safe rate of peripheral IV potassium?
why: Faster rates risk arrhythmias and need cardiac monitoring (central line).

q: What is the maximum sodium rise in 24 hours when correcting chronic hyponatraemia?
why: Faster correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.

q: What is the first-line treatment for SIADH?
why: Tolvaptan is a specialist option; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms.

q: How many rescue breaths are given in paediatric BLS?
why: Paediatric arrests are usually hypoxic, so ventilation comes first.

q: What head position opens an infant's airway?
why: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck; over-extension can obstruct the soft trachea. Older children: "sniffing" position.

q: What is a normal heart rate for an infant under 1?
why: Normal ranges fall with age; tachycardia is an early sign of shock.

q: What is the APLS weight estimate for a child aged 1–5?
why: Used for drug and fluid doses when weight is unknown.

q: What is the fluid bolus for a shocked child?
why: Reassess after each bolus; overload is a risk.

q: Where should the leader of a resuscitation team ideally stand?
acc: back / foot / end / not hands on
model: Back from the patient (e.g. at the foot of the bed), hands off.
why: Keeping an overview lets the leader plan, allocate tasks and summarise.

q: Name a role that nurses especially lead in recognising a deteriorating child.
why: Nurses spend the most time with patients and often notice deterioration first.

q: What does CUS stand for in speaking up?
why: Graded assertiveness lets any team member raise concerns.

q: Should "units" be abbreviated on a drug chart?
why: "U" can be misread as zero, causing tenfold overdoses (insulin, heparin).

q: How should 5 milligrams be written to avoid errors?
why: "5.0 mg" can be misread as 50 mg; but write leading zeros, e.g. 0.5 mg.

q: What must every PRN prescription include besides drug, dose and route?
model: Indication, minimum interval and maximum dose in 24 hours.
hint: How often and how much at most.
why: Prevents overdose from repeated administration.

q: What is the Cockcroft–Gault constant for men?
why: CrCl = (140 − age) × weight × 1.23 ÷ creatinine; women use 1.04.

q: Calculate CrCl: man, 70 years, 70 kg, creatinine 120 µmol/L.
When should creatinine clearance be used rather than eGFR?
model: For dosing renally cleared or narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (e.g. DOACs, gentamicin).
why: Drug trials used CrCl; eGFR is for CKD staging.

q: Which reference gives detailed drug dosing in renal impairment and dialysis?
why: Also the BNF renal impairment sections and pharmacists.

q: What must be taken before giving antibiotics in urosepsis?
why: Don't delay antibiotics beyond 1 hour; cultures guide later narrowing.

q: Which IV antibiotic often used in urosepsis needs levels and caution in AKI?
why: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic; dose by weight and CrCl and check levels.

q: Which antibiotic class is used for urosepsis with a previous ESBL organism?
why: ESBL-producing organisms resist most penicillins and cephalosporins.

q: Why is a renal ultrasound urgent in urosepsis?
model: To find obstruction (an infected obstructed kidney needs drainage).
why: Antibiotics alone fail without source control (nephrostomy or stent).

q: Why are close contacts of meningococcal disease given antibiotics?
model: To eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent secondary cases.
hint: The bacteria live in the throat of contacts.
why: Close contacts share the invasive strain and have a much higher risk, mostly in the first 7 days.

q: When should suspected meningococcal disease be notified to public health?
model: On clinical suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.
why: Early notification lets the health protection team trace contacts and give prophylaxis quickly.

q: Which antibiotic is first choice for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis?
why: It is suitable for all ages and in pregnancy; rifampicin is an alternative but interacts with the pill and turns secretions orange.

q: Over what period before onset must contact have occurred for prophylaxis to be offered?
model: The 7 days before the case's onset.
why: Household and intimate kissing contacts in that window are offered prophylaxis.

q: Are classroom contacts routinely given meningococcal prophylaxis?
model: No (unless the health protection team identifies a cluster).
why: Their risk is only slightly raised compared with household contacts.

q: Which side effect of rifampicin should contacts be warned about?
model: Orange-red urine, tears and stained contact lenses; reduced contraceptive pill effectiveness.
why: Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer.

q: What clinical feature distinguishes encephalitis from meningitis?
acc: altered mental / confusion / behaviour / consciousness / personality
model: Altered mental state (confusion, behaviour change, reduced consciousness).
hint: Brain function, not just the coverings.
why: Encephalitis involves the brain tissue itself; meningitis causes headache, neck stiffness and photophobia with preserved cognition early on.

q: Which imaging is best for suspected encephalitis?
why: CT is often normal early; MRI shows temporal lobe changes in HSV and other patterns.

q: What CSF white cell type predominates in viral encephalitis?
why: Bacterial meningitis gives neutrophils; very early viral CSF may show neutrophils.

q: Is CSF glucose low in viral encephalitis?
why: Low CSF glucose suggests bacterial, TB or fungal infection.

q: What CSF finding suggests TB meningitis?
acc: very high protein / low glucose + lymphocyte / high protein
model: Lymphocytes with very high protein and very low glucose.
hint: Like viral cells, but the sugar is used up.
why: TB meningitis is subacute, often with cranial nerve palsies; send AFB stain, culture and PCR.

q: Which lobe does HSV encephalitis typically affect?
why: HSV-1 reactivation spreads along trigeminal/olfactory pathways to the temporal lobes, causing haemorrhagic necrosis.

q: What is the treatment for suspected HSV encephalitis?
model: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times daily, started immediately.
why: Treat for 14–21 days; adjust for renal function and keep hydrated to avoid crystal nephropathy.

q: What is the gold-standard test for HSV encephalitis?
why: It is highly sensitive and specific, though it can be negative very early.

q: Name a long-term complication of HSV encephalitis.
acc: memory / amnesia / epilepsy / seizure / personality / behaviour / dysphasia / cognitive
model: Memory impairment, epilepsy, personality change, dysphasia, cognitive deficits.
why: Temporal lobe and hippocampal damage underlie the memory and behaviour problems.

q: Which autoimmune encephalitis can follow HSV encephalitis?
hint: An antibody against a glutamate receptor.
why: About a fifth of patients develop new psychiatric or movement symptoms weeks later; treat with immunotherapy.

q: Which tumour is linked to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis?
hint: A germ cell tumour in young women.
why: The tumour contains neural tissue expressing NMDA receptors; removal and immunotherapy lead to recovery.

q: Which encephalitis causes faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatraemia?
hint: An antibody against a potassium-channel complex protein.
why: It typically affects older men and responds to immunotherapy.

q: Which demyelinating encephalitis follows infection or vaccination in children?
why: Multifocal demyelination, usually monophasic, treated with steroids.

q: Should antibiotics be delayed for a CT or LP in suspected meningitis?
why: Give antibiotics within 1 hour; LP results are still useful after antibiotics (PCR).

q: Name a sign that should delay LP because of raised intracranial pressure.
acc: papilloedema / focal / reduced consciousness / gcs / seizure / bradycardia / pupil / posturing
model: Papilloedema, focal neurological signs, reduced or fluctuating consciousness, new seizures, bradycardia with hypertension.
hint: Signs of pressure inside the skull.
why: LP can cause brain herniation when ICP is raised.

q: Why is LP avoided in extensive purpura?
model: The patient needs resuscitation for meningococcal sepsis, and coagulopathy makes LP risky.
why: LP adds little when the diagnosis is clinically clear.

q: Name a common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates.
acc: group b / gbs / agalactiae / e coli / escherichia / listeria
model: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli or Listeria.
why: They are acquired from the maternal genital and gut flora at birth.

q: Which is the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in adults?
hint: Also the commonest cause of pneumonia.
why: Often follows otitis, sinusitis or pneumonia; dexamethasone reduces complications.

q: Why is amoxicillin added to empirical meningitis treatment in people over 60?
why: Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins and affects older and immunocompromised people with weaker cell-mediated immunity.

q: Why do children under 2 respond poorly to polysaccharide vaccines?
model: Polysaccharides are T-cell-independent antigens, which infants respond to poorly.
why: Conjugating to a protein carrier gives a T-dependent response with memory.

q: What is the commonest cause of meningitis overall?
why: Viral meningitis is usually self-limiting; HSV-2 can cause recurrent meningitis.

q: Which steroid is given with antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis?
why: It reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae, especially in pneumococcal meningitis.

q: What is a common side effect of the infant MenB vaccine?
why: Prophylactic paracetamol is given with the infant doses.

q: Who is offered the MenACWY vaccine?
hint: Year 9 pupils and new starters in higher education.
why: Carriage peaks in young adults; vaccinating them reduces carriage and protects others (herd immunity).

q: Why are conjugate vaccines better than polysaccharide vaccines?
acc: memory / t dependent / carriage / herd / under 2 / infant
model: They produce T-dependent immunity with memory, work in infants and reduce carriage.
hint: Think lasting protection and protecting others.
why: Polysaccharide vaccines give short-lived protection and don't work in under-2s.

q: Which vaccine protects against TB meningitis in children?
why: Given to at-risk infants; it protects best against severe childhood forms (meningitis, miliary TB).

q: Why should live vaccines be avoided in significant immunosuppression?
model: The attenuated organism can cause disease.
why: E.g. MMR, BCG, rotavirus, varicella.

q: What is the commonest long-term complication of bacterial meningitis?
why: Arrange audiology within 4 weeks of recovery.

q: What is Kernig's sign?
model: Pain and resistance on extending the knee with the hip flexed.
why: Stretching inflamed nerve roots causes meningeal irritation pain.

q: Name the components of Cushing's triad.
why: A late sign of raised ICP and impending herniation.

q: Which electrolyte disturbance is common in meningitis?
why: ADH release from brain inflammation; monitor sodium and fluid balance.

q: Which cranial nerve palsy is a false localising sign of raised ICP?
why: Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to stretching.

q: Does alcohol improve essential tremor or Parkinsonian tremor?
why: Many patients notice a small drink reduces their tremor; Parkinson's tremor doesn't respond.

q: When is a Parkinsonian tremor most obvious?
why: It lessens with movement; essential tremor is worst on posture and action.

q: Which drug is first line for essential tremor?
why: Both reduce tremor amplitude.

q: Which scan distinguishes essential tremor from Parkinson's when unsure?
hint: A SPECT scan of the striatum.
why: It's normal in essential tremor and reduced in Parkinson's.

q: Where are neurons lost in Parkinson's disease?
why: Loss of dopaminergic neurons projecting to the striatum underlies the motor features.

q: Which motor feature is essential for diagnosing Parkinson's?
why: Plus rest tremor and/or rigidity.

q: Name a non-motor feature that can precede Parkinson's motor signs.
acc: anosmia / smell / rem sleep / constipation / depression
model: Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression.
hint: Loss of a sense, or acting out dreams.
why: These reflect early α-synuclein pathology outside the substantia nigra.

q: What is the earliest motor sign of Parkinson's on handwriting?
model: Micrographia (small, cramped writing that gets smaller).
why: Reflects bradykinesia with decrement in amplitude.

q: Early falls and vertical gaze palsy suggest which condition?
why: A tauopathy with axial rigidity and poor levodopa response.

q: Early severe autonomic failure with parkinsonism suggests what?
why: Postural hypotension, urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction early, sometimes with cerebellar signs.

q: Dementia within a year of parkinsonism with visual hallucinations suggests what?
why: Patients are very sensitive to antipsychotics.

q: Which antiemetic commonly causes drug-induced parkinsonism?
why: Both are dopamine D2 antagonists.

q: Which drug is most effective for Parkinson's motor symptoms?
why: It's first line when motor symptoms affect quality of life; long-term use causes dyskinesias and fluctuations.

q: Name a side effect specific to dopamine agonists.
acc: impulse / gambling / hypersexual / shopping / sleep / somnolence
model: Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality) and excessive daytime sleepiness.
why: Warn patients and families before starting.

q: Which antiemetic is safe in Parkinson's?
why: It doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier, so it doesn't block central dopamine (check QT).

q: What is the risk of suddenly stopping Parkinson's drugs?
why: PD drugs are time-critical; if nil by mouth, use a rotigotine patch or NG tube.

q: Which drug treats levodopa-induced dyskinesias?
why: It's an NMDA antagonist with weak dopaminergic effects.

q: What causes Huntington's disease?
model: A CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene (chromosome 4).
why: Autosomal dominant with anticipation; chorea, dementia and psychiatric symptoms.

q: What is tardive dyskinesia?
acc: orofacial / chewing / lip / involuntary + antipsychotic / antipsychotic
model: Involuntary orofacial movements (chewing, lip-smacking) after long-term antipsychotics.
hint: A late effect of dopamine blockade.
why: It may persist after stopping the drug; switching to clozapine or using tetrabenazine-like drugs may help.

q: Which blood test is checked in restless legs syndrome?
why: Iron deficiency is a treatable cause; also check renal function and pregnancy.

q: What is the treatment for acute dystonia from metoclopramide?
why: An anticholinergic that rapidly reverses drug-induced dystonia.

q: What is a "sensory trick" in dystonia?
model: Touching a body part (e.g. the chin) to relieve the dystonic posture.
hint: Contact with the skin relieves it.
why: It's characteristic of dystonia (geste antagoniste).

q: How long does an untreated migraine attack last?
why: Cluster attacks last 15–180 minutes.

q: What is the acute treatment of choice for cluster headache?
why: Oral analgesics are too slow.

q: Which drug prevents cluster headache, requiring ECG monitoring?
why: It can cause heart block, so ECGs are checked at baseline and after dose changes.

q: Which contraceptive is contraindicated in migraine with aura?
why: It increases ischaemic stroke risk (UKMEC 4).

q: Name a migraine preventive drug.
why: Offered when attacks are frequent or disabling; topiramate is teratogenic.

q: How does a cluster headache patient behave during an attack?
why: Migraine sufferers prefer to lie still in a dark room.

q: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil suggests what?
model: Compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
why: Parasympathetic fibres run superficially, so compression affects the pupil early; needs urgent CT angiography.

q: Which nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia worse on looking down?
why: Superior oblique weakness; patients tilt the head away to compensate.

q: Partial ptosis with a small pupil suggests what?
why: Loss of sympathetic supply; painful Horner's suggests carotid dissection.

q: What does optic neuritis typically cause besides visual loss?
acc: pain on eye movement / pain / colour / red desaturation / rapd
model: Pain on eye movement, colour desaturation and an RAPD.
why: Linked with MS: arrange MRI.

q: What condition causes papilloedema in a young obese woman with normal imaging?
why: Raised CSF opening pressure; treat with weight loss and acetazolamide to protect vision.

q: What visual field defect does a temporal lobe lesion cause?
why: It damages Meyer's loop ("pie in the sky").

q: What is Lhermitte's sign?
model: An electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion.
why: Seen with cervical cord demyelination (MS).

q: What is Uhthoff's phenomenon?
model: Worsening of MS symptoms with heat (e.g. hot bath, exercise).
why: Demyelinated axons conduct less well when warm.

q: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young person suggests what?
why: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

q: What CSF finding supports MS?
model: Oligoclonal bands in CSF but not serum.
why: They show intrathecal antibody production and can substitute for dissemination in time.

q: What MRI lesion pattern is typical of MS?
model: Periventricular white matter lesions (Dawson's fingers), plus juxtacortical, infratentorial and cord lesions.
why: Lesions perpendicular to the ventricles.

q: Which antibody test helps exclude neuromyelitis optica?
why: NMOSD needs different treatment; some MS drugs worsen it.

q: What is the commonest MS course at onset?
why: About 85% start this way; many later become secondary progressive.

q: How long must new symptoms last to count as an MS relapse?
model: More than 24 hours (without fever or infection).
why: Shorter or infection-related worsening may be a pseudo-relapse.

q: Which MS type progresses from onset without relapses?
why: About 10–15%, older onset, men and women equally.

q: How is a disabling MS relapse treated?
model: High-dose methylprednisolone (oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or IV).
hint: A high-dose short course of an anti-inflammatory.
why: Speeds recovery but doesn't alter long-term disability; exclude infection first.

q: Which MS drug carries a risk of PML?
why: Risk is linked to JC virus antibodies and treatment duration.

q: Which drug treats spasticity in MS?
why: A GABA-B agonist; physiotherapy and botulinum toxin also help.

q: When is intermittent self-catheterisation advised in MS?
model: When the post-void residual is over 100 mL.
why: Antimuscarinics alone can worsen retention.

q: Name a precipitant of MS relapse.
acc: infection / postpartum / stress / heat / smoking / vitamin d / stopping
model: Infection, the postpartum period, stress, stopping DMTs.
why: Relapse rates fall in pregnancy and rise in the 3 months after birth.

q: What is a pseudo-relapse in MS?
