acc: infection / heat / fever / temporary / old symptom
model: Temporary worsening of old symptoms due to infection, fever, heat or stress.
why: Treat the trigger (e.g. UTI) rather than giving steroids.

q: What is a thunderclap headache?
acc: 1 minute / one minute / within a minute / sudden / instant
model: A severe headache reaching peak intensity within 1 minute.
hint: Like being hit on the head.
why: Subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

q: When should an LP be done to look for xanthochromia after a thunderclap headache?
why: Bilirubin from red cell breakdown takes time to form.

q: A new headache in someone over 50 with jaw claudication suggests what?
why: Start high-dose steroids immediately to prevent blindness.

q: What headache features suggest raised intracranial pressure?
model: Worse in the morning, lying down, coughing or straining, with vomiting.
why: ICP rises when lying flat and with Valsalva.

q: What causes medication overuse headache?
model: Taking analgesics or triptans on too many days (≥10–15 days a month).
why: Treatment is withdrawal of the overused drug.

q: Describe a tension-type headache.
model: Bilateral, pressing or tight band-like headache, mild–moderate, not worsened by activity.
hint: Like a hat that's too small.
why: No nausea; may have mild photophobia or phonophobia.

q: Is neuroimaging needed for a typical migraine without red flags?
why: NICE advises against imaging typical primary headaches.

q: What CSF finding is typical of Guillain–Barré syndrome?
model: High protein with a normal cell count.
hint: One CSF value is up, another isn't.
why: Albuminocytological dissociation; nerve conduction shows demyelination.

q: Which bedside test monitors respiratory function in Guillain–Barré?
why: A falling FVC predicts respiratory failure before oxygen sats fall.

q: Which antibody is found in most patients with myasthenia gravis?
why: Others have anti-MuSK; CT chest for thymoma.

q: Which drug prolongs survival in MND?
why: A glutamate inhibitor that extends survival by a few months; NIV also improves survival.

q: Within what time should steroids be given in Bell's palsy?
why: Prednisolone improves recovery; protect the eye.

q: What distinguishes MND from other weakness on examination?
model: Mixed UMN and LMN signs with no sensory loss.
why: Eye movements and sphincters are usually spared.

q: Which way does the uvula deviate in a vagus palsy?
model: Away from the side of the lesion.
why: The intact levator veli palatini pulls it.

q: Name a sign of pseudobulbar palsy.
acc: brisk jaw / jaw jerk / spastic tongue / emotional / labile / donald
model: Brisk jaw jerk, spastic tongue, emotional lability, "Donald Duck" speech.
why: It's an UMN (bilateral corticobulbar) lesion, often from bilateral strokes.

q: Name a sign of bulbar palsy.
model: Wasted, fasciculating tongue, nasal speech, absent gag.
why: An LMN lesion of IX–XII (e.g. MND, myasthenia, brainstem stroke).

q: What is the difference between dysarthria and dysphasia?
model: Dysarthria is a problem of articulation (motor speech); dysphasia is a problem of language.
why: Dysphasia localises to the dominant cortex; dysarthria can come from anywhere along the motor pathway.

q: Which test directly visualises swallowing with barium?
why: FEES (endoscopic evaluation) is an alternative.

q: What does a "bovine" cough suggest?
hint: A nerve looping under the aortic arch.
why: Causes include lung cancer, thyroid surgery and aortic aneurysm.

q: After how many weeks of pregnancy can pre-eclampsia be diagnosed?
why: New hypertension before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing (chronic) hypertension or a molar pregnancy.

q: What is first-line antihypertensive treatment in pre-eclampsia?
why: Avoid in asthma; nifedipine and methyldopa are alternatives. ACE inhibitors are avoided antenatally.

q: Which drug prevents and treats eclamptic seizures?
why: Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output; calcium gluconate reverses toxicity.

q: What does HELLP stand for?
model: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets.
why: A severe form of pre-eclampsia; delivery is the treatment.

q: Who should take aspirin from 12 weeks to prevent pre-eclampsia?
acc: high risk / previous / ckd / diabetes / hypertension / lupus / sle / antiphospholipid
model: Women with one high-risk factor (previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, SLE/APS, diabetes, chronic hypertension) or two moderate risks.
hint: A history of hypertensive pregnancy, or chronic disease.
why: Aspirin 75–150 mg nightly until birth reduces risk.

q: What is the definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia?
why: Timing balances maternal risk against fetal prematurity; steroids if preterm.

q: Which reflex sign suggests severe pre-eclampsia?
why: Reflects cerebral irritability before eclampsia; also monitored for magnesium toxicity (loss of reflexes).

q: Painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus at 32 weeks suggests what?
why: Never do a digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded on ultrasound.

q: Painful bleeding with a tender, hard uterus suggests what?
why: Bleeding may be concealed, so shock can be out of proportion to visible loss.

q: What are the 4 Ts of postpartum haemorrhage?
why: Uterine atony (tone) causes about 70%.

q: What is the first drug given for uterine atony?
why: Then ergometrine (not in hypertension), carboprost (not in asthma), misoprostol and tranexamic acid.

q: Which test measures the size of fetomaternal haemorrhage?
why: It guides the anti-D dose for Rhesus-negative women.

q: What hCG rise over 48 hours suggests a viable intrauterine pregnancy?
why: A suboptimal rise or plateau suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy.

q: Name a criterion for methotrexate in ectopic pregnancy.
model: hCG <1500, unruptured, no significant pain, no fetal heartbeat, mass <35 mm.
why: Otherwise laparoscopic salpingectomy.

q: By how much does cardiac output rise in pregnancy?
why: Stroke volume and heart rate both rise; SVR falls from progesterone.

q: Why is mild anaemia normal in pregnancy?
model: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass (dilution).
why: Hb thresholds are 110 g/L in the first trimester and 105 g/L later.

q: What acid–base state is normal in pregnancy?
why: Progesterone increases tidal volume and minute ventilation, lowering PaCO₂.

q: Why might a "normal" creatinine of 90 µmol/L be abnormal in pregnancy?
model: GFR rises ~50%, so creatinine is normally lower.
why: A creatinine of 90 may indicate renal impairment in pregnancy.

q: Why does insulin resistance rise in later pregnancy?
why: It diverts glucose to the fetus and can cause gestational diabetes.

q: Why does pregnancy increase VTE risk?
model: It's a hypercoagulable state (more clotting factors, less protein S), plus venous stasis.
why: Risk is highest postpartum; PE is a leading cause of maternal death.

q: Does a fetus have legal personality in England and Wales?
why: It can't be murdered in utero and has no rights that override the mother's.

q: Can a competent pregnant woman refuse a caesarean if the fetus may die?
why: Her autonomy prevails; St George's v S found forced caesarean unlawful.

q: Which Act allows a child to sue for injury caused before birth?
why: The child must be born alive; a mother is only liable for negligent driving.

q: Within how many days must a birth be registered in England and Wales?
why: Stillbirths at or after 24 weeks must also be registered.

q: Which case established that a competent woman can refuse a caesarean even if her fetus will die?
model: Re MB (1997) (also St George's v S, 1998).
why: In Re MB, needle phobia made her temporarily incapacitated, so treatment was lawful.

q: Which Act creates the offence of child destruction?
why: It protects a fetus capable of being born alive.

q: Which case set the modern consent standard using an obstetric example?
why: Doctors must disclose material risks, such as shoulder dystocia in a diabetic mother.

q: How many doctors must sign for a non-emergency abortion?
why: They must agree in good faith that a ground applies; one is enough in an emergency.

q: What is the time limit under ground C of the Abortion Act?
why: Ground C (risk to the woman's health) accounts for about 98% of abortions.

q: Which ground allows termination at any gestation for serious fetal abnormality?
hint: A letter near the end of the list.
why: Substantial risk the child would be seriously handicapped.

q: Can a father legally prevent an abortion?
why: Paton v BPAS and C v S.

q: Can a doctor with a conscientious objection refuse to participate in an abortion?
model: Yes, except in an emergency, but they must refer.
why: Section 4 of the Abortion Act; GMC requires prompt referral.

q: What is the Bolam test?
model: Practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion.
why: Bolitho adds that the opinion must be logically defensible.

q: Can parents recover the costs of raising a healthy child after a failed vasectomy?
hint: A healthy child isn't seen as a loss.
why: They may get damages for the pregnancy and a conventional award (Rees).

q: Can parents recover the extra costs of raising a disabled child after negligence?
why: Costs attributable to the disability are recoverable.

q: Is a "wrongful life" claim by the child recognised in England?
hint: The child can't claim it shouldn't exist.
why: Courts won't compare existence with non-existence.

q: What is the time limit for most negligence claims?
model: 3 years from the date of knowledge.
why: For children, the clock starts at 18.

q: What three measurements make up the combined test?
model: Nuchal translucency, hCG and PAPP-A (with age).
hint: An ultrasound and two blood markers.
why: Done at 11–14 weeks; gives a chance of trisomies.

q: What result counts as "higher chance" on Down syndrome screening?
hint: One in a hundred and fifty.
why: Women are offered NIPT or invasive testing.

q: Is NIPT a diagnostic test?
why: Confined placental mosaicism causes false positives, so confirm with CVS or amniocentesis.

q: What combined-test pattern suggests Down syndrome?
acc: high hcg + low papp / hcg + papp
model: High hCG, low PAPP-A and increased nuchal translucency.
why: In Edwards and Patau both hCG and PAPP-A are low.

q: What is the risk to each child if both parents carry an autosomal recessive condition?
why: 50% will be carriers, 25% unaffected non-carriers.

q: When can amniocentesis be done?
why: CVS is done at 11–14 weeks; both carry ~0.5% miscarriage risk.

q: Name a prerequisite for an assisted vaginal birth.
acc: fully dilated / ruptured / cephalic / position / engaged / analgesia / bladder
model: Fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, known position, head ≤1/5 palpable, analgesia, empty bladder.
why: Missing a prerequisite risks failure and trauma.

q: What is the decision-to-delivery target for a category 1 caesarean?
why: Category 1 means immediate threat to the life of the woman or fetus.

q: Which instrument is not used before 34 weeks?
why: Risk of cephalohaematoma and intracranial haemorrhage in preterm babies.

q: Name a risk of caesarean section for future pregnancies.
model: Placenta praevia or accreta, uterine rupture.
why: The uterine scar affects placentation and labour.

q: Which neonatal complication is more common after ventouse?
why: Suction lifts the scalp; subgaleal bleeding can cause shock.

q: What weight loss defines hyperemesis gravidarum?
why: With dehydration and ketosis; give antiemetics, fluids and thiamine.

q: Itching of the palms and soles without a rash in late pregnancy suggests what?
why: Check bile acids and LFTs; very high bile acids increase stillbirth risk.

q: Which vitamin is given to prevent Wernicke's in hyperemesis?
why: Prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine.

q: Which antibiotic is avoided in the first trimester?
why: It's a folate antagonist (neural tube defects).

q: What are the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes on OGTT?
why: NICE thresholds; OGTT at 24–28 weeks for women with risk factors.

q: What does G3 P1+1 mean?
model: Three pregnancies (including this one), one birth ≥24 weeks, one loss before 24 weeks.
hint: G counts one thing, P another.
why: Gravidity counts pregnancies; parity counts births after 24 weeks.

q: When is the anomaly scan done?
why: The dating scan is at 11–14 weeks.

q: Why should you ask about domestic abuse when the woman is alone?
model: So she can disclose safely without the abuser present.
why: Abuse often starts or escalates in pregnancy.

q: Which psychiatric history puts a woman at high risk of postpartum psychosis?
why: Needs perinatal mental health input and a plan.

q: At what gestation is the fundus at the umbilicus?
why: Just palpable at 12 weeks, xiphisternum at 36.

q: How is engagement of the fetal head described?
model: In fifths palpable above the pelvic brim.
why: ≤2/5 palpable means engaged.

q: Why plot SFH on a customised chart?
model: To detect fetal growth restriction, adjusted for maternal height, weight, ethnicity and parity.
hint: Adjusted for the mother's height, weight and parity.
why: SFH below the 10th centile or static growth needs a scan.

q: Name a cause of breathlessness in pregnancy that must not be missed.
why: Physiological breathlessness has normal sats and examination.

q: What is the threshold for treating anaemia in the first trimester?
why: Below 105 g/L in the second and third trimesters.

q: Why is asymptomatic bacteriuria treated in pregnancy?
model: It can progress to pyelonephritis and preterm labour.
why: Dilated ureters make ascending infection more likely.

q: Name a sign specific to Graves' disease.
acc: exophthalmos / proptosis / pretibial / acropachy / bruit / ophthalmoplegia
model: Exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy, thyroid bruit.
why: Caused by TSH-receptor antibodies acting on orbital and skin fibroblasts.

q: What is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in the UK?
why: Anti-TPO antibodies; iodine deficiency is commonest worldwide.

q: Which antithyroid drug is used in the first trimester?
why: Carbimazole is teratogenic in early pregnancy; switch after the first trimester (PTU is hepatotoxic).

q: What should happen to levothyroxine when a woman becomes pregnant?
why: Requirements rise early; hypothyroidism harms fetal neurodevelopment.

q: Which drug used for bipolar disorder causes hypothyroidism?
why: Monitor TFTs every 6 months.

q: High TSH with low free T4 means what?
why: The failing thyroid can't respond to TSH.

q: Low TSH with low free T4 suggests what?
model: Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid syndrome.
why: Check other pituitary hormones.

q: Which antibody confirms Graves' disease?
why: Anti-TPO is typical of Hashimoto's.

q: What does low uptake on a thyroid scan with thyrotoxicosis suggest?
why: Hormone leaks from a damaged gland rather than being overproduced.

q: When should TSH be rechecked after a levothyroxine dose change?
why: TSH takes this long to reach a new steady state.

q: Why is TSH low in early pregnancy?
why: Use trimester-specific reference ranges.

q: Name a nail sign of iron deficiency.
why: Other iron deficiency signs: angular stomatitis, glossitis, hair loss.

q: Which neurological syndrome is caused by B12 deficiency?
model: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (and peripheral neuropathy).
hint: Dorsal columns and pyramidal tracts together.
why: Dorsal column (proprioception, vibration) and corticospinal tract involvement; can occur without anaemia.

q: Why is chronic anaemia often well tolerated?
model: Compensation: increased cardiac output and 2,3-DPG (right shift of the O₂ dissociation curve).
why: Rapid blood loss gives symptoms at higher Hb levels.

q: Jaundice with anaemia and splenomegaly suggests what?
why: Red cell breakdown raises unconjugated bilirubin; check LDH, haptoglobin and DAT.

q: Which hormone stimulates red cell production, and where is it made?
why: Peritubular cells release EPO in response to hypoxia; CKD causes anaemia.

q: What does a raised reticulocyte count indicate?
model: The marrow is responding (bleeding or haemolysis, or recovery after treatment).
why: A low count with anaemia means a production problem.

q: What does a leucoerythroblastic film suggest?
model: Marrow infiltration (e.g. metastases, myelofibrosis, haematological malignancy).
why: Nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells are pushed out into the blood.

q: Where is bone marrow usually sampled in adults?
why: Aspirate for cell morphology and trephine for architecture.

q: How long does a red blood cell normally survive?
why: Old cells are removed by splenic macrophages; haem becomes bilirubin.

q: Which enzyme deficiency causes haemolysis triggered by fava beans?
why: Without NADPH, red cells can't reduce glutathione and are damaged by oxidants (Heinz bodies, bite cells).

q: Which red cell membrane disorder causes spherocytes?
why: Spectrin or ankyrin defects make cells spherical and rigid, so the spleen destroys them.

q: What are the globin chains in adult haemoglobin A?
model: Two α and two β chains.
why: HbF is α₂γ₂; HbA₂ is α₂δ₂.

q: Give a mechanism of anaemia other than reduced production.
acc: destruction / haemoly / loss / bleed / ineffective / dilution / pool
model: Increased destruction (haemolysis), blood loss, ineffective production, pooling or dilution.
why: Classifying by mechanism guides tests (reticulocytes, haemolysis screen).

q: What blood film finding suggests microangiopathic haemolysis?
why: Seen in DIC, HUS, TTP and with mechanical valves.

q: What do Howell–Jolly bodies indicate?
why: The spleen normally removes nuclear remnants from red cells.

q: Why can ferritin be normal despite iron deficiency?
model: It's an acute-phase protein, raised in inflammation.
why: Check transferrin saturation (<20%) in inflamed patients.

q: Which test detects antibody-coated red cells in autoimmune haemolysis?
hint: Antiglobulin added to the patient's washed red cells.
why: Positive in autoimmune haemolysis and transfusion reactions.

q: Name three results of a positive haemolysis screen.
model: Raised LDH, raised unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin (and raised reticulocytes).
hint: Enzyme up, pigment up, binding protein down.
why: Haptoglobin binds free Hb and is used up.

q: What Hb electrophoresis finding confirms β-thalassaemia trait?
why: Reduced β chains mean more α₂δ₂.

q: Why is alternate-day oral iron dosing used?
model: Hepcidin rises for ~24 hours after a dose, so alternate days improves absorption.
hint: A liver hormone peaks after each dose.
why: Also fewer side effects.

q: How long should oral iron continue after Hb normalises?
why: To replenish iron stores (ferritin).

q: Name a drug whose absorption is reduced by oral iron.
acc: levothyroxine / tetracycline / doxycycline / ciprofloxacin / quinolone / bisphosphonate
why: Iron chelates them in the gut; separate doses by a few hours.

q: Why must B12 be replaced before folate in combined deficiency?
model: Folate alone can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration.
why: Folate corrects the anaemia but not the neurological damage.

q: What is the maintenance regimen for hydroxocobalamin in pernicious anaemia?
model: 1 mg IM every 2–3 months for life.
hint: Lifelong IM injections, a few times a year.
why: After loading (three times weekly for 2 weeks); oral B12 isn't absorbed without intrinsic factor.

q: What is the Hb target with ESAs in CKD?
why: Higher targets increased stroke and cardiovascular events in trials.

q: Which electrolyte can fall when B12 treatment starts in severe megaloblastic anaemia?
why: Rapid new red cell production takes up potassium.

q: Which hormone causes anaemia of chronic disease?
hint: A liver peptide that degrades ferroportin.
why: Inflammation (IL-6) raises hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption and release from macrophages (ferroportin).

q: What ferritin level is typical in anaemia of chronic disease?
why: Iron is trapped in stores; serum iron and TIBC are low.

q: What causes the large cells in megaloblastic anaemia?
why: B12 and folate are needed for thymidine synthesis.

q: Which virus causes an aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease?
why: It infects erythroid progenitors, halting red cell production.

q: What is aplastic anaemia?
why: Often autoimmune; treated with ATG + ciclosporin or stem cell transplant.

q: What Hb threshold is used for restrictive transfusion in most adults?
why: 80 g/L in acute coronary syndrome (NICE NG24).

q: How many units of red cells should a non-bleeding adult receive before reassessing?
why: Single-unit transfusion reduces unnecessary exposure.

q: Which patients need irradiated blood?
model: After stem cell transplant, Hodgkin lymphoma, purine analogues (e.g. fludarabine).
why: Prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.

q: What should be treated instead of transfusing in stable iron deficiency anaemia?
why: Transfusion has risks and doesn't treat the cause.

q: At what fibrinogen level is cryoprecipitate given in major haemorrhage?
why: Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen.

q: Can a person who has received a blood transfusion donate blood in the UK?
why: A precaution against vCJD transmission.

q: Name a risk to discuss when consenting for transfusion.
acc: taco / trali / reaction / infection / allergic / wrong blood / fever
model: Reactions (fever, allergy), TACO, TRALI, wrong blood, very low infection risk.
why: Consent must include risks, benefits and alternatives.

q: Within how many hours must a unit of red cells be completed after leaving storage?
why: Longer risks bacterial growth.

q: Which fluid can run through the same line as blood?
why: Glucose solutions cause haemolysis; calcium-containing fluids cause clotting.

q: Which drug may be prescribed with each unit for a patient at risk of TACO?
why: Reduces circulatory overload risk in heart or renal failure.

q: What is the "two-sample rule"?
model: First-time patients need two separate group samples taken at different times.
why: Detects wrong-blood-in-tube errors before transfusion.

q: When should observations be taken during a transfusion?
model: Before, 15 minutes after starting each unit, and at the end.
hint: A quarter of an hour in.
why: Severe reactions usually occur early.

q: Why must blood samples be labelled at the bedside?
why: Never pre-label tubes or label away from the patient.

q: What causes an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction?
model: ABO incompatibility (usually wrong blood to wrong patient).
why: Pre-formed antibodies lyse donor cells within minutes.

q: What is the first action in any suspected transfusion reaction?
why: Keep the line open with saline, ABCDE, check identity, call for help.

q: Hypertension, raised JVP and pulmonary oedema during transfusion suggest what?
why: Treat with furosemide and oxygen; TRALI causes hypotension and doesn't respond to diuretics.

q: Which blood component is most often contaminated with bacteria?
why: They're stored at room temperature.

q: Which patients may have anaphylaxis to blood products?
why: They need IgA-deficient components.

q: Where are serious transfusion reactions reported?
why: The UK haemovigilance scheme.

q: Which questionnaire assesses daytime sleepiness?
why: A score above 10 suggests excessive sleepiness (e.g. OSA).

q: What is post-exertional malaise?
model: Worsening of symptoms after physical or mental exertion.
why: A key feature of ME/CFS.

q: Why ask about diet in a fatigue history?
model: To identify deficiencies (e.g. vegan diet → B12; low iron).
why: Nutritional causes are reversible.

q: Name a red flag in a fatigue history.
acc: weight loss / night sweat / lymph / bleed / fever / lump
model: Weight loss, night sweats, fever, lumps, bleeding.
why: They suggest malignancy, lymphoma or TB.

q: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
model: Attributing new symptoms to an existing diagnosis (e.g. mental illness or learning disability).
why: A thorough systems review guards against it.

q: Name a first-line blood test for unexplained fatigue.
acc: fbc / tft / thyroid / hba1c / ferritin / crp / esr / u&e / lft / calcium / coeliac
model: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFTs, HbA1c, ferritin, CRP/ESR, calcium, coeliac serology.
why: Cover common treatable causes.

q: Which Clinical Frailty Scale score indicates frailty?
why: Guides decisions about investigations and care.

q: Name a "frailty syndrome".
model: Falls, delirium, immobility, incontinence, medication side effects.
why: Atypical presentations of illness in frail people.

q: What is a comprehensive geriatric assessment?
model: A multidimensional, MDT assessment of medical, functional, psychological and social needs.
why: Improves outcomes in frail older people.

q: Which older-age inflammatory condition causes fatigue and shoulder and hip girdle stiffness?
why: High ESR/CRP; responds dramatically to low-dose prednisolone.

q: What is the normal platelet count?
why: Thrombocytosis is often reactive (bleeding, iron deficiency, inflammation).

q: A patient on carbimazole has a sore throat. What blood test is urgent?
why: Carbimazole can cause agranulocytosis; stop the drug if neutropenic.

q: What should iron deficiency anaemia in a 65-year-old man prompt?
model: GI investigation for cancer (suspected cancer pathway).
why: Occult GI blood loss from colorectal or gastric cancer.

q: Name a drug causing neutropenia.
acc: carbimazole / clozapine / methotrexate / chemotherapy / azathioprine / sulfasalazine
why: Check FBC if infection symptoms develop.

q: What is the commonest cause of microcytic anaemia?
why: Usually blood loss (menstrual, GI) or poor intake/absorption.

q: Name a non-megaloblastic cause of macrocytosis.
acc: alcohol / liver / hypothyroid / reticulocyt / myelodysplas / mds
model: Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia.
why: B12 and folate are normal.

q: Which drug interferes with folate and causes macrocytosis?
why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.

q: What Mentzer index suggests thalassaemia trait?
why: Thal trait has a high red cell count for its Hb.

q: Name a cause of normocytic anaemia.
acc: ckd / kidney / chronic disease / blood loss / bleed / haemoly / mixed / marrow / pregnan
model: CKD, anaemia of chronic disease, acute blood loss, haemolysis, mixed deficiency.
hint: Think organ failure or long-term illness.
why: Check reticulocytes, renal function and inflammatory markers.

q: What ferritin level confirms iron deficiency?
why: Ferritin may be falsely normal in inflammation.

q: Which serology test should be done in unexplained iron deficiency?
model: Coeliac serology (tTG IgA with total IgA).
why: Coeliac disease causes iron malabsorption.

q: Which antibody test confirms pernicious anaemia?
hint: The factor needed to absorb B12.
why: Highly specific; parietal cell antibodies are sensitive but non-specific.

q: Which test helps decide if normocytic anaemia is a production or destruction problem?
why: High = bleeding or haemolysis; low = production failure.

q: Which investigation finds the cause of iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman?
acc: colonoscopy + ogd / endoscopy / ogd / colonoscopy / ct colonography
model: Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) and colonoscopy (or CT colonography).
why: To exclude GI malignancy.

q: What is the most common cancer in the UK?
why: BCC is very common but rarely metastasises; it is often excluded from cancer registry totals.

q: Which layer of the epidermis forms the main barrier?
why: Corneocytes embedded in lipids, held together by proteins such as filaggrin, prevent water loss and allergen entry.

q: Which epidermal cells present antigen?
hint: Dendritic cells named after a German anatomist.
why: They take up allergens and drive type IV reactions in allergic contact dermatitis.

q: Which investigation identifies the cause of allergic contact dermatitis?
why: Allergens are applied under occlusion and read at 48 and 96 hours (type IV reaction).

q: How should a suspected fungal skin infection be sampled?
model: Skin scrapings (or nail clippings/hair) for microscopy and culture.
why: Swabs are poor for dermatophytes.

q: Which questionnaire measures the impact of skin disease on quality of life?
why: Used alongside severity scores (e.g. PASI) to decide on systemic treatment.

q: What proportion of people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis?
why: Screen yearly with the PEST questionnaire; early treatment prevents joint damage.

q: Name a metabolic comorbidity of psoriasis.
acc: obesity / diabetes / dyslipid / hypertension / metabolic syndrome / nafld
model: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension (metabolic syndrome), NAFLD.
why: Systemic inflammation raises cardiovascular risk.

q: What is the "atopic march"?
acc: eczema + asthma / allergic / food allergy / hay fever
model: Progression from eczema in infancy to food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis.
hint: Skin first, then airways and gut.
why: A leaky skin barrier allows sensitisation through the skin.

q: Which protein's mutations cause barrier dysfunction in atopic eczema?
why: Loss-of-function mutations impair the stratum corneum, increasing water loss and allergen entry.

q: Pemphigus vulgaris antibodies target which protein?
why: Loss of keratinocyte adhesion causes intraepidermal, flaccid blisters.

q: Bullous pemphigoid antibodies target which structure?
hint: Anchors the basal layer to the basement membrane.
why: The split is subepidermal, so blisters are tense.

q: How long does epidermal turnover take in psoriasis?
why: Rapid turnover produces thick plaques with silvery scale.

q: What is the essential feature for diagnosing atopic eczema?
why: UK Working Party criteria: itch plus 3 or more other features.

q: Where does eczema typically affect infants?
model: Face, scalp and extensor surfaces (sparing the nappy area).
why: Older children and adults get flexural eczema.

q: Which bacterium colonises eczematous skin?
why: Infection causes flares with crusting and weeping; treat with flucloxacillin if needed.

q: What should be used instead of soap in eczema?
why: Soaps strip lipids and worsen the barrier.

q: Which topical drug class avoids steroid side effects on the face in eczema?
hint: Also used to prevent transplant rejection.
why: They don't cause skin atrophy.

q: Which biologic is used for severe atopic eczema?
why: It blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling (Th2).

q: Describe the typical appearance of a nodular BCC.
model: A pearly papule with a rolled edge and telangiectasia, often centrally ulcerated.
why: BCCs are locally destructive ("rodent ulcer") but rarely metastasise.

q: What does ABCDE stand for in melanoma?
model: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution.
why: Changing lesions need suspected cancer referral.

q: Which measurement best predicts melanoma prognosis?
why: Depth of invasion in mm determines spread risk and excision margins.

q: What score on the Glasgow 7-point checklist triggers a suspected cancer referral?
why: Major features (size, shape, colour change) score 2; minor features score 1.

q: Which type of melanoma affects palms, soles and nails, especially in darker skin?
hint: Named for its site at the extremities.
why: Often diagnosed late.

q: Name a risk factor for cutaneous SCC.
acc: uv / sun / immunosuppress / transplant / actinic / scar / wound / hpv
model: UV exposure, immunosuppression (e.g. transplant), actinic keratoses, chronic wounds or scars.
why: SCC can metastasise; refer urgently.

q: What is Bowen's disease?
acc: squamous cell carcinoma in situ / scc in situ / in situ
why: Full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without invasion; treat with 5-FU, cryotherapy or excision.

q: Describe a seborrhoeic keratosis.
hint: Looks like it could be peeled off.
why: Very common and benign in older adults.

q: What is the "dimple sign"?
model: Dimpling when a dermatofibroma is pinched.
why: Dermatofibromas are firm benign nodules, often on the legs.

q: Why should a pyogenic granuloma be sent for histology?
why: Both can be rapidly growing red bleeding nodules.

q: What is the natural history of an infantile haemangioma?
model: Grows for months, then gradually involutes.
why: Propranolol if near the eye, airway or ulcerating.

q: What is the cause of itch worse after a hot bath with a high haematocrit?
why: Aquagenic pruritus; check FBC and JAK2.

q: Name a systemic cause of itch without a rash.
acc: cholestasis / liver / pbc / ckd / renal / uraemi / iron / polycythaemia / lymphoma / thyroid / hiv / drug / opioid
model: Cholestasis, CKD, iron deficiency, polycythaemia, lymphoma, thyroid disease, drugs.
hint: Consider organ failure or a blood disorder.
why: Investigate with FBC, ferritin, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose and CXR.

q: Which drug treats itch from cholestasis?
why: It binds bile acids in the gut.

q: Who must be treated when someone has scabies?
model: All household and close contacts, at the same time.
why: Otherwise reinfection is common; repeat permethrin after 7 days.

q: Which cancer is linked to malignant acanthosis nigricans?
why: Benign acanthosis nigricans is linked to insulin resistance.

q: What are Gottron's papules a sign of?
why: Violaceous papules over the knuckles; screen for underlying cancer.

q: Name an autoimmune condition associated with vitiligo.
model: Autoimmune thyroid disease (also type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's).
why: Check TFTs.

q: What are "exclamation mark" hairs a sign of?
why: Autoimmune T-cell attack on hair follicles; often regrows.

q: What must be checked before applying compression for a venous leg ulcer?
hint: Compare leg and arm blood pressures.
why: Compression on a leg with significant arterial disease can cause ischaemia; full compression needs an ABPI of about 0.8–1.3.

q: Name a cause of erythema nodosum.
acc: sarcoid / strep / tb / tuberculosis / ibd / crohn / pregnan / pill / contracept / drug
model: Sarcoidosis, streptococcal infection, TB, IBD, pregnancy, drugs.
why: Tender red nodules on the shins (panniculitis).

q: Which skin condition is associated with coeliac disease?
why: Itchy vesicles on extensors; IgA deposits; gluten-free diet and dapsone.

q: Describe a pyoderma gangrenosum ulcer.
model: Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined edge.
why: Associated with IBD and RA; avoid debridement (pathergy).

q: What is the first-line treatment for localised impetigo?
why: NICE prefers it to topical antibiotics to limit resistance; flucloxacillin if widespread.

q: Which bacterium most commonly causes cellulitis?
hint: Also causes tonsillitis and scarlet fever.
why: Flucloxacillin covers both.

q: What feature suggests necrotising fasciitis?
acc: pain out of proportion / out of proportion / crepitus
model: Pain out of proportion to the signs, rapid spread, crepitus, systemic toxicity.
why: A surgical emergency needing debridement.

q: Describe tinea corporis.
model: An annular scaly patch with an active edge and central clearing.
hint: Its common name is a misnomer: no worm involved.
why: Topical steroids worsen it (tinea incognito).

q: Which fungal infection shows satellite lesions?
why: Intertrigo in skin folds with satellite papules and pustules.

q: What is the treatment for scabies?
model: Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body, repeated after 7 days.
why: Treat all contacts; ivermectin for crusted scabies.

q: Molluscum contagiosum lesions have what characteristic shape?
why: A poxvirus; resolves spontaneously.

q: How long does an individual urticarial wheal last?
why: Longer-lasting lesions suggest urticarial vasculitis.

q: Which angioedema occurs without urticaria and doesn't respond to antihistamines?
why: No mast cell involvement; hereditary type is C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.

q: What body surface area defines TEN?
why: SJS is under 10%; 10–30% is overlap.

q: Name a drug commonly causing SJS/TEN.
acc: allopurinol / carbamazepine / lamotrigine / phenytoin / sulfonamide / co trimoxazole / nevirapine / nsaid
why: Usually 1–4 weeks after starting; stop the drug immediately.

q: Are blisters in bullous pemphigoid tense or flaccid?
why: The split is subepidermal, so the roof is thick.

q: Which blistering disease starts in the mouth?
why: Flaccid blisters and erosions; Nikolsky positive.

q: What is erythroderma?
model: Erythema affecting more than 90% of the skin.
why: Skin failure: hypothermia, fluid loss, infection, heart failure.

q: Which drug reaction causes eosinophilia, fever, facial swelling and hepatitis?
hint: An acronym that sounds like clothing.
why: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, 2–8 weeks after starting.

q: What emergency causes punched-out erosions in a child with eczema?
why: Give aciclovir and refer the same day.

q: Which lesion distinguishes acne from rosacea?
why: Rosacea has papules and pustules without comedones.

q: What is first-line treatment for mild-to-moderate acne?
model: A 12-week topical combination (e.g. adapalene with benzoyl peroxide).
why: NICE NG198.

q: Why is isotretinoin prescribed under a pregnancy prevention programme?
why: Women must use effective contraception and have pregnancy tests.

q: Which psychiatric side effect is monitored with isotretinoin?
model: Mood changes, depression and suicidal thoughts.
why: Ask about mood at each review.

q: Which oral antibiotic is used for moderate-to-severe rosacea?
why: Also topical ivermectin; avoid triggers.

q: Name a trigger for rosacea flushing.
acc: alcohol / spicy / heat / sun / hot drink
model: Alcohol, spicy food, heat, sunlight, hot drinks.
why: Avoiding triggers reduces flushing.

q: In a hospital inpatient with a new rash, what should you check first?
model: The drug chart for new medicines.
why: Drug reactions are the commonest cause of new inpatient rashes.

q: Why can erythema be harder to recognise in skin of colour?
model: It may look violaceous, dark brown or grey rather than red.
why: Rely on texture, warmth and comparison with the patient's normal skin.

q: What is the first-line topical treatment for chronic plaque psoriasis?
model: A potent topical steroid plus a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol).
why: Once daily for up to 4 weeks.

q: Name a drug that can trigger or worsen psoriasis.
acc: lithium / beta blocker / antimalarial / hydroxychloroquine / nsaid / steroid withdrawal
model: Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, withdrawal of oral steroids.
why: Ask about drugs in a flare.

q: Which type of psoriasis follows a streptococcal sore throat?
why: Small "raindrop" plaques on the trunk.

q: What is the commonest contact allergen?
why: Jewellery, belt buckles, watches.

q: Describe the lesions of lichen planus.
model: Purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules (Wickham's striae).
why: Often on the wrists; oral lacy white patches.

q: Name a very potent topical steroid.
why: Used for pemphigoid and thick plaques; avoid on the face.

q: How much area does one fingertip unit cover?
why: One FTU is about 0.5 g.

q: Name a side effect of long-term topical steroids.
acc: atrophy / thin / striae / telangiectasia / perioral / tinea incognito
model: Skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis.
why: Use the lowest effective potency.

q: A child has honey-crusted lesions around the mouth. What is the likely diagnosis?
why: S. aureus or S. pyogenes; very contagious.

q: A 70-year-old has a pearly nodule with a rolled edge. How urgent is the referral?
why: BCCs rarely metastasise; suspected melanoma and SCC need urgent referral.

q: Name a technique for taking a history from someone with expressive dysphasia.
acc: closed / yes no / time / writing / gesture / picture
model: Closed (yes/no) questions, extra time, gestures, pictures or writing.
why: Comprehension is usually preserved.

q: What should you establish first in a patient with speech impairment?
model: Whether it's dysarthria, dysphasia or dysphonia.
hint: Which part of speech is affected?
why: It determines how to adapt your communication.

q: What feature in the history suggests myasthenia gravis as the cause of dysarthria?
acc: fatig / worse end of day / worse with use
model: Fatigability (worse with use or at the end of the day).
why: Check for fatigable ptosis and diplopia.

q: Which additional assessment would you propose if a patient with dysarthria coughs when drinking?
model: A swallowing assessment (bedside screen, then SALT).
why: Dysphagia risks aspiration pneumonia.

q: Which cognitive test might you add to a neurological examination?
why: Cognitive impairment changes the differential and management.

q: Expressive dysphasia with right-sided weakness localises to which hemisphere?
hint: Where Broca's area is in most people.
why: Broca's area is in the dominant frontal lobe.

q: In the presentation, why should you state the lesion's likely location?
model: Localising the lesion links the findings to a site and narrows the differential and imaging.
why: E.g. "localises to the left MCA territory".

q: Progressive dysarthria with a fasciculating tongue and brisk reflexes suggests what?
why: Mixed UMN and LMN signs without sensory loss.

q: Name a metabolic cause of sudden speech disturbance that must be checked immediately.
why: It mimics stroke; check capillary glucose in every case.

q: Slurred scanning speech with nystagmus and ataxia localises where?
why: Causes include MS, alcohol, stroke and drugs.

q: What is the difference between a macule and a papule?
model: A macule is flat; a papule is raised.
why: Both are small (<1 cm).

q: What is a vesicle larger than 0.5 cm called?
why: Seen in pemphigoid, burns and bullous impetigo.

q: What is the difference between an erosion and an ulcer?
model: An erosion is partial epidermal loss; an ulcer extends into the dermis.
why: Ulcers may scar.

q: What is lichenification?
model: Thickened skin with exaggerated markings from chronic rubbing or scratching.
why: Typical of chronic eczema.

q: What does it mean if a rash doesn't blanch?
why: Non-blanching rash with fever suggests meningococcal sepsis.

q: What does "annular" mean in describing a rash?
why: E.g. tinea corporis, granuloma annulare.

q: What lighting is best for skin examination?
why: Colour and texture are easier to see.

q: Why examine the whole skin even for a single lesion?
model: Patients often have other unnoticed lesions (e.g. melanoma on the back).
why: Full skin checks find extra cancers.

q: A rapidly growing tender keratotic nodule on sun-damaged skin is likely what?
why: Refer urgently; keratoacanthoma looks similar.

q: Painful grouped vesicles in a band on one side of the trunk suggest what?
why: Reactivation of VZV in a dermatome; aciclovir within 72 hours.

q: Should a swab be used to diagnose tinea?
why: Fungal microscopy and culture need scale.

q: How should a wound be prepared before swabbing?
model: Clean surface debris with sterile saline (not antiseptic).
why: Antiseptics kill organisms and give false negatives.

q: Which swab technique samples 1 cm² of viable wound tissue with pressure?
why: Better correlation with tissue bacterial load.

q: How is a vesicle sampled for HSV PCR?
model: De-roof the vesicle and swab the base firmly.
why: The base contains infected cells; use viral transport medium.

q: Where is an MRSA screening swab taken?
model: The anterior nares (plus groin/perineum or wounds per policy).
why: The nose is the main carriage site.

q: Which receptor tests are done on a breast cancer biopsy?
model: Oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2.
hint: Hormone receptors and a growth factor receptor.
why: Receptor status decides endocrine and HER2-targeted therapy; triple-negative tumours lack all three.

q: What imaging is used first for a breast lump in a woman under 40?
why: Young breasts are dense, so mammography is less sensitive; mammography is added from 40.

q: What is the commonest histological type of breast cancer?
why: About 75–80%; invasive lobular is ~10–15% and often multifocal.

q: When should a woman with a breast lump be referred on the suspected cancer pathway?
model: Aged 30 or over with an unexplained breast lump.
why: NICE NG12; also ≥50 with unilateral nipple discharge or retraction.

q: Which procedure assesses the axilla in clinically node-negative breast cancer?
why: Avoids full axillary clearance (and lymphoedema) if the first draining node is clear.

q: What is Paget's disease of the nipple?
model: An eczema-like nipple change caused by underlying breast cancer (DCIS spreading into the nipple epidermis).
why: Unilateral nipple "eczema" needs biopsy.

q: Which endocrine drug is used for ER-positive breast cancer in premenopausal women?
why: A SERM; aromatase inhibitors don't work if the ovaries are still active.

q: Why should women on tamoxifen report vaginal bleeding?
why: It's an oestrogen agonist on the endometrium.

q: What bone problem do aromatase inhibitors cause?
why: They lower oestrogen further; check DEXA and give bisphosphonates if needed.

q: Which side effect of trastuzumab needs regular echocardiograms?
why: Echo every 3 months during treatment.

q: What is neutropenic sepsis and how fast should antibiotics be given?
model: Fever (>38 °C) with neutropenia after chemotherapy: IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
why: Piperacillin–tazobactam is commonly used; it's an oncological emergency.

q: Which chemotherapy class causes cardiotoxicity?
why: Dose-dependent cardiomyopathy.

q: Who usually acts as key worker for breast cancer patients?
model: The breast care nurse (clinical nurse specialist).
why: Provides information, support and continuity.

q: Name a long-term physical problem after axillary surgery or radiotherapy.
why: Lymphatic drainage is disrupted; compression, skin care and physio help.

q: Name a psychosocial effect of gynaecological cancer treatment.
acc: body image / sexual / fertility / menopause / anxiety / depression / relationship / fear of recurrence / dyspareunia
model: Loss of fertility, early menopause, sexual dysfunction, body image changes, anxiety and depression.
why: Offer psychosexual support and fertility preservation before treatment.

q: What can prevent vaginal stenosis after pelvic radiotherapy?
why: Used regularly after treatment to maintain vaginal length and comfort.

q: Which women are invited for NHS breast screening?
model: Women aged 50–70 (up to their 71st birthday), every 3 years.
why: Mammography; women over 71 can self-refer.

q: What is the main harm of breast screening?
hint: Treating cancers that would never have caused harm.
why: About 3 women overdiagnosed for each death prevented (Marmot review).

q: What is the primary test in UK cervical screening?
why: Only HPV-positive samples go on to cytology; HPV is more sensitive than cytology.

q: How often are HPV-negative 25–49-year-olds recalled in Wales?
why: High HPV test sensitivity makes longer intervals safe.

q: Why is there no national ovarian cancer screening programme?
model: Trials (UKCTOCS) showed no reduction in mortality.
why: CA125 and ultrasound screening caused harm through surgery for false positives.

q: Name a Wilson and Jungner screening criterion.
acc: important / latent / early / test / acceptable / treatment / cost / natural history / facilities
model: Important problem, detectable early stage, acceptable test, effective treatment, known natural history, cost-effective.
hint: Consider the condition, the screening tool and what follows.
why: Screening must do more good than harm.

q: What is a "breast mouse"?
hint: It moves away from your fingers.
why: Highly mobile, smooth, firm lump in young women.

q: What does bloody discharge from a single duct suggest?
hint: A benign growth in a duct.
why: Needs imaging and possibly excision.

q: What causes peau d'orange?
model: Blockage of dermal lymphatics by tumour.
why: Skin oedema around hair follicles gives an orange-peel appearance.

q: Why does breast cancer cause skin dimpling?
model: Tumour infiltrates and shortens Cooper's (suspensory) ligaments.
hint: Fibrous bands from skin to fascia.
why: The skin is pulled inwards.

q: What should you suspect if "mastitis" doesn't respond to antibiotics?
why: Tumour in dermal lymphatics causes a red, swollen, warm breast.

q: Name a drug that causes gynaecomastia.
acc: spironolactone / digoxin / finasteride / cannabis / cimetidine / oestrogen / ketoconazole
why: They alter the oestrogen:androgen balance.

q: What is the commonest gynaecological cancer in the UK?
why: Usually presents early with postmenopausal bleeding.

q: Postmenopausal bleeding in a woman aged 55+ needs what?
model: A suspected cancer referral (transvaginal ultrasound ± biopsy).
why: Endometrial thickness >4 mm needs biopsy.

q: Which blood test is done for persistent bloating in a woman over 50?
why: If ≥35 IU/mL, arrange a pelvic ultrasound.

q: What is the classic symptom of cervical cancer?
why: The friable tumour bleeds on contact.

q: Name a risk factor for endometrial cancer.
acc: obesity / unopposed / nulliparity / tamoxifen / pcos / late menopause / diabetes / lynch / hrt
model: Obesity, unopposed oestrogen, PCOS, tamoxifen, nulliparity, Lynch syndrome.
why: Excess oestrogen stimulates the endometrium.

q: Which skin condition predisposes to vulval cancer?
why: Chronic inflammation leads to differentiated VIN and SCC.

q: Which HPV proteins inactivate p53 and Rb?
why: Loss of tumour suppressors drives CIN to invasive cancer.

q: Where does high-grade serous ovarian cancer often originate?
why: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma; this is why salpingectomy reduces risk.

q: Why does ovarian cancer usually present late?
model: It spreads across the peritoneum early with vague symptoms.
why: Most present at stage III–IV with ascites.

q: Which ovarian tumour causes Meigs' syndrome?
why: Ascites and pleural effusion that resolve after removal.

q: Which ovarian tumour secretes oestrogen?
why: Causes postmenopausal bleeding or precocious puberty; inhibin is a marker.

q: What type of endometrial cancer is oestrogen-dependent?
why: Arises from atypical hyperplasia; type 2 (serous) is aggressive and p53-mutated.

q: What is the commonest histological type of cervical cancer?
why: Arises at the transformation zone; adenocarcinoma is ~20%.

q: What is the standard surgery for early endometrial cancer?
hint: Remove the womb, tubes and ovaries.
why: Usually laparoscopic, ± node assessment and adjuvant radiotherapy.

q: What chemotherapy is standard for ovarian cancer?
hint: A heavy-metal-based drug plus a taxane.
why: After or before debulking surgery; PARP inhibitors for maintenance.

q: How is CIN treated?
model: LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone).
hint: A heated wire removes the abnormal area.
why: Small increase in preterm birth risk in later pregnancies.

q: How is locally advanced cervical cancer treated?
model: Chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin with external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy).
why: Surgery is for early stages.

q: Which maintenance drugs benefit BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer?
why: Synthetic lethality in cells that can't repair DNA by homologous recombination.

q: Which receptor does ondansetron block?
why: Best for chemotherapy- and radiotherapy-induced nausea; can prolong QT.

q: Which antiemetic acts as a prokinetic?
why: D₂ antagonism plus 5-HT₄ agonism speeds gastric emptying.

q: Which antiemetic is best for vestibular nausea?
why: H₁ and muscarinic blockade in the vestibular pathway.

q: Which antiemetic class blocks substance P?
why: Used for highly emetogenic chemotherapy, especially delayed nausea.

q: What is the main serious side effect of metoclopramide in young women?
why: Treat with procyclidine; limit to 5 days.

q: Which triple combination prevents nausea with highly emetogenic chemotherapy?
model: A 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron), an NK1 antagonist (aprepitant) and dexamethasone.
why: Evidence shows better complete response than single agents.

q: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone?
model: The area postrema (floor of the fourth ventricle).
hint: In the medulla, outside the blood–brain barrier.
why: It lies outside the blood–brain barrier, so it detects toxins and drugs.

q: Name a sign that should raise concern about domestic abuse.
acc: inconsistent / delayed / partner / repeated / protected / pattern / missed
model: Injuries inconsistent with the story, delayed presentation, a partner who won't leave or answers for the patient.
why: Also injuries to protected areas, repeated attendances, depression and self-harm.

q: When does domestic abuse often start or escalate?
hint: A time of change in the relationship.
why: Ask about abuse at antenatal appointments.

q: Who should interpret when you ask about abuse?
model: A professional interpreter (never a family member).
why: Family may be the abuser or filter the answers.

q: Which risk assessment tool is used in domestic abuse?
why: High-risk cases are referred to MARAC.

q: What is a MARAC?
model: A Multi-Agency Risk Assessment Conference for high-risk domestic abuse.
why: Police, health, social care and IDVAs share information and plan safety.

q: Can a competent adult decline action after disclosing abuse?
model: Yes, unless children are at risk or there's serious risk of harm to others.
why: Respect autonomy; offer support and a safety plan.

q: Which Act made coercive control a criminal offence?
why: Controlling or coercive behaviour in intimate or family relationships.

q: When is a domestic abuse victim at greatest risk of homicide?
why: Also pregnancy, strangulation, threats to kill.

q: Name a type of abuse other than physical.
acc: sexual / emotional / psychological / financial / economic / neglect / coercive / discriminatory / organisational
model: Sexual, emotional, financial, coercive control, neglect.
why: Abuse often involves several types.

q: Which non-fatal act strongly predicts later domestic homicide?
why: It became a specific offence in 2022.

q: Which speculum is used to view the cervix?
why: A bivalve speculum.

q: What does cervical motion tenderness suggest?
why: Do a pregnancy test and NAAT swabs.

q: Describe the uterine positions found on bimanual examination.
why: Most uteri are anteverted; a fixed retroverted uterus suggests endometriosis.

q: How is uterine size described on examination?
why: E.g. "14-week size" for fibroids.

q: A friable cervix with contact bleeding needs what?
why: Cervical cancer must be excluded.

q: What is the empirical outpatient treatment for PID?
model: Ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days.
why: Covers chlamydia, gonorrhoea and anaerobes (BASHH).

q: Thin grey fishy discharge with pH >4.5 suggests what?
why: Clue cells on microscopy; treat with metronidazole.

q: Frothy yellow-green discharge with a strawberry cervix suggests what?
why: An STI: treat patient and partners with metronidazole.

q: What is a cervical ectropion?
model: Columnar epithelium visible on the ectocervix (red ring around the os).
why: Common with the pill and pregnancy; can cause post-coital bleeding.

q: Name a family history feature that warrants genetics referral in breast cancer.
acc: ovarian / male / under 40 / young / bilateral / brca / ashkenazi / multiple
model: Breast cancer under 40, male breast cancer, ovarian cancer, bilateral cancer, several affected relatives, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.
why: Suggests BRCA or other high-risk genes.

q: Why ask about the menstrual cycle with a breast lump?
model: Cyclical lumps and pain suggest benign fibrocystic change.
hint: Lumps that come and go with periods.
why: Re-examine after a period if unsure.

q: Why ask a woman to press her hands on her hips during breast inspection?
model: It contracts pectoralis major, showing tethering or fixation.
why: Tumours fixed to muscle move with contraction.

q: Name the axillary tail of the breast.
why: Breast tissue extends towards the axilla; cancers can arise there.

q: Which breast should you examine first?
why: It gives a baseline for comparison.

q: Which test reproduces tennis elbow pain?
model: Cozen's test (resisted wrist extension) or Mill's test.
why: Stresses the common extensor origin.

q: What is the normal range of elbow flexion?
why: Full extension is 0°.

q: Tingling in the ring and little fingers with a positive Tinel's at the elbow suggests what?
why: Worse with prolonged elbow flexion.

q: Which muscle is involved in a painful arc from 60° to 120°?
why: Its tendon is compressed under the acromion.

q: Loss of passive external rotation suggests what?
why: The capsule contracts; active and passive range are both reduced.

q: Which nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation?
why: It wraps around the surgical neck; check the regimental badge area.

q: Which tendons are involved in de Quervain's tenosynovitis?
acc: abductor pollicis longus / apl + extensor pollicis brevis / epb
model: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.
why: First dorsal compartment; positive Finkelstein's test.

q: Why can a scaphoid fracture lead to avascular necrosis?
why: Proximal fragments lose supply.

q: Which imaging finds an occult scaphoid fracture?
why: Initial X-rays are often normal; immobilise until excluded.

q: Which shoulder injury needs early orthopaedic referral?
acc: acute traumatic cuff tear / traumatic tear / cuff tear
model: An acute traumatic rotator cuff tear in a younger patient.
why: Early repair gives better results.

q: Which test confirms carpal tunnel syndrome?
why: Useful before surgery or if the diagnosis is unclear.

q: What is the table-top test used for?
why: Inability to place the hand flat suggests referral for surgery.

q: What should a joint examination presentation finish with?
why: E.g. "consistent with subacromial impingement; I'd arrange physiotherapy".

q: How should range of movement be presented?
why: E.g. "abduction limited to 90 degrees actively, full passively".

q: What is the commonest cause of abnormal LFTs in the UK?
model: MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, formerly NAFLD).
why: About 1 in 3 adults have it, driven by obesity and type 2 diabetes.

q: What is the biggest cause of liver disease deaths in the UK?
why: Liver deaths have risen sharply over decades, unlike most major diseases.

q: Describe the progression of chronic liver injury.
model: Steatosis → hepatitis → fibrosis → cirrhosis → decompensation and HCC.
why: Earlier stages can reverse if the cause is removed.

q: What is the UK weekly low-risk alcohol limit?
model: 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days.
why: UK Chief Medical Officers' guidance for men and women.

q: What weight loss can improve MASLD?
why: Reduces steatosis, inflammation and can reverse fibrosis.

q: Name a lifestyle risk factor for hepatitis C.
model: Injecting drug use (sharing equipment), unregulated tattoos.
why: Blood-borne transmission.

q: Name a sign of decompensated liver disease.
acc: jaundice / ascites / encephalopathy / asterixis / varic / bleed
why: Decompensation markedly worsens prognosis.

q: Name a precipitant of hepatic decompensation.
acc: infection / bleed / alcohol / constipation / sedative / opioid / diuretic / dehydration / sbp / drug
model: Infection (including SBP), GI bleeding, alcohol, constipation, sedative drugs, dehydration.
hint: Think about what stresses a failing liver.
why: Look for and treat the trigger.

q: Which five features make up the Child–Pugh score?
model: Bilirubin, albumin, INR (or PT), ascites, encephalopathy.
hint: Three blood tests, two clinical features.
why: Grades cirrhosis severity (A–C).

q: Why do spider naevi and gynaecomastia occur in liver disease?
why: Also palmar erythema and testicular atrophy.

q: What AST:ALT ratio suggests alcohol-related liver disease?
why: Alcohol damages mitochondria (AST) and depletes pyridoxal phosphate (ALT production).

q: Which hepatitis B marker shows current infection?
why: Anti-HBs indicates immunity; anti-HBc IgM indicates acute infection.

q: What proportion of neonates infected with hepatitis B develop chronic infection?
why: Versus ~5% of adults: hence vaccination and immunoglobulin for babies of infected mothers.

q: How is chronic hepatitis C treated?
why: Finding undiagnosed people is now the main challenge.

q: Which hepatitis is linked to undercooked pork in the UK?
why: Usually mild; chronic in the immunosuppressed.

q: Which metabolite causes liver injury in paracetamol overdose?
why: Normally neutralised by glutathione; acetylcysteine replenishes it.

q: Name an antibiotic that causes cholestatic jaundice.
hint: A penicillin combined with clavulanic acid.
why: Can appear weeks after stopping.

q: Do people need an address or ID to register with a GP?
why: NHS guidance: anyone can register without proof of address or ID.

q: What is "tri-morbidity" in homeless health?
model: Coexisting physical illness, mental illness and substance misuse.
why: Common in homeless people and needs joined-up care.

q: What should never happen at hospital discharge for a homeless patient?
model: Discharge to the street without a plan.
why: Hospital homeless teams and the duty to refer to housing services help.

q: Name a harm-reduction intervention for people who inject drugs.
acc: needle / naloxone / opioid substitution / methadone / buprenorphine
model: Needle exchange, take-home naloxone, opioid substitution therapy.
why: Reduces overdose deaths and blood-borne viruses.

q: What proportion of the liver's blood comes from the portal vein?
why: The hepatic artery provides the remaining ~25% (more oxygenated).

q: Where do oesophageal varices form in portal hypertension?
acc: left gastric + azygos / left gastric / azygos
model: At the anastomosis between left gastric (portal) and azygos/oesophageal (systemic) veins.
why: Rupture causes massive haematemesis.

q: In which direction does the spleen enlarge?
acc: right iliac / rif / towards the umbilicus / diagonally
model: Down and medially towards the right iliac fossa.
why: Start palpating in the RIF.

q: Which vaccines are given after splenectomy?
model: Pneumococcal, meningococcal (ACWY, B), Hib and annual flu.
why: Risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria.

q: What is the hepatorenal pouch of Morison?
model: The space between the liver and right kidney, the lowest point in the supine abdomen.
why: Free fluid collects here (seen on FAST scan).

q: What is the common reward pathway in addiction?
model: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens).
hint: From the midbrain to the ventral striatum.
why: Drugs of abuse raise dopamine here.

q: When do alcohol withdrawal seizures usually occur?
why: Delirium tremens peaks at 48–72 hours; chlordiazepoxide prevents both.

q: How does cocaine cause chest pain?
why: Treat with benzodiazepines and GTN; avoid beta-blockers.

q: Which drug is a partial μ-opioid agonist used for opioid substitution?
why: Ceiling effect on respiratory depression; can precipitate withdrawal.

q: Which electrolyte disturbance is linked with MDMA?
model: Hyponatraemia (from SIADH and excess water intake).
hint: SIADH plus drinking lots of water.
why: SIADH plus drinking large volumes of water.

q: What is cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome relieved by?
why: Cyclical vomiting in heavy long-term cannabis users; stopping cannabis cures it.

q: Which recreational drug causes B12 deficiency?
why: It inactivates B12, causing subacute combined degeneration.

q: Which bladder complication is linked to ketamine use?
why: Causes pain, frequency and a small contracted bladder.

q: Which drug class reduces portal pressure in patients with varices?
why: Reduces variceal bleeding risk; banding is an alternative.

q: Which drug treats ascites in cirrhosis?
why: Counteracts secondary hyperaldosteronism; large-volume paracentesis with albumin if tense.

q: How often should patients with cirrhosis have HCC surveillance?
why: Early HCC can be cured.

q: Which drug treats hepatic encephalopathy?
why: Reduces ammonia production and absorption in the gut.

q: What ascitic fluid neutrophil count diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
why: Treat with IV antibiotics; give prophylaxis afterwards.

q: Which clotting factors are vitamin K-dependent?
hint: The mnemonic is a year in the 1970s.
why: The liver makes them; INR rises in liver failure and vitamin K deficiency.

q: What does phase II drug metabolism do?
model: Conjugation (e.g. glucuronidation) to make drugs water-soluble.
why: Phase I (CYP450) usually comes first.

q: Which enzyme converts alcohol to acetaldehyde?
hint: Named after the substrate it oxidises.
why: Aldehyde dehydrogenase then converts acetaldehyde to acetate.

q: How does disulfiram work?
model: It blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up if alcohol is drunk.
why: Causes flushing, nausea and palpitations: an aversive effect.

q: Why can benzodiazepines be dangerous in liver disease?
model: Reduced clearance can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
why: Use lower doses or shorter-acting drugs (e.g. oxazepam).

q: Why does liver failure cause encephalopathy?
hint: A nitrogen waste product builds up.
why: Ammonia and other toxins affect brain function.

q: Name a CYP450 enzyme inducer.
acc: rifampicin / carbamazepine / phenytoin / st john / alcohol
model: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort, chronic alcohol.
why: Speeds metabolism of other drugs (e.g. reduces the pill's effect).

q: Pale stools, dark urine and itching suggest which type of jaundice?
why: Conjugated bilirubin can't reach the gut; it's excreted in urine.

q: What is Charcot's triad?
acc: fever + jaundice + pain / rigor + jaundice + ruq
hint: Three features of bile duct infection.
why: Ascending cholangitis: an emergency needing antibiotics and biliary drainage.

q: What is Courvoisier's law?
model: A palpable, painless gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones.
hint: A palpable organ in a jaundiced patient.
why: Suggests pancreatic head or distal bile duct cancer.

q: Mild unconjugated jaundice during fasting or illness suggests what?
why: Reduced UGT1A1 activity; benign.

q: What does a pulsatile liver suggest?
why: Systolic backflow transmits to the liver.

q: What are Kayser–Fleischer rings a sign of?
why: Copper deposition in Descemet's membrane.

q: What is asterixis a sign of in liver disease?
why: A flapping tremor with outstretched hands.

q: How would you explain cirrhosis in plain language?
model: The liver has become scarred after long-term damage.
why: Avoid jargon and check understanding.

q: Name a symptom to safety-net for in cirrhosis.
acc: yellow / jaundice / swelling / confusion / vomiting blood / black stool / melaena
model: Yellow eyes, tummy swelling, confusion, vomiting blood or black stools.
why: Signs of decompensation needing urgent care.

q: What does OARS stand for in motivational interviewing?
model: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries.
why: Core skills to draw out change talk.

q: What is the "righting reflex"?
model: The urge to tell or persuade the patient to change.
why: It provokes resistance; MI resists it.

q: Name a stage in the stages of change model.
acc: precontemplation / pre contemplation / contemplation / preparation / action / maintenance / relapse
why: Prochaska and DiClemente; match your approach to the stage.

q: Why shouldn't a dependent drinker stop alcohol suddenly without support?
model: Risk of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.
hint: The brain is used to it.
why: Needs medically assisted withdrawal with chlordiazepoxide and thiamine.

q: Name a drug to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence.
why: Used with psychosocial support.

q: What is "developing discrepancy" in MI?
model: Highlighting the gap between current behaviour and the patient's goals or values.
hint: Where they are vs where they want to be.
why: Motivation grows from the patient's own reasons.

q: What should you do if you use the wrong pronoun for a patient?
model: Apologise briefly, correct yourself and move on.
why: Long apologies draw more attention.

q: Which protected characteristic in the Equality Act covers trans people?
why: Discrimination in services is unlawful.

q: How can you invite a patient to share their pronouns?
model: Introduce yourself with your own pronouns, or ask directly.
why: Shows respect and avoids assumptions.

q: When is it appropriate to ask about a patient's gender transition history?
model: Only when it's clinically relevant (e.g. medications, anatomy, screening).
why: Explain why you're asking; never out of curiosity.

q: Which hormone therapy increases VTE risk?
why: Relevant for trans women taking oestrogen.

q: Which side effect of testosterone therapy needs blood monitoring?
why: Increases thrombosis risk.

q: Which organ remains after vaginoplasty and still needs consideration?
why: Prostate disease remains possible.

q: Name a barrier trans people face in accessing healthcare.
acc: discrimination / misgender / wait / screening / stigma / knowledge / outed / cost
model: Discrimination, misgendering, long waits for gender clinics, missed screening invitations, lack of clinician knowledge.
why: Negative experiences lead to delayed care.

q: Why might a trans man miss cervical screening?
model: Screening invitations are based on recorded gender.
hint: The recall system uses the gender on file.
why: Practices should arrange screening manually.

q: How many unprovoked seizures usually define epilepsy?
model: Two, more than 24 hours apart (or one with a high recurrence risk).
why: ILAE definition; one seizure with ≥60% recurrence risk (e.g. epileptiform EEG, structural lesion) also counts.

q: What EEG pattern is typical of childhood absence epilepsy?
why: Absences can be provoked by hyperventilation in clinic.

q: Which epilepsy syndrome causes morning jerks in teenagers?
why: Triggered by sleep deprivation and alcohol; usually lifelong treatment.

q: What EEG pattern is seen in infantile spasms?
why: West syndrome; often linked to tuberous sclerosis.

q: What is the commonest cause of temporal lobe epilepsy?
why: Often responds to surgery if drug-resistant.

q: Why is an eyewitness account so important in transient loss of consciousness?
model: The patient usually can't remember the event.
why: Ask witnesses about colour, movements and recovery; videos help.

q: Name a red flag that suggests cardiac syncope.
acc: exert / lying / palpitation / chest pain / family / sudden death / ecg
model: Syncope on exertion or lying down, palpitations or chest pain, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG.
why: Needs urgent cardiology assessment.

q: Which test must every patient with transient loss of consciousness have?
why: Look for long QT, Brugada, WPW, heart block, ischaemia.

q: What does a déjà vu aura before an event suggest?
why: The aura is the start of the seizure.

q: Which sign is most specific for a generalised tonic–clonic seizure: lateral or tip tongue biting?
why: Seizures cause biting of the side of the tongue.

q: How long do jerks usually last in convulsive syncope?
why: Brief irregular jerks are common in syncope and don't mean epilepsy.

q: Name a feature suggesting a dissociative (functional) seizure.
acc: eyes closed / asynchronous / side to side / pelvic / wax / prolonged
model: Eyes closed, asynchronous movements, side-to-side head shaking, pelvic thrusting, waxing and waning.
why: Video EEG telemetry confirms the diagnosis.

q: What is the gold-standard test to distinguish epileptic from dissociative seizures?
hint: Recording both video and brain activity.
why: Captures a typical event with simultaneous EEG.

q: Describe the recovery after a generalised seizure.
model: Prolonged postictal confusion and drowsiness, headache, aching muscles.
why: Syncope recovery is quick.

q: What are automatisms in a focal impaired-awareness seizure?
model: Repetitive movements such as lip-smacking, chewing or fiddling.
why: Typical of temporal lobe seizures.

q: Why must valproate be avoided in women who could become pregnant?
model: It's highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, developmental disorders).
why: Prescribing requires a Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

q: What is the first-line drug for absence seizures?
why: It blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels.

q: Which serious side effect requires slow titration of lamotrigine?
why: Faster titration or co-prescribing valproate raises the risk.

q: Which antiepileptic causes hyponatraemia?
why: SIADH-like effect.

q: Which antiepileptic follows zero-order kinetics?
why: Small dose increases cause large level rises; narrow therapeutic index.

q: Name a psychiatric side effect of levetiracetam.
why: Ask about mood at review.

q: What is the first drug for status epilepticus in hospital?
why: Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if no IV; repeat once.

q: When does a seizure become status epilepticus?
model: When it lasts 5 minutes or more (or repeated seizures without recovery).
why: Treat at 5 minutes.

q: Name a second-line drug for established status epilepticus.
why: Given if seizures continue after two benzodiazepine doses.

q: Which antiepileptics reduce the effect of the combined pill?
model: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate at higher doses).
why: Use an IUD/IUS or injection instead.

q: How long must a car driver usually be seizure-free with epilepsy?
why: DVLA rules; 6 months after a first unprovoked seizure with normal tests.

q: What folic acid dose is given in pregnancy for women on antiepileptics?
why: Higher-dose folic acid reduces neural tube defect risk.

q: What is the inheritance of Huntington's disease?
why: CAG repeat in HTT; each child has a 50% risk.

q: What is genetic anticipation?
model: Earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations.
hint: Children are affected sooner than parents.
why: Due to expanding trinucleotide repeats.

q: Which sign shows a child uses their hands to climb up their legs to stand?
why: Proximal leg weakness, classically Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

q: Which protein is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
why: Out-of-frame deletions in DMD; X-linked recessive.

q: Which genetic condition causes inability to release a handshake?
why: CTG repeat in DMPK; also cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac conduction defects.

q: What is the inheritance of spinal muscular atrophy?
why: Causes a floppy infant with tongue fasciculations.

q: Name a skin sign of neurofibromatosis type 1.
acc: cafe au lait / café / freckling / neurofibroma
why: Six or more café-au-lait macules is a diagnostic criterion.

q: Which repeat causes Friedreich's ataxia?
why: In FXN (frataxin); ataxia, absent reflexes, upgoing plantars, cardiomyopathy.

q: Name a skin sign of tuberous sclerosis.
model: Ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas.
why: Also epilepsy and learning disability.

q: Which neurological level gives a sensory level and sphincter problems?
why: With bilateral UMN signs below the level.

q: What do "crossed signs" localise to?
why: Cranial nerve signs on one side, limb signs on the other.

q: What time course suggests a vascular cause?
why: Stroke, haemorrhage.

q: Fatigable weakness without sensory loss localises to where?
why: E.g. myasthenia gravis.

q: Proximal symmetrical weakness without sensory loss suggests disease where?
why: E.g. polymyositis, steroid myopathy, thyroid disease.

q: What GCS score indicates the airway may need protecting?
why: "GCS 8, intubate".

q: What does a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in coma suggest?
model: Third nerve compression from uncal herniation.
why: A neurosurgical emergency.

q: What breathing pattern suggests metabolic acidosis in coma?
why: Deep sighing breaths, e.g. DKA.

q: What is decerebrate posturing?
model: Extension of arms and legs to pain.
why: Indicates midbrain/pons damage (worse than decorticate flexion).

q: What should be checked first in any unconscious patient?
why: Hypoglycaemia is common and quickly reversible.

q: What should be given with glucose to a malnourished or alcohol-dependent comatose patient?
why: Glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.

q: Which drug levels should be checked in unexplained coma?
why: Co-ingested overdoses are common and treatable.

q: What is the doll's eye reflex used to test?
why: Eyes moving opposite to head turns indicate an intact brainstem.

q: Name a quiz mode in this app useful for targeting weak topics.
why: Revisiting weak items with spaced repetition improves retention.

q: Which older group has the highest suicide rate?
why: Especially if widowed, isolated, with chronic illness, pain or alcohol misuse.

q: What is "depressive pseudodementia"?
model: Cognitive impairment caused by depression that mimics dementia.
why: It improves when depression is treated.

q: Name a screening tool for depression in older adults.
why: Focuses less on physical symptoms.

q: Name a psychotic feature of severe depression in older adults.
why: Psychotic depression needs urgent specialist input.

q: Name a blood test to exclude a physical cause of low mood.
acc: tft / thyroid / b12 / folate / calcium / fbc / u&e / glucose / hba1c
model: TFTs, B12, folate, calcium, FBC, U&E, HbA1c.
why: Hypothyroidism, anaemia, hypercalcaemia and hyponatraemia can cause low mood.

q: Name a drug that can cause low mood.
acc: beta blocker / propranolol / steroid / isotretinoin / levetiracetam / benzodiazepine / opioid / interferon
model: Beta-blockers, steroids, isotretinoin, levetiracetam, benzodiazepines, opioids.
why: Review the medication list.

q: Which electrolyte abnormality causes "moans and groans"?
why: Low mood, abdominal pain, constipation, polyuria, renal stones.

q: Which liver enzyme is most liver-specific?
why: AST also comes from muscle, heart and red cells.

q: What does a raised GGT with raised ALP indicate?
model: The ALP is from the liver (biliary).
why: Normal GGT with high ALP suggests bone.

q: Which LFT reflects acute changes in synthetic function?
why: Clotting factors have short half-lives; albumin reflects chronic function.

q: What R ratio suggests a hepatocellular pattern?
why: R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN); ≤2 is cholestatic.

q: Name a test in a non-invasive liver screen.
acc: hepatitis / ana / ama / smooth muscle / ferritin / caeruloplasmin / antitrypsin / immunoglobulin / coeliac
model: Hepatitis B and C serology, autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, AMA), ferritin, caeruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin, immunoglobulins.
why: Finds treatable causes.

q: Which antibody is positive in primary biliary cholangitis?
why: Middle-aged women with itch and cholestatic LFTs; treat with ursodeoxycholic acid.

q: Name a cause of ALT over 1000.
acc: viral / hepatitis / paracetamol / ischaemi / shock / autoimmune
model: Viral hepatitis, paracetamol overdose, ischaemic hepatitis.
why: Very high transaminases mean acute hepatocellular necrosis.

q: Isolated raised ALP with normal GGT suggests a source where?
why: E.g. Paget's disease, metastases, healing fracture, osteomalacia.

q: Which condition of IBD causes cholestatic LFTs and beaded ducts on MRCP?
why: Associated with ulcerative colitis; risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

q: What should you do first for a cholestatic LFT pattern?
model: Ultrasound to look for dilated ducts.
why: Dilated ducts → MRCP/CT/ERCP; non-dilated → AMA, drug review.

q: Isolated raised unconjugated bilirubin with normal LFTs in a young adult suggests what?
why: Benign; exclude haemolysis.

q: What does FAST stand for?
model: Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 999.
why: A pre-hospital screen for stroke; ROSIER is used in A&E.

q: What is the first imaging test in suspected acute stroke?
why: Excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis.
