q: Within what time from onset can thrombolysis be given for ischaemic stroke?
why: Benefit is greatest the earlier it's given.

q: Which patients are candidates for mechanical thrombectomy?
model: Those with a large vessel occlusion (e.g. ICA, M1, basilar).
why: Within 6 h, or up to 24 h if imaging shows salvageable brain.

q: What antiplatelet regimen follows an ischaemic stroke?
model: Aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks, then clopidogrel 75 mg long term.
hint: One drug short term, another long term.
why: Start once haemorrhage is excluded (24 h after thrombolysis).

q: Within what time should a swallow screen be done after stroke?
model: Within 4 hours, before any oral intake.
why: Dysphagia causes aspiration pneumonia.

q: Which VTE prevention method is used in immobile stroke patients?
why: Compression stockings don't help after stroke.

q: How soon should a suspected TIA be assessed by a specialist?
why: Stroke risk is highest in the first days; give aspirin 300 mg immediately.

q: When is carotid endarterectomy recommended after stroke or TIA?
model: For symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50–99%, ideally within 2 weeks.
hint: Significant narrowing on the side of symptoms.
why: Benefit falls quickly with delay.

q: How long must a car driver stop driving after a stroke or TIA?
why: DVLA rule for car licences; longer for HGV.

q: How is warfarin reversed in intracerebral haemorrhage?
acc: prothrombin complex / pcc / beriplex + vitamin k / vitamin k
model: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K.
why: Rapid reversal limits haematoma growth.

q: What proportion of strokes are ischaemic?
why: About 15% are haemorrhagic.

q: What is the ischaemic penumbra?
model: Brain tissue around the infarct core that is underperfused but still salvageable.
hint: The tissue that can still be rescued.
why: Rapid reperfusion aims to save it.

q: What is the biggest modifiable risk factor for stroke?
why: Drives atherosclerosis, small vessel disease and intracerebral haemorrhage.

q: Which arrhythmia causes cardioembolic stroke?
why: Thrombus forms in the left atrial appendage; anticoagulation reduces risk by ~2/3.

q: What causes lacunar infarcts?
model: Small vessel disease (lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries).
why: Linked to hypertension and diabetes.

q: What causes lobar haemorrhages in older people?
hint: A protein deposited in vessel walls.
why: Amyloid weakens cortical vessel walls.

q: Neck pain with Horner's and stroke in a young person suggests what?
hint: A tear in the artery wall.
why: May follow minor neck trauma.

q: What causes most subarachnoid haemorrhages?
why: At the circle of Willis; risk factors include smoking, hypertension and ADPKD.

q: Why is the exact onset time important in acute stroke?
model: It determines eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy.
why: For wake-up strokes, use the time last seen well.

q: Name a stroke mimic.
acc: hypoglycaemia / seizure / todd / migraine / sepsis / functional / tumour / subdural / bell / ms
model: Hypoglycaemia, seizure (Todd's paresis), migraine, sepsis, functional disorder, tumour.
why: Always check glucose.

q: What are the three features of a TACS?
acc: weakness + hemianopia + higher / hemiparesis + hemianopia + higher cortical
model: Unilateral weakness/sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction.
why: Oxford classification; all three = total anterior circulation stroke.

q: Which artery's occlusion causes leg weakness more than arm weakness?
why: It supplies the medial cortex (leg area).

q: Which stroke causes homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing?
why: The macula has dual (MCA/PCA) supply.

q: What is lateral medullary syndrome?
model: A PICA (or vertebral) stroke: ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, Horner's, ataxia, dysphagia.
why: Crossed signs localise to the brainstem.

q: Name a feature of a lacunar stroke.
acc: pure motor / pure sensory / ataxic hemiparesis / sensorimotor
model: Pure motor or pure sensory stroke, sensorimotor stroke or ataxic hemiparesis.
why: No cortical signs or visual field defect.

q: Why might tone and reflexes be reduced immediately after a stroke?
model: Acute "neural shock": UMN signs develop over days.
why: Initially flaccid, later spastic.

q: What is the single most important intervention for all stroke patients?
model: Admission to a specialist stroke unit.
why: Reduces death and dependency for all stroke types.

q: How effective is thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion?
model: About 1 in 3 treated patients gain functional independence.
hint: A small number needed to treat.
why: One of the most effective treatments in medicine.

q: Why are DOACs preferred over warfarin for AF after stroke?
model: Lower risk of intracranial haemorrhage (and no INR monitoring).
hint: A feared complication inside the skull.
why: Similar or better stroke prevention.

q: What surgery improves survival in malignant MCA infarction?
why: Relieves raised ICP from massive oedema; best within 48 h.

q: Why is CT the first scan in acute stroke?
hint: Blood shows up white straight away.
why: Blood is hyperdense immediately; early ischaemia may not show.

q: Which RA symptom do patients often report as the most disabling, besides pain?
why: Driven by systemic inflammation, poor sleep and low mood; often under-recognised.

q: Which vaccines must be avoided on biologic therapy?
why: Risk of vaccine-strain infection; give non-live vaccines (flu, pneumococcal, recombinant shingles).

q: Which MDT member provides splints and aids for daily activities in RA?
why: Joint protection, adaptations and splints help function.

q: Which cytokine do the biologics adalimumab and etanercept block?
hint: A cytokine named after its effect on tumours.
why: TNF drives synovial inflammation and joint destruction; blocking it reduces disease activity but raises infection risk.

q: Which finger joints are typically spared in RA?
why: DIP involvement suggests OA or psoriatic arthritis.

q: What is the first-line DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis?
why: Given once weekly with folic acid on a different day.

q: Which antibiotic must be avoided with methotrexate?
why: Both are folate antagonists, causing bone marrow suppression.

q: What must be screened for before starting a TNF inhibitor?
why: TNF blockade can reactivate TB; also check hepatitis B and C.

q: What triad defines Felty's syndrome?
hint: An enlarged organ and low white cells.
why: Risk of recurrent infections.

q: What X-ray finding is the earliest sign in RA?
model: Soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteopenia.
why: Erosions and joint space loss come later.

q: Which DMARD needs annual eye screening after 5 years?
why: Retinopathy risk; it's safe in pregnancy.

q: Which DAS28 score indicates remission?
hint: Just over two and a half.
why: Treat-to-target aims for remission or low disease activity (<3.2).

q: Name a classic RA finger deformity.
acc: swan neck / boutonniere / boutonnière / ulnar deviation / z thumb
model: Swan neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation, Z-thumb.
why: From tendon and ligament damage by synovitis.

q: What bone biochemistry is typical of osteomalacia?
acc: low phosphate + high alp / alp + vitamin d
model: Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, low vitamin D, high PTH.
hint: Think mineralisation failure and a compensating gland.
why: Vitamin D deficiency impairs mineralisation and triggers secondary hyperparathyroidism.

q: What are Looser's zones?
why: Lucent bands of unmineralised osteoid.

q: Name a feature of rickets in a child.
acc: bow / rosary / wrist / bossing / delayed walking / genu varum
model: Bowed legs, rachitic rosary, widened wrists, frontal bossing, delayed walking.
why: Defective mineralisation of growing bone.

q: What is the typical blood result in Paget's disease?
model: Isolated raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate.
why: Excessive bone turnover.

q: What is the treatment for symptomatic Paget's disease?
why: Reduces bone pain by suppressing osteoclasts.

q: Name a complication of Paget's disease.
acc: deaf / fracture / osteoarthritis / osteosarcoma / heart failure / spinal stenosis / deformity
model: Deafness, fractures, deformity, OA, spinal stenosis, osteosarcoma, high-output heart failure.
why: Enlarged weak bone compresses nerves and alters joints.

q: Which form of vitamin D is given in CKD?
why: The kidney can't perform 1α-hydroxylation.

q: How do glucocorticoids reduce inflammation at the gene level?
model: They bind cytoplasmic receptors, move to the nucleus and alter gene transcription (e.g. blocking NF-κB).
why: Reduces cytokines, COX-2 and inflammatory mediators.

q: What dose of prednisolone is equivalent to 20 mg hydrocortisone?
why: Prednisolone is about 4 times as potent.

q: Which steroid has almost no mineralocorticoid activity?
why: Useful for cerebral oedema without fluid retention.

q: What must patients on long-term steroids carry?
why: Alerts clinicians to adrenal insufficiency risk.

q: What happens if long-term steroids are stopped abruptly?
why: The HPA axis is suppressed; treat with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg.

q: Name a musculoskeletal side effect of long-term steroids.
why: Give bone protection for courses ≥3 months.

q: What are steroid "sick day rules"?
model: Double the dose during illness with fever (IM hydrocortisone if vomiting).
why: Stress increases cortisol requirements.

q: Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
why: ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA tracks activity.

q: What inflammatory marker pattern is typical of active SLE?
acc: esr + crp / high esr + normal crp
why: A raised CRP suggests infection or serositis.

q: Which drug should all SLE patients take unless contraindicated?
why: Reduces flares and improves survival.

q: What does CREST stand for?
model: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.
why: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis; anticentromere antibodies.

q: How is scleroderma renal crisis treated?
why: Malignant hypertension and AKI; avoid high-dose steroids.

q: Name a skin sign of dermatomyositis.
model: Heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, shawl sign, mechanic's hands.
why: Screen for underlying cancer.

q: Which antibodies are found in Sjögren's syndrome?
why: Anti-Ro in pregnancy risks congenital heart block.

q: Which test measures tear production in Sjögren's?
why: Less than 5 mm of wetting in 5 minutes is abnormal.

q: What should be done immediately for suspected GCA?
why: Prevents blindness; don't wait for biopsy.

q: Name a symptom of GCA.
acc: jaw claudication / headache / scalp / visual / temporal
model: Temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual disturbance.
why: Over-50s with raised ESR/CRP.

q: What dose of prednisolone treats polymyalgia rheumatica?
why: A dramatic response within days supports the diagnosis.

q: Which ANCA is associated with GPA?
why: MPA is usually p-ANCA (MPO).

q: Which organs does GPA classically affect?
acc: upper airway + lung + kidney / sinus + lung + kidney
model: Upper airway (sinuses, nose), lungs and kidneys.
why: Saddle nose, haemoptysis, rapidly progressive GN.

q: Which infection is linked with polyarteritis nodosa?
why: Medium vessel vasculitis with microaneurysms on angiography; ANCA negative.

q: What is the vessel-size classification of vasculitis called?
why: Large, medium and small vessel vasculitides.

q: Name a differential for symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis.
acc: parvovirus / viral / psoriatic / sle / lupus / gout / reactive / pmr / hepatitis
model: Viral arthritis (parvovirus B19), psoriatic arthritis, SLE, gout, PMR.
why: Serology and examination help distinguish.

q: Name a poor prognostic factor in RA.
acc: ccp / rf / erosion / smok / crp / extra articular
model: Anti-CCP/RF positivity, early erosions, high CRP, smoking, extra-articular disease.
why: Justifies early aggressive treatment.

q: Which antiemetic should be avoided in Parkinson's disease?
why: Central dopamine blockade worsens parkinsonism; use domperidone.

q: Why is early defibrillation so important in VF?
model: Survival falls with every minute without defibrillation.
why: VF deteriorates to asystole; high-quality CPR buys time.

q: What is pulseless electrical activity?
model: Organised electrical activity on the monitor without a palpable pulse.
hint: The rhythm looks compatible with life.
why: Look for reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts).

q: When is adrenaline given in a non-shockable arrest?
model: As soon as IV/IO access is obtained, then every 3–5 minutes.
why: In shockable rhythms it's given after the 3rd shock.

q: How often should compressors swap during CPR?
why: Fatigue reduces quality.

q: What is the compression depth for adults?
why: At 100–120 per minute with full recoil.

q: What does a sudden rise in end-tidal CO₂ during CPR suggest?
why: Waveform capnography also confirms tube placement.

q: When should amiodarone 150 mg be given in a shockable arrest?
hint: Two shocks after the first dose.
why: 300 mg after the 3rd, 150 mg after the 5th.

q: Name one of the 4 Hs.
acc: hypoxia / hypovolaemia / hyperkalaemia / hypokalaemia / hypothermia / metabolic
why: Reversible causes to treat during CPR.

q: What is the target oxygen saturation after ROSC?
why: Avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia.

q: Which test detects an Achilles tendon rupture?
why: No plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed.

q: What does the "too many toes" sign suggest?
why: Seen from behind: forefoot abduction shows extra toes laterally.

q: What should the heels do when a patient stands on tiptoe?
why: Failure suggests tibialis posterior dysfunction or a rigid flatfoot.

q: Which test elicits a click in Morton's neuroma?
why: Between the 3rd and 4th toes typically.

q: Which device tests protective sensation in the diabetic foot?
why: Loss of sensation predicts ulcer risk.

q: Heel pain worst on the first steps in the morning suggests what?
why: Tender at the medial calcaneal tubercle.

q: Which ankle ligament is most commonly sprained?
why: Inversion injury.

q: Name a criterion in the Ottawa ankle rules.
acc: malleolus / fifth metatarsal / navicular / weight bear / 5th
model: Bony tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of a malleolus, base of 5th metatarsal or navicular, or inability to weight-bear 4 steps.
why: Identifies who needs an X-ray.

q: What causes a hot, swollen, deformed midfoot in a person with diabetic neuropathy?
why: Needs urgent offloading and diabetic foot team review.

q: Name a cause of pes cavus.
acc: charcot marie / cmt / friedreich / spina / neurolog
model: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, Friedreich's ataxia, spinal dysraphism.
why: A high arch often signals a neurological cause.

q: Which drug class predisposes to Achilles tendon rupture?
why: Also corticosteroids.

q: How urgently should a diabetic foot ulcer be referred?
model: Urgently to the MDT diabetic foot service (within 1 working day); emergency if sepsis or critical ischaemia.
why: Delays lead to amputation.

q: What test confirms gout if the diagnosis is uncertain?
model: Joint aspiration for negatively birefringent urate crystals.
why: Also excludes septic arthritis.

q: When should serum urate be checked after a gout attack?
why: Urate can be normal during an attack.

q: What imaging confirms a stress fracture or osteomyelitis of the foot?
why: X-rays may be normal early.

q: What should a foot and ankle examination presentation end with?
model: A summary, most likely diagnosis and plan.
why: E.g. "consistent with Achilles rupture; I'd refer to orthopaedics today".

q: What are the three diagnostic criteria for DKA?
model: Ketones ≥3 mmol/L, glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes), and pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L.
why: JBDS criteria: ketonaemia, hyperglycaemia and acidosis.

q: What rate of fixed-rate IV insulin is used in DKA?
hint: A tenth of a unit per kg.
why: Soluble insulin (e.g. Actrapid); continue the usual long-acting insulin.

q: When should 10% glucose be added in DKA treatment?
model: When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L.
why: Insulin must continue to clear ketones without causing hypoglycaemia.

q: How much potassium is added per litre if K⁺ is 3.5–5.5 mmol/L in DKA?
why: Insulin drives potassium into cells; total body potassium is depleted.

q: Why does DKA cause Kussmaul breathing?
model: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis (blowing off CO₂).
hint: The lungs try to correct the pH.
why: Deep, sighing breaths.

q: Which diabetes drug class can cause euglycaemic DKA?
hint: They make glucose leak into the urine.
why: Glucose may be near-normal, so check ketones in unwell patients on these drugs.

q: What defines resolution of DKA?
hint: Two blood values back towards normal.
why: Then switch to SC insulin with a meal.

q: Which serious DKA complication mainly affects children?
why: Headache, confusion, bradycardia; avoid over-rapid fluid replacement.

q: What random glucose with symptoms diagnoses diabetes?
why: Fasting ≥7.0 or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol are alternatives.

q: Why is HbA1c unreliable for diagnosing type 1 diabetes?
model: Onset is rapid, so HbA1c (which reflects ~3 months) may not have risen.
why: Diagnose type 1 clinically and refer the same day.

q: Which antibodies support a type 1 diabetes diagnosis?
acc: gad / ia 2 / znt8 / islet / insulin autoantibod
model: GAD, IA-2, ZnT8 and insulin autoantibodies.
why: Also low C-peptide; useful in atypical cases.

q: What HbA1c target does NICE recommend for most adults with type 1 diabetes?
why: Individualise to avoid hypoglycaemia.

q: What does "time in range" mean in CGM?
model: The percentage of time glucose is between 3.9 and 10 mmol/L.
why: Target >70%.

q: Name a check done at the annual diabetes review.
acc: retina / eye / foot / acr / albumin / egfr / bp / lipid / weight
model: Retinal screening, foot check, urine ACR and eGFR, BP, lipids, weight.
why: Detects complications early.

q: Which immune cells destroy β-cells in type 1 diabetes?
model: T cells (especially CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells).
why: Autoantibodies are markers rather than the main cause of damage.

q: Which HLA types increase type 1 diabetes risk?
why: Genetic susceptibility plus environmental triggers.

q: What proportion of β-cells are lost before symptoms appear?
why: Stage 3 disease.

q: Which trial showed intensive glucose control reduces microvascular complications in type 1 diabetes?
why: With more hypoglycaemia; follow-up (EDIC) showed lasting benefit.

q: Name an autoimmune condition associated with type 1 diabetes.
model: Autoimmune thyroid disease, coeliac disease, Addison's, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo.
why: Screen thyroid annually and coeliac if symptoms.

q: What is insulitis?
model: Lymphocytic (T-cell) infiltration of the pancreatic islets.
hint: Seen on histology early in type 1.
why: The histological hallmark of early type 1 diabetes.

q: Which islet cells are preserved in type 1 diabetes?
why: Unopposed glucagon worsens hyperglycaemia and ketogenesis.

q: At roughly what blood glucose does glycosuria start?
why: The renal threshold for glucose reabsorption.

q: What renal lesion is characteristic of diabetic nephropathy?
why: Follows mesangial expansion; albuminuria is the earliest sign.

q: Why does uncontrolled diabetes cause blurred vision?
hint: Glucose-driven water shifts in the eye.
why: Resolves as glucose normalises.

q: Which body appraises new medicines in Wales when NICE hasn't?
model: The All Wales Medicines Strategy Group (AWMSG).
why: Supported by the All Wales Therapeutics and Toxicology Centre.

q: Do NICE technology appraisals apply in Wales?
why: NHS Wales must make NICE- and AWMSG-recommended medicines available within 2 months.

q: How can a clinician get a medicine that isn't routinely available for one patient in Wales?
why: Approved if there's significant clinical benefit and reasonable value for money.

q: Which agency licenses medicines in the UK?
why: Licensing covers quality, safety and efficacy, not cost-effectiveness.

q: What is the usual NICE cost-effectiveness threshold?
why: Higher thresholds for end-of-life and very rare conditions.

q: What is the first treatment for a conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow?
acc: 15 / 20 / fast acting / juice / glucose tablet / sugar
model: 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. fruit juice or glucose tablets).
why: Recheck after 10–15 minutes, then give a starchy snack.

q: How is hypoglycaemia treated in an unconscious patient without IV access?
why: Less effective in alcohol excess or liver disease.

q: Should basal insulin be stopped during illness in type 1 diabetes?
why: Stopping it causes DKA; check ketones and take extra insulin if needed.

q: What is DAFNE?
model: Dose Adjustment For Normal Eating, a structured education course.
why: Teaches carbohydrate counting and insulin adjustment.

q: What glucose level should drivers on insulin have before driving?
why: DVLA advice: check before and every 2 hours on long drives.

q: Which drug class is started for albuminuria in diabetes?
why: Reduces intraglomerular pressure and slows nephropathy.

q: What is the onset of action of rapid-acting insulin analogues?
why: Given just before meals.

q: Which insulin is used in IV infusions?
why: Used in FRIII and VRIII.

q: Name a long-acting insulin analogue.
why: Provides flat basal insulin over ~24 hours.

q: What causes lumpy injection sites with erratic absorption?
model: Lipohypertrophy from repeated injections in the same place.
why: Rotate sites.

q: Why should insulin never be drawn up with an IV syringe?
model: Risk of a large dosing error (IV syringes are marked in mL, not units).
why: Use insulin pens or insulin syringes.

q: How does insulin lower serum potassium?
acc: na k atpase / into cells / shift / sodium potassium
model: It stimulates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting potassium into cells.
why: Used to treat hyperkalaemia.

q: Why do long-acting analogues cause less nocturnal hypoglycaemia than NPH?
model: They have a flat profile without a peak.
why: NPH peaks at 4–8 hours, often overnight.

q: What is the first step in interpreting an ABG?
model: Look at the pH (acidaemia or alkalaemia).
why: Then PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, compensation and anion gap.

q: How is the anion gap calculated?
acc: sodium / na + chloride / cl + bicarbonate / hco3
why: A raised gap suggests ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure or toxins.

q: What does GALS stand for?
why: A quick MSK screen.

q: Which test detects a small knee effusion?
why: The patellar tap detects large effusions.

q: Which test detects a fixed flexion deformity of the hip?
why: Flexing the opposite hip flattens the lumbar lordosis; the tested thigh lifting off the couch shows a fixed flexion deformity.

q: Immediate knee swelling after a twisting injury suggests which injury?
why: Meniscal tears swell over hours.

q: An overweight 13-year-old with knee pain and reduced hip internal rotation has what until proven otherwise?
acc: sufe / slipped upper femoral / slipped capital
why: Hip pathology can present as knee pain; urgent X-ray (frog-leg lateral).

q: What is Osgood–Schlatter disease?
model: Traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in adolescents.
why: Pain and swelling below the knee with activity; self-limiting.

q: A shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall suggests what?
acc: neck of femur / hip fracture / nof
why: Needs surgery within 36 hours.

q: Which knee condition can mimic a DVT when it ruptures?
why: Popliteal cyst associated with OA or RA.

q: What does a locked knee that won't fully extend suggest?
model: A bucket-handle meniscal tear (or loose body).
why: Needs urgent orthopaedic referral.

q: Does NICE recommend X-rays to diagnose typical osteoarthritis?
why: ≥45 with activity-related joint pain and short morning stiffness.

q: What are the core treatments for osteoarthritis?
why: Topical NSAIDs for knee and hand OA.

q: Name a Kocher criterion for septic arthritis of the hip in children.
why: More criteria = higher probability.

q: What must happen before antibiotics in a hot swollen joint?
why: Unless the patient is septic and unstable.

q: Within what time should hip fracture surgery happen?
why: Delays increase mortality.

q: How should a meniscal tear with an extension block be managed?
why: A bucket-handle tear may need early repair.

q: Name a Schneiderian first-rank symptom.
acc: third person / running commentary / thought echo / insertion / withdrawal / broadcast / passivity / delusional perception
model: Third-person auditory hallucinations, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, passivity phenomena, delusional perception.
why: Suggestive of schizophrenia but not diagnostic on their own.

q: How long must symptoms last for schizophrenia (ICD-11)?
why: Shorter episodes are classed as acute and transient psychotic disorder.

q: Why do negative symptoms matter for prognosis in schizophrenia?
model: They cause much of the long-term disability and respond poorly to antipsychotics.
why: Psychosocial interventions and rehabilitation help.

q: Name an organic cause of psychosis.
acc: delirium / cannabis / amphetamine / steroid / encephalitis / epilepsy / tumour / sle / thyroid / dementia / alcohol
model: Delirium, drugs (cannabis, stimulants, steroids), encephalitis, temporal lobe epilepsy, tumour, SLE, thyroid disease.
why: Visual hallucinations and impaired cognition suggest an organic cause.

q: What MSE finding suggests a patient is hallucinating during the interview?
model: Responding to unseen stimuli (pausing, looking around, appearing to listen).
why: Ask gently what they're hearing.

q: What is "knight's move" thinking?
model: Derailment or loosening of associations: jumps between unconnected ideas.
why: A formal thought disorder seen in schizophrenia.

q: Name a risk factor for violence in psychosis.
acc: command / persecutory / substance / previous violence / non adherence
model: Command hallucinations, persecutory delusions, substance misuse, previous violence, non-adherence.
why: Previous violence is the strongest predictor.

q: When is suicide risk highest in schizophrenia?
model: Early in the illness and soon after discharge from hospital.
why: Also with depression and insight into deterioration.

q: What distinguishes neurotic from psychotic disorders?
model: Insight and reality testing are preserved in neurotic disorders.
why: People know their fears or thoughts are excessive.

q: What are compulsions in OCD?
model: Repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to reduce anxiety from obsessions.
why: E.g. washing, checking, counting.

q: What characterises panic disorder?
model: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about further attacks.
why: Often leads to agoraphobia.

q: What is agoraphobia?
model: Fear and avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult (crowds, public transport, leaving home).
why: Often accompanies panic disorder.

q: Social anxiety disorder is fear of what?
acc: scrutiny / embarrass / humiliat / judged / negative evaluation
model: Scrutiny, embarrassment or negative evaluation by others.
why: Treated with individual CBT or an SSRI.

q: Which brain structure is overactive in anxiety disorders?
why: Reduced prefrontal control fails to dampen fear responses.

q: Why does hyperventilation in panic cause tingling fingers?
why: Also light-headedness and carpopedal spasm.

q: How does avoidance maintain anxiety?
acc: negative reinforcement / relief / never learn / extinction
model: It relieves anxiety short-term (negative reinforcement), so the fear is never disconfirmed.
hint: It feels better in the moment.
why: Exposure therapy targets this.

q: Which brain circuit is implicated in OCD?
hint: A loop through the basal ganglia.
why: Overactivity drives intrusive thoughts and urges.

q: What is the cognitive model of panic?
why: E.g. palpitations interpreted as a heart attack, escalating anxiety.

q: Name a physical cause to exclude in a patient with anxiety.
acc: thyroid / caffeine / alcohol withdrawal / hypoglycaemia / arrhythmia / phaeochromocytoma / asthma / stimulant
model: Hyperthyroidism, caffeine, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, arrhythmias, phaeochromocytoma.
why: Check TFTs and ask about substances.

q: Which screening tool assesses generalised anxiety?
why: PHQ-9 for depression; PCL-5 for PTSD.

q: In OCD, are obsessions usually recognised as the person's own thoughts?
why: Unlike thought insertion in psychosis.

q: Which dopamine pathway's overactivity causes positive psychotic symptoms?
why: D₂ blockade here treats hallucinations and delusions.

q: Blockade of which dopamine pathway causes extrapyramidal side effects?
why: Causes dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia.

q: Why do antipsychotics raise prolactin?
model: They block dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, which normally inhibits prolactin.
why: Causes galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction.

q: Which antipsychotic is used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia?
why: After trials of two antipsychotics including one atypical.

q: Why does clozapine require regular blood tests?
why: FBC weekly at first, then less often.

q: Name a feature of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
model: Fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion, very high CK.
why: Stop the antipsychotic; cool and support; dantrolene.

q: Which antipsychotic is a dopamine partial agonist?
why: Less prolactin rise and weight gain.

q: Which antipsychotic most causes weight gain and diabetes?
why: Monitor weight, glucose and lipids.

q: Which drug class mainly causes psychosis via NMDA blockade?
why: Supports the glutamate hypothesis of schizophrenia.

q: What psychological treatment is first line for OCD?
model: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP).
why: Gradually facing triggers without performing compulsions.

q: What is the treatment of choice for specific phobias?
why: Uses a fear hierarchy.

q: Name a low-intensity intervention in stepped care.
acc: guided self help / computerised / online / psychoeducation
model: Guided self-help, computerised CBT, psychoeducational groups.
why: Step 2 for mild to moderate anxiety and depression.

q: What is EMDR used for?
why: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing.

q: Does NICE recommend risk assessment scales to predict suicide?
why: They're poor predictors; use a needs-based psychosocial assessment and safety plan.

q: What is the difference between static and dynamic risk factors?
model: Static factors can't change (e.g. previous attempts); dynamic factors can (e.g. substance use, hopelessness).
why: Management targets dynamic factors.

q: What does "concordance" mean?
model: A partnership in which patient and clinician agree treatment together.
why: Preferred to "compliance", which implies obedience.

q: Name a strategy to improve antipsychotic adherence.
acc: depot / long acting / shared / psychoeducation / simplif / side effect / motivational
model: Depot (long-acting injectable) antipsychotics, shared decision-making, managing side effects, simplifying regimens.
why: Non-adherence causes relapse.

q: What is Cotard's syndrome?
model: A nihilistic delusion of being dead or rotting.
why: Seen in severe psychotic depression.

q: Name a core feature of mania.
acc: elevated / irritable / energy / sleep / pressured / grandiose / disinhibit / flight
model: Elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, disinhibition.
hint: The opposite of depression, and more.
why: Lasting at least a week or needing admission.

q: How does hypomania differ from mania?
model: It's milder (≥4 days), without psychosis or marked impairment.
why: Defines bipolar II with depression.

q: What is flight of ideas?
model: Rapidly moving between ideas with loose links (e.g. rhymes, puns).
why: Typical of mania.

q: Why is psychotic depression a medical emergency in some cases?
model: Food and fluid refusal and high suicide risk.
why: ECT may be needed.

q: What distinguishes bipolar I from bipolar II?
model: Bipolar I has at least one manic episode; bipolar II has hypomania with depression.
why: Both involve recurrent mood episodes.

q: What is rapid cycling in bipolar disorder?
model: Four or more mood episodes a year.
why: Harder to treat; avoid antidepressants.

q: What commonly triggers a manic episode?
model: Sleep loss (also antidepressants, steroids, substances, childbirth).
why: Circadian disruption is central.

q: What is the usual target lithium level for maintenance?
why: Sampled 12 hours after the dose.

q: Name a sign of lithium toxicity.
acc: coarse tremor / ataxia / vomiting / diarrhoea / confusion / dysarthria / seizure
model: Coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, slurred speech, seizures.
why: Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides.

q: Which blood tests are monitored every 6 months on lithium?
acc: u&e / egfr / renal / thyroid / tft / calcium
model: Renal function (U&E/eGFR), thyroid function and calcium.
hint: Two organs lithium damages, plus a mineral.
why: Lithium causes CKD, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism.

q: What causes polyuria on lithium?
acc: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus / diabetes insipidus / adh
hint: The collecting ducts stop responding to a hormone.
why: Lithium reduces renal response to ADH.

q: Name an indication for ECT.
acc: severe depression / life threatening / stupor / psychotic depression / catatonia / mania / treatment resistant
model: Severe life-threatening depression, psychotic depression, catatonia, severe mania, treatment resistance.
why: Works faster than drugs in severe cases.

q: What is a common side effect of ECT?
why: Usually short-term.

q: How do benzodiazepines act on the GABA-A receptor?
model: They increase the frequency of chloride channel opening (positive allosteric modulation).
why: Barbiturates increase duration.

q: Why should benzodiazepines be prescribed only short-term?
why: Usually 2–4 weeks; taper slowly to stop.

q: Which drugs increase lithium levels?
model: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazide diuretics.
why: They reduce renal lithium clearance.

q: Which section of the MHA covers irreversible treatments like psychosurgery?
why: Requires both consent and an independent second opinion.

q: Name the three components of anxiety.
why: Each is a target for treatment.

q: What should patients be warned about when starting an SSRI for anxiety?
hint: An early side effect that mimics the illness.
why: Effects take 2–4 weeks; side effects often settle.

q: How long should an SSRI continue after remission of an anxiety disorder?
why: Reduces relapse; taper slowly.

q: Which SSRI side effect matters in older people?
why: Check sodium.

q: What is the main focus of worry in GAD?
why: Not focused on one situation.

q: What appearance clue might suggest OCD?
model: Chapped, red hands from excessive washing.
why: Contamination obsessions with washing compulsions.

q: What is first-line drug treatment for GAD?
hint: Also used for depression and PTSD.
why: Alternatives: another SSRI, SNRI or pregabalin.

q: Which drug is used for physical symptoms of performance anxiety?
why: Reduces tremor and palpitations.

q: Should benzodiazepines be used long term in panic disorder?
why: Associated with worse long-term outcomes.

q: Which tricyclic is used for OCD?
why: Strongly serotonergic.

q: How do SSRI doses for OCD compare with those for depression?
why: OCD responds more slowly.

q: How long does a Section 2 of the Mental Health Act last?
why: For assessment; not renewable.

q: How long does a Section 3 last initially?
why: For treatment; renewable.

q: Which section lets a doctor hold an informal inpatient?
why: Section 5(4) is the nurse's holding power (6 hours).

q: Which section lets police take someone from a public place to a place of safety?
why: Section 135 needs a warrant to enter private premises.

q: Who must be involved in a Section 2 or 3 application along with doctors?
why: Usually a social worker.

q: Can the MHA be used to treat an unrelated physical illness without consent?
why: Use the Mental Capacity Act if the patient lacks capacity.

q: Which section gives free aftercare after a Section 3?
why: Health and social care must provide it.

q: Does having a mental illness mean a patient lacks capacity?
why: Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed.

q: What is the "least restrictive" principle?
model: Choosing the option that limits the patient's rights and freedom least.
hint: Limit freedom as little as possible.
why: A core principle of MHA and MCA practice.

q: Name an ethical principle of medical ethics.
why: The four principles.

q: Name a digital mental health intervention available in Wales.
model: SilverCloud online CBT (or NHS 111 option 2 crisis support).
why: Self-referral, no GP needed.

q: Name a concern about digital mental health tools.
acc: exclusion / privacy / data / evidence / safety / inequ
model: Digital exclusion, data privacy, variable evidence and safety.
why: Not everyone has access or skills.

q: Name a patient factor that makes a consultation challenging.
acc: anger / distress / intoxicat / cognitive / expectation / pain / language / mental
model: Anger or distress, intoxication, cognitive impairment, pain, unrealistic expectations, language barriers.
why: Recognising them helps you adapt.

q: Name a clinician factor that contributes to difficult consultations.
acc: fatigue / stress / time / burnout / bias / confidence
model: Fatigue, stress, time pressure, burnout, biases.
why: Self-awareness helps.

q: Name a warning sign of impending violence.
acc: raised voice / pacing / clenched / staring / threat / space
model: Raised voice, pacing, clenched fists, staring, invading personal space, threats.
why: Act early: de-escalate or leave.

q: Name a physical cause of agitation not to miss.
acc: hypoxia / hypoglycaemia / delirium / intoxicat / withdrawal / head injury / sepsis / pain
model: Hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, delirium, intoxication or withdrawal, head injury, sepsis.
why: Avoid diagnostic overshadowing.

q: Where should you sit when seeing a potentially aggressive patient?
model: Where both of you can reach an exit (don't block theirs).
why: Know where the alarm is.

q: What body position is recommended during de-escalation?
model: Side-on, open posture, hands visible, beyond arm's length.
why: Less threatening and safer.

q: What should you do first when a patient is angry about waiting?
why: E.g. "I can see you're really frustrated."

q: Name a drug used for rapid tranquillisation.
model: IM lorazepam, or haloperidol with promethazine.
why: Only after de-escalation and oral options fail.

q: What is a "hot debrief"?
model: A brief team debrief immediately after an incident.
why: Check wellbeing and learn; formal reflection later.

q: Name a sign of burnout.
model: Emotional exhaustion, cynicism (depersonalisation), reduced sense of accomplishment.
why: Seek support early.

q: Name a support service for doctors in Wales.
acc: health for health / hhp / occupational / bma / gp
model: Health for Health Professionals Wales (also occupational health, BMA support).
why: Confidential support for doctors and students.

q: Name a re-experiencing symptom of PTSD.
why: The core symptom cluster.

q: Why should you avoid pressing for detail of trauma in an initial history?
model: It can re-traumatise; let the patient control the pace.
why: Trauma-informed care.

q: What substance problem commonly coexists with PTSD?
why: It isn't a barrier to trauma-focused treatment.

q: Name the three core symptom clusters of PTSD in ICD-11.
acc: re experienc + avoid + threat / intrusion + avoidance + hyperarousal
model: Re-experiencing, avoidance, and a sense of current threat (hyperarousal).
why: Lasting several weeks with functional impairment.

q: What extra features define complex PTSD?
model: Affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and relationship difficulties.
hint: Three extra problems after prolonged trauma.
why: Usually after prolonged or repeated trauma.

q: What is first-line treatment for PTSD in adults?
acc: trauma focused cbt / tf cbt / cbt
why: EMDR is an alternative for non-combat trauma.

q: Which drugs are used for PTSD if medication is preferred?
why: Not first line.

q: Should single-session psychological debriefing be offered after trauma?
why: Active monitoring or trauma-focused CBT instead.

q: Which drug class should be avoided in PTSD?
why: May worsen outcomes and cause dependence.

q: In the MSE, what is recorded under "mood"?
model: The patient's subjective description in their own words.
why: Affect is your objective observation.

q: Under which MSE heading do delusions belong?
why: Thought form covers the flow and connection of thoughts.

q: Under which MSE heading are hallucinations recorded?
why: Record the modality and whether second or third person.

q: By what age should a child walk independently before it's a red flag?
why: Check CK in boys to exclude Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

q: What does hand preference before 12 months suggest?
model: Weakness of the other side (e.g. hemiplegic cerebral palsy).
why: Handedness normally develops after 18 months or so.

q: Which assessment detects cerebral palsy early in high-risk infants?
why: Allows diagnosis before 5 months corrected age and earlier therapy.

q: By what age should a baby sit unsupported?
why: Median age is 6–8 months; not sitting by 9 months needs referral.

q: What is cerebral palsy?
acc: non progressive / permanent + movement / movement + posture
model: A permanent disorder of movement and posture from a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain.
why: The lesion doesn't progress, but the motor picture changes with growth.

q: What brain lesion causes spastic diplegia in premature babies?
why: Damages fibres to the legs that run close to the ventricles.

q: What is the commonest type of cerebral palsy?
why: Pyramidal (UMN) involvement.

q: Which orthopaedic problem needs regular X-ray surveillance in CP?
why: Spastic adductors and hip flexors pull the hip out.

q: Name a treatment for spasticity in CP.
acc: baclofen / botulinum / botox / rhizotomy / physio / orthos
model: Baclofen, botulinum toxin, physiotherapy, orthoses, selective dorsal rhizotomy.
why: Reduces tone and prevents contractures.

q: Name a condition associated with CP besides motor problems.
acc: epilepsy / learning / visual / hearing / feeding / scoliosis / drool
model: Epilepsy, learning disability, visual or hearing impairment, feeding problems, scoliosis.
why: CP is often more than a movement disorder.

q: What is the approximate prevalence of autism in children?
why: Diagnosed 3–4 times more often in boys; girls are under-recognised.

q: Name the two core domains of autism.
model: Social communication/interaction difficulties and restricted, repetitive behaviours and interests.
why: Both must be present from early development.

q: Why are girls with autism under-diagnosed?
why: Interests may appear more socially typical.

q: Which observational assessment is used in autism diagnosis?
why: With a parental interview (ADI-R) and school information.

q: Which genetic conditions are associated with autism?
model: Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis, Down syndrome.
why: Examine skin and consider genetic testing.

q: Does the MMR vaccine cause autism?
why: The original claim was fraudulent and large studies show no link.

q: What is the commonest cause of limp in a 3–8-year-old?
hint: Follows a cold; settles in a week or two.
why: Often follows a viral illness; a diagnosis of exclusion.

q: What is a toddler's fracture?
model: A spiral fracture of the tibia in a toddler.
why: After a twist or minor fall; may not show on initial X-ray.

q: Which hip condition affects obese adolescent boys?
why: Can present with knee pain only.

q: Why must you examine the hip in a child with knee pain?
model: Hip pain is often referred to the knee (obturator and femoral nerves).
why: SUFE and Perthes can present this way.

q: Which sign of proximal weakness suggests Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
why: Plus calf pseudohypertrophy and very high CK.

q: What skin sign over the lower back suggests spinal dysraphism?
model: A sacral dimple or hair tuft.
hint: Look at the base of the spine.
why: Tethered cord can cause limp, foot deformity and bladder problems.

q: Name a neurological cause of limp in a child.
acc: cerebral palsy / duchenne / sma / neuropathy / tethered / tumour / ataxia / guillain
model: Cerebral palsy, Duchenne, peripheral neuropathy, tethered cord, posterior fossa tumour.
why: Check tone, reflexes, CK and spine.

q: Why are adolescents prone to SUFE?
model: The growth plate is weak during the growth spurt, especially with obesity or hormonal factors.
why: The epiphysis slips through the physis.

q: Why is septic arthritis more common in infants?
model: Metaphyseal vessels cross the growth plate, so osteomyelitis spreads into the joint.
why: Infants can't localise pain, so they just won't move the limb.

q: Why does Perthes disease affect children aged 4–8?
model: The femoral head's blood supply is precarious at this age.
hint: Think about the femoral head's supply.
why: Leads to avascular necrosis.

q: Name a Kocher criterion for septic arthritis.
why: More criteria = higher probability.

q: Which X-ray view is essential when SUFE is suspected?
model: A frog-leg lateral view of both hips.
why: The slip may not show on an AP view.

q: Which test distinguishes septic arthritis from transient synovitis definitively?
model: Joint aspiration (Gram stain, culture, cell count).
why: Ultrasound shows an effusion but can't tell which.

q: What does a positive ANA in JIA mean for monitoring?
model: Higher risk of uveitis: regular eye screening.
why: Uveitis is often asymptomatic.

q: Which blood test helps detect leukaemia presenting as a limp?
why: Cytopenias or blasts.

q: Which organism causes septic arthritis in children under 4, besides S. aureus?
why: Hard to culture; PCR helps.

q: How long must arthritis last to diagnose JIA?
hint: About a month and a half.
why: In a child under 16 with no other cause.

q: What is the treatment for SUFE?
why: Prevent further slip; avoid weight-bearing.

q: Which newborn tests screen for DDH?
why: Ultrasound by 6 weeks if risk factors.

q: Name a risk factor for DDH.
model: Breech presentation, family history, female sex, first-born, oligohydramnios.
why: Selective ultrasound screening.

q: Which bone tumour causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs?
why: Benign; prostaglandin-mediated pain.

q: Name an X-ray feature of osteosarcoma.
why: Metaphyseal tumour around the knee in adolescents.

q: What IQ threshold defines learning disability?
model: An IQ below 70 (with impaired adaptive functioning, starting in childhood).
why: All three criteria are required.

q: What is the commonest genetic cause of learning disability?
why: Fragile X is the commonest inherited cause.

q: From what age are annual health checks offered to people with learning disabilities?
why: To address health inequalities.

q: What is the difference between a learning disability and a learning difficulty?
model: A learning difficulty (e.g. dyslexia) doesn't affect general intellect.
why: Learning disability involves global intellectual impairment.

q: At what age do babies usually start to smile socially?
hint: About a month and a half.
why: No social smile by 8 weeks is a red flag.

q: At what age does a fine pincer grip develop?
why: Inferior pincer at 9 months.

q: What should loss of previously acquired skills prompt?
why: Regression suggests neurodegenerative, metabolic or autistic regression.

q: At what age can a child copy a circle?
why: Cross at 4, square at 4, triangle at 5.

q: At what age do children usually use two-word phrases?
why: No two-word phrases by 2½ years is a red flag.

q: What age should be used for developmental assessment of a baby born at 30 weeks until age 2?
why: Subtract the weeks of prematurity.

q: What sweat chloride level is diagnostic of cystic fibrosis?
why: 30–59 is intermediate; confirm with CFTR genetics.

q: Which newborn screening marker is raised in CF?
why: Followed by CFTR variant testing and a sweat test.

q: Which neonatal bowel presentation suggests CF?
why: Occurs in 10–20% of babies with CF.

q: What is the inheritance of cystic fibrosis?
why: CFTR gene on chromosome 7; carrier frequency ~1 in 25.

q: Why are most men with CF infertile?
model: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
why: Sperm are made and can be retrieved for ICSI.

q: What type of channel is CFTR?
why: Dysfunction causes thick, dehydrated secretions.

q: Which organism causing chronic lung infection in CF is associated with poor prognosis and cross-infection?
why: CF patients are segregated to prevent spread.

q: Name a consequence of pancreatic insufficiency in CF.
model: Steatorrhoea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, faltering growth.
why: Treated with pancreatic enzymes and vitamins A, D, E, K.

q: What is CF-related diabetes treated with?
why: Due to pancreatic islet damage; common in adults.

q: What is DIOS in CF?
hint: The adult equivalent of meconium ileus.
why: Thick intestinal contents block the terminal ileum in older patients.

q: How does ivacaftor work?
model: It's a CFTR potentiator that increases channel opening.
why: Combined with correctors (elexacaftor, tezacaftor) for F508del.

q: How does dornase alfa help in CF?
model: It cleaves neutrophil DNA in sputum, thinning it.
why: Improves mucus clearance.

q: Why is nebulised hypertonic saline used in CF?
model: It rehydrates the airway surface liquid.
why: Helps mucociliary clearance.

q: What must people with CF take with every meal?
why: Replaces lipase for fat absorption.

q: Which long-term antibiotic has anti-inflammatory benefits in CF?
why: Reduces exacerbations, especially with Pseudomonas.

q: Which CFTR modulator combination is used for patients with F508del?
why: Transformative improvements in lung function and weight.

q: Name a long-term problem in children born extremely preterm.
acc: cerebral palsy / learning / adhd / autism / retinopathy / bronchopulmonary / chronic lung / hearing / growth
model: Cerebral palsy, learning difficulties, ADHD, retinopathy of prematurity, chronic lung disease.
why: Risk rises with lower gestation.

q: Are vaccines given at corrected or chronological age in preterm babies?
why: Development and growth use corrected age until 2.

q: What lung condition commonly follows extreme prematurity?
model: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (chronic lung disease of prematurity).
why: May need home oxygen; RSV protection.

q: What is diagnostic overshadowing in learning disability?
model: Attributing symptoms or behaviour change to the learning disability rather than illness.
why: Leads to missed diagnoses.

q: Name a physical access barrier for people with intellectual disabilities.
model: Inaccessible buildings, couches, scales or waiting areas.
why: Reasonable adjustments are required by law.

q: Which Act requires reasonable adjustments in healthcare?
why: Includes longer appointments and easy-read information.

q: What document tells clinicians how a person with learning disability communicates?
acc: hospital passport / health passport / communication passport
why: Describes communication, likes, dislikes and needs.

q: Name a visual communication aid.
acc: easy read / picture / makaton / symbol / sign
why: Supports understanding.

q: Who should you address first in a consultation with a person with learning disability and their carer?
why: Then involve the carer with consent.

q: Name an early social sign of autism in a toddler.
acc: name / eye contact / point / joint attention / smile / pretend
model: Not responding to name, reduced eye contact, not pointing to share interest, little pretend play.
why: Joint attention is usually present by 12–18 months.

q: What is echolalia?
model: Repeating words or phrases spoken by others.
why: A feature of autism.

q: Name a repetitive behaviour seen in autism.
model: Hand flapping, rocking, spinning, lining up toys.
why: Stereotyped movements and insistence on sameness.

q: What test must every child assessed for autism have?
why: Hearing loss can mimic autism.

q: Which genetic condition causes regression and hand-wringing in girls?
why: MECP2 mutation; slowing head growth.

q: How does developmental language disorder differ from autism?
model: Social interest and non-verbal communication are preserved.
why: The problem is language rather than social interaction.

q: Which syndrome causes acquired loss of language with an abnormal EEG?
why: Acquired epileptic aphasia.

q: Name a post-diagnostic support for a child with autism.
acc: parent / salt / speech / ot / education / idp / ehcp / sleep / camhs / social care / respite
model: Parent programmes, SALT, OT, educational support (IDP), sleep support, CAMHS, social care.
why: Support is tailored to the child and family.

q: Should medication be used to treat the core features of autism?
hint: Think about what drugs can and can't change.
why: Antipsychotics only for severe behaviours that challenge, with psychosocial support.

q: Which hormone is used for sleep problems in autistic children?
why: After sleep hygiene measures.

q: Which part of the brain is affected in dyskinetic CP?
why: Causes dystonia, chorea and athetosis.

q: What causes ataxic CP?
why: Hypotonia, poor balance and intention tremor.

q: What does GMFCS describe?
why: Level I walks without limitation; V is wheelchair-transported.

q: Which neonatal condition causes dyskinetic CP via bilirubin?
why: Bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia.

q: Name a red flag that a child's "CP" may be something else.
acc: progress / regress / family / normal mri / fluctuat
model: Progression or regression, family history, normal MRI, fluctuating symptoms.
why: Consider metabolic, genetic and neuromuscular causes.

q: Which treatable condition mimics CP with diurnal variation?
why: Dramatic response to levodopa.

q: What is the most important investigation for suspected CP?
why: Abnormal in most children with CP.

q: Which blood test helps distinguish neuromuscular disease from CP?
why: Very high in muscular dystrophies.
